items.title: Why Are Canon Lenses White? The Science Behind the Sideline Icon
items.summary_what: Why Are Canon Lenses White? The Science Behind the Sideline Icon: When you head to a sporting event, you will inevitably see a sea of big white lenses.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: When you head to a sporting event, you will inevitably see a sea of big white lenses. For decades, it was Canon lenses 99% of the time. There were likely some people in marketing who were happy to see their lenses a different color than Nikon. Today? There are a lot of Sony lenses being used that also use their version of the white paint. Nikon has had a lens here or there, but all of their current lenses are black. Reverse marketing? So, while the white paint will always be part of Canon's branding, maybe less so today, there are real scientific reasons that Canon continues to evolve the white paint that most take for granted. Why Canon lenses are white is always one of the first questions budding photographers ask, and the simple answer is usually “to deal with heat.” That statement is true, but it's a bit more complex than that. The Problem with Sunshine Sometimes the sun can be a big problem for camera lenses. You will see accurate information out there about long lenses accentuating heatwaves, which is a regular occurrence for wildlife and outdoor sports photographers. Sometimes those heatwaves are from the environment; sometimes they can be from the heat coming off the lens itself. I think we all know that dark surfaces absorb light and turn it into heat, whereas lighter and whiter lenses reflect more light from the surface, reducing the impact of the heat generated. Conventional white Before 2018 Sunlight (infrared) Lens barrel ↑ Paint layer Titanium oxide (white pigment) Carbon black (tints the white) Carbon black soaks up infrared, so much of the sun's heat passes into the lens barrel. Heat-shield coating 2018 onward Sunlight (infrared) Lens barrel ↑ Paint layer Silica-coated titanium oxide Infrared-reflective pigment (replaces carbon black) Infrared is reflected away instead of absorbed, so far less heat reaches the barrel: 20% less temperature rise, according to Canon. Simplified illustration based on Canon Europe's description of the two paint formulations. Particle sizes and counts are not to scale. We call them white lenses, but they're a few shades off-white. If the lenses were pure white, you'd get some pretty nasty, bright reflections coming off the surface. Blinding yourself or the person beside you isn't the best thing. For the purpose of this exercise, we'll still call it “Canon White.” This coating has been 60 years in the making, and Canon continues to work to improve it. More Than 60 Years of White Canon first used a lighter color on its broadcast camera lenses in 1960, including the Canon TV 2000mm f/11 . The lens looked like 18% gray in color, and the signature “Canon White” would come about 15 years later. It wasn't until 1976 that Canon introduced white lenses to their SLR lineup. The goal was simple: reduce the heat on the surface of the lens to minimize thermal expansion and contraction. Canon TV 2000mm f/11 // Credit: Canon Inc. There was another big reason for the switch to reflective coatings for Canon: the proliferation of fluorite and synthetic fluorite elements. Fluorite is great at controlling chromatic aberrations, but it is more affected by heat than other glass element types. The white paint development was enough to keep the performance of the fluorite elements right where they wanted it to be. The Australian Open Problem It wasn't until the early 2000s that Canon realized what they had been doing with surface coatings wasn't enough and that it was time to make the white paint better. There were a lot of complaints from photographers using the EOS-1D at the Australian Open about autofocus performance issues. Canon tested the cameras and found nothing wrong with any of them. Canon sent a technician into the stands with the photographers to monitor the temperature of the cameras and lenses, and it turned out things were cooking. If you just lie on a lounger at the pool in 30°C weather under a high sun, most of us would feel a bit warm. That's what Canon discovered. Photographers aren't in the sun for half an hour; it can be an all-day affair. Canon had just discovered that too much heat was present inside the lens and that had effected the performance of the autofocus system. It was time to get back into R&D on the paint used for the surface of a camera lens barrel. The Sea of White // Credit: Canon Ireland Time for a New “Canon White” In 2018, Canon introduced a new heat-shield coating. The brief was demanding: the coating had to block more heat than ever, resist scratches and abrasion, avoid discoloring after long exposure to sunlight, feel good in the hand without being rough, and still look unmistakably like “Canon White.” This kind of technology can take a long time to develop, testing both optical performance in the field and the feasibility of manufacturing the coating in large quantities. Canon first looked at existing heat-shielding coatings, including ones used in the construction industry. None were tough enough. They couldn't handle the vibration and knocks a working lens takes, and a small bump could damage them. So, Canon decided to develop its own. What Changed? The original white paint got its shade by mixing white titanium oxide with carbon black. Carbon black is what absorbed infrared light. The new version swapped the carbon black for an infrared-reflective pigment, so sunlight’s infrared bounces off instead of soaking in. The titanium oxide is now also coated with silica. The new coating is more resistant to scratches and UV fading, too. As we know, it's not indestructible, and at some point, you're going to get one of those lovely chunks gouged out of the coating to expose the metal below. We like those battle scars around here, but not everyone does. The Shade of White Getting the right shade of white was a process. Engineers tested a pile of samples and spent time adjusting the shade, texture, the level of sheen, and even how much coating was applied to see what influence it had on the finished color and overall performance. In the end, Canon picked the color by eye because they couldn't quantify aesthetic outcomes with definitive data on the shade and application. Testing the performance was also a massive task. Canon engineers placed temperature sensors inside and outside the barrel, testing the old and new coatings side by side. They figured out that there were many slight variables with a direct impact on heat: things like small differences in the angle of the lens or whether or not there was a breeze. How much the new white helps Temperature rise of a lens in sunlight, conventional Canon white = 100 Conventional white paint titanium oxide + carbon black 100 Heat-shield coating (2018) silica-coated titanium oxide + IR-reflective pigment 80 −20% temperature rise Swapping the infrared-absorbing carbon black for an infrared-reflecting pigment means less of the sun's heat soaks into the lens. Source: Canon Europe. Canon quotes only the relative reduction, not absolute temperatures, so the bars are indexed rather than in °C. Through exhaustive testing, Canon concluded that the new coating reduced temperatures in the lens by about 20%. Does it Matter Today? Canon notes that modern RF lenses can be more prone to heat issues due to smaller barrel surface areas and fewer internal elements to distribute the heat load. Modern high-resolution image sensors can also reveal far more anomalies than film or early digital sensors. At 45MP, every atmospheric disturbance has a greater visual impact than on an older 12MP sensor. It’s similar to the days of mirror-slap on tripods: vibration blur was far more noticeable on a 50MP body than on a 24MP body. Lens Hoods Play a Role The coating on the lens hood plays a big role in battling the effects of heat. If the lens hood on a “Big White” were black, the front barrel would absorb heat directly at the entrance pupil, creating internal heat haze or a “mirage” effect inside the glass. So not only do lens hoods protect your glass from impacts and flare, they also play a critical role in keeping internal temperatures down. Keep in mind: the longer your focal length, the more exaggerated these heat-based anomalies become. Even on a smaller lens like the RF 100-500mm f/4.5-7.1L IS USM, which has far less surface area than an RF 600mm f/4L IS USM, the 500mm reach makes the heat-shield coating essential on both the barrel and hood. The coating debuted in 2018 on the EF 400mm f/2.8L IS III USM and EF 600mm f/4L IS III USM. The first RF lens to receive it was the RF 70-200mm f/2.8L IS USM in 2019, a compact zoom frequently relied upon by sports photographers under blazing summer heat. Canon White Through the Years More than 60 years of Canon white: why Canon's telephoto lenses are white, and how the paint went from a simple heat reflector to a purpose-built infrared-reflecting coating. 1960 Origin Broadcast lenses go white Canon first uses white on its broadcast camera lenses, including the TV2000mm F11. 1976 SLR era White comes to SLR lenses White is first used on Canon SLR lenses to reflect heat and minimise thermal expansion and contraction. That is especially important for heat-sensitive synthetic fluorite elements, which Canon pioneered in the 1960s. Early 2000s Field report The Australian Open problem Photographers shooting with the EOS-1D report autofocus problems. The cameras test fine, so a Canon technician sits with them and logs temperatures. The culprit turns out to be heat building up in lenses that sit in the sun for hours. 2018 Breakthrough New heat-shield coating Canon debuts its own coating on the EF 400mm f/2.8L IS III and EF 600mm f/4L IS III. It replaces IR-absorbing carbon black with an IR-reflective pigment and uses silica-coated titanium oxide, cutting temperature rise by 20% compared with the conventional paint. 2019 RF era First RF lens with the coating The RF 70-200mm F2.8 L IS USM becomes the first RF-mount lens to wear the new white, followed by the RF 70-200mm F4 L IS USM. Today Now Across the RF super-telephotos, and the hoods The coating is now used on lenses such as the RF 400mm F2.8, RF 600mm F4 and RF 100-500mm. It is also applied to their lens hoods, so a hot hood doesn't create heat haze inside the lens. Source: Canon and Canon Europe. The 20% figure is Canon's own comparison with its previous white paint. Why Aren't Smaller Lenses White? There are a few reasons why this paint color is saved for the bigger lenses. Smaller lenses have less surface area to soak up heat.. A lens like an RF 24-70mm f/2.8L IS USM isn't likely to be sitting baking in the sun on a tripod at an event. As mentioned earlier, the longer the focal length, the more likely you'll be able to see the negative effects of heat. Yes, there are the RF 100-400mm f/5.6-8 IS, RF 600mm f/11 and the RF 800mm f/11 black lenses in Canon's lineup, but they're not targeted at professionals who will be dealing with the sun for longer periods of time. Black is also better for videography to keep surface reflections to a minimum. Black is a bit more “stealth” when shooting events like a wedding. We imagine that the black coating is cheaper to use than the “Canon White” coating. In Closing The question of the white paint and why it exists has been asked for decades past and will be asked in the future, and for those of us that like to know why something is done the way it is, we think this topic will always be interesting. Canon could be working on the next iteration of this technology, as they seem to be a company that spends a lot of resources on the “little things”. Sure, one of those little things is going to be branding, but sometimes you get added benefits to advances in your technology. It has been 60 years of engineering just to try and keep the lenses cooler, and if they find a better way to do it, expect a new coating or two down the line.

items.title: Nikon Z5IIC review: an awkward viewfinderless camera design that’s heavy in the hand, heavy on specs, and light on your wallet
items.summary_what: Nikon Z5IIC review: an awkward viewfinderless camera design that’s heavy in the hand, heavy on specs, and light on your wallet: The Nikon Z5IIC launched following rumors of a Nikon camera without a viewfinder.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: The Nikon Z5IIC launched following rumors of a Nikon camera without a viewfinder. While there were whispers of a fixed-lens full-frame compact camera and a stills-focused Nikon ZR , nobody could have predicted a ‘viewfinderless’ clone of the Nikon Z5 II . Viewfinderless cameras have always been divisive. Photography purists cite the stability and sun-glare-free nature of shooting through the viewfinder as too crucial to pass up. But plenty of modern photographers ignore their EVF in favor of their mirrorless cameras’ rear LCD and a more dynamic method of shooting. What works for you, works. But the big question I’ll be trying to answer is what benefits the Nikon Z5IIC’s viewfinderless design brings to the table. One such benefit is price. With reports of the Nikon Z5 reaching the end of its lifecycle , the Nikon Z5IIC could soon become the most affordable entry point into Nikon’s full-frame mirrorless lineup at $1,399.95 / £1,349 / AU$2,399 (body only). And that entry point is exactly what Nikon is targeting. The ‘C’ in the camera’s name is supposed to represent ‘Casual’, which is why the Nikon Z5IIC is also the very first full-frame Z-series camera to feature Scene Modes. I took the Nikon Z5IIC for a spin around the beautiful city of Bath to find out how its viewfinderless design fared in a street photography setting. Read on for a deep dive into the camera’s specs and to find out how it performed in real-world scenarios. (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Nikon Z5IIC vs Z5II: Specifications Nikon Z5IIC Nikon Z5 II Effective pixels 24.5MP BSI CMOS (full-frame) 24.5MP BSI CMOS (full-frame) ISO sensitivity Stills: 100–64000, (50-204,800 expanded) Video: 100–51200, Hi 2.0 Stills: 100–64000, (50-204,800 expanded) Video: 100–51200, Hi 2.0 Engine EXPEED 7 EXPEED 7 File format (Photo) RAW/JPEG/HEIF RAW/JPEG/HEIF Phase detection AF area Single-point AF: 273 points Auto-area AF: 299 points Single-point AF: 273 points Auto-area AF: 299 points Subject detection 10 types 9 types AF detection -10 EV -10EV Continuous shooting speed Electronic front-curtain shutter: 14 fps (CH+) Electronic shutter: 30 fps (C30) Electronic front-curtain shutter: 14 fps (CH+) Electronic shutter: 30 fps (C30) Vibration reduction 5-axis in-body VR: Up to 7.5 stops 5-axis in-body VR: Up to 7.5 stops Shutter speed 1/8000–30 sec (extendable up to 900 sec) 1/8000–30 sec (extendable up to 900 sec) Video frame size/frame rate 4K 60p (cropped) 4K 30p Full HD 120p 4K 60p (cropped) 4K 30p Full HD 120p Video compression N-RAW, H.265/264 N-RAW, H.265/264 Video recording mode N-Log, HLG, SDR N-Log, HLG, SDR Monitor 3.2-inch, approx. 1040k-dot vari-angle 3.2-inch, approx. 2100k-dot vari-angle Media slot SD (UHS-II) x1 SD (UHS-II) x2 Battery EN-EL15c (Rechargeable Li-ion) EN-EL15c (Rechargeable Li-ion) Dimensions (W×H×D) 5.3 x 3.3 x 2.9 in (134 × 80.5 × 72 mm) 5.3 x 4 x 2.9 in (134 x 100.5 x 72 mm) Weight (camera body only) 19 oz. / 538 g (body-only) 24.7 oz. / 620 g (body-only) Nikon Z5IIC: Price The Nikon Z5IIC is priced at $1,399.95 / £1,349 / AU$2,399 (body only). Compare that to the Nikon Z5 II , which is typically listed around $1,599 / £1,499 / AU$2,699, and that’s a decent saving of around $200 / £150 / AU$300. But one thing I’ve had in mind is where the Z5IIC will end up. As time goes on, we could see that body-only price creep towards the $1,000 mark. You can also opt to choose from various kits or bundles, such as the Nikon Z5IIC + Nikon Z 24-50mm f/4-6.3 ($1,699.95 / £1,609 / AU$2,949). This prime-sized zoom is a great choice for the camera’s viewfinderless design. While the Nikon Z5IIC + Nikon Z 24-200mm f/4-6.3 VR ($TBC / £2,049 / AU$3,699) might seem like a great all-in-one option, I’d be wary of any lens bigger than the Nikon Z 24-120mm f/4 S , which I used during my review. When you stack the Nikon Z5IIC against the Panasonic Lumix S9 and Sony A7C II , it’s priced between them. Overall, I think it’s competitively priced given its specs and the economic challenges the consumer tech industry is currently facing. Nikon Z5IIC: Design & Handling The Nikon Z5IIC largely follows the same formula as every other mainline Z-series camera: it’s solid, bulky, has a deep grip, and plenty of physical controls. The big difference is that it doesn’t have a faux pentaprism bump in which to house an electronic viewfinder. It’s less bulky and inherently more ‘riggable’ than any other full-frame Z-series camera (Nikon ZR aside). This allows it to occupy marginally less space in a backpack, weigh marginally less in the hand, look marginally less professional and intimidating, and cost marginally less than its blueprint, the Nikon Z5 II. The big question I had when using this camera was: Is ‘marginal’ enough to warrant the downgrade in functionality? I get it. Not every photographer wants to use a viewfinder, and there’s nothing wrong with that at all. If you’re prepared for bright, sunny conditions reflecting off the rear LCD and that doesn’t faze you, who am I to tell you otherwise? But the difference here is that the Nikon Z5IIC is a beefy, full-frame camera and that does change things. (Image credit: Mike Harris wearing a t-shirt and jeans holding the Nikon Z5IIC on a green background) Take the Panasonic Lumix S9 for example; a viewfinderless full-frame camera that’s roughly 135g lighter than the Nikon Z5IIC. That does make a difference. I’ve handed the Z5IIC off to various colleagues, and they’ve all been surprised by the same thing: its weight. The camera’s body weighs 538 g, which is a not-insignificant 82 g lighter than the Nikon Z5 II. And yet, the way you handle a viewfinderless camera is just different . Peer through a viewfinder and you’ll instinctively cradle a larger camera with both hands, but viewfinderless cameras need to be held farther from the body. The Z5IIC might be lighter than the Nikon Z5 II, but I noticed its weight more. That’s not to say the weight is a constant pain point, but it is a consideration. I used the camera with the Nikon Z 40mm f/2 and Nikon Z 24-120mm f/4 S. The latter is as heavy and bulky as I’d want to go for regular, handheld shooting. And even then, this is a relatively hefty setup for an everyday carry. (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Use the Nikon Z5IIC for video, though, and the form factor isn’t an issue. Again, you tend to hold a camera differently when shooting video. Your forefinger doesn’t have to rest on the shutter button, meaning you can hold it in any way that feels comfortable to you. And of course, if you mainly shoot stills from a tripod, the form factor won’t be an issue at all, and most tripod users compose via the rear screen anyway. Ultimately, the lack of a viewfinder won’t be a turnoff for everyone, but the size and weight of the camera could be. I recommend trying it on for size in your local camera shop before buying, and considering very carefully what lenses you want to use with it. A telephoto-friendly camera this is not. A disappointing oversight from Nikon on paper is the Z5IIC’s rear screen. It’s actually lower resolution than the Nikon Z5II’s 2100k-dot screen (it’s 1040k dots). This really is a curious decision from Nikon and one that I can only assume was a budgetary measure. Still, you’d think the rear screen on a viewfinderless camera would be a core spec. And yet, despite my displeasure, if I’m going to be truly honest, I didn’t find this to be an issue out in the field. An oversight, yes, but not one that will impact the camera’s day-to-day usability. (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Now that I’ve addressed the elephant in the room, let’s move on to some of the positives, of which there are plenty. As you’d expect from a mainline Z-series camera, the entire body feels solid. It’s built from magnesium alloy and durable-feeling plastics, while the grip is deep and covered in Nikon’s grippy leatherette. It’s also weather sealed, and while I’m not going to leave a $1399.95 / £1,349 camera out in a downpour, the UK’s dreadful weather meant I spent a lot of time using the Z5IIC in light showers. I never advise letting any camera get saturated, but I felt entirely confident using the Z5IIC in wet conditions. As per usual, Nikon has churned out a utilitarian device that’s built like a tank. But what’s unheard of from a mainline Z-series camera is that the Z5IIC comes in two colors. That’s right, it’s not just all-black with the classic red stripe; you can also opt for a silver variant. This paint job is only applied to the top plate, giving the camera a definite Sony A7C II vibe. Some of my colleagues think the silver looks plasticky, but as somebody who often moans about silver cameras looking cheap, I’d opt for the silver variant. Consider me a fan. (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) On the aforementioned top plate, you’ll find a fairly minimalist setup that’s functionally almost identical to the Nikon Z5 II. You’ve got a chunky mode dial that’s satisfyingly stiff, albeit slightly different to the Nikon Z5II’s in that it has only two U options instead of three. This is to facilitate the new Scene Mode icon (more on that later). Like the Z5 II, there’s also a very handy Picture Control button. Simply tap it and use the rear command dial to scroll through 31 ‘looks’ which are applied to images in real time. The left side of the top plate is typically bare, but without the viewfinder bump, it might have been nice to have included an ISO or exposure comp dial. Moving on to the rear, it’s standard fare except for the lack of a joystick. This is a real backwards step as far as I’m concerned. I can’t imagine it would have been an expensive addition. It simply means you’re forced to use the d-pad, which isn’t always as comfortable for your thumb, when holding the camera to accommodate its viewfinderless design. Thankfully, though, the buttons are solid and pleasantly spongy. Future / Mike Harris Future / Mike Harris Future / Mike Harris Future / Mike Harris Future / Mike Harris Future / Mike Harris The Nikon Z5IIC has a single SD-card slot, which is a downgrade from the Z5 II. However, this isn’t a pro-grade camera, and if you’re a stickler for pro features, you’re going to want a viewfinder anyway. As such, I think this is a sensible cost-saving measure that won’t bother most, especially with the ever-increasing price of memory cards these days. On the front of the camera, you’ve got two Fn buttons, which can be reached by extending your middle and forefinger from the grip, so they can be activated one-handed. And, like other Z-series cameras, the Z5IIC’s controls are highly customizable, so you can make the setup work for you. The camera uses Nikon’s standard EN-EL15c rechargeable Li-ion battery. According to the CIPA Shot Rating, it’s rated for 350 shots, which isn’t much different from the Nikon Z5II’s 330-380. During use, I can confirm that the battery held up as well as could be expected. Any concerns you might have about the rear LCD always being on can be easily dispelled. Firstly, by getting into the habit of switching your camera off when not in use. And secondly, by the fact that a standard mirrorless is constantly switching between an EVF and a rear LCD, the power usage isn’t going to be much different. Nikon Z5IIC: Performance Nikon’s second-generation Z-series lineup consists of the Nikon Z9 at the very top of the pyramid, with varying degrees of tech trickling down to other cameras in the range. As such, all of Nikon’s cameras boast very solid core performances and the Nikon Z5IIC is no different. In a world of high-megapixel sensors, you could look down upon the Z5IIC’s 24.5-MP sensor, but like all of Nikon’s full-frame image files, the stills you get from the Z5IIC really are top tier. RAW files stand up to generous cropping and are extremely pliable in post; they’re just an all-around treat to work with. And if editing RAW files isn’t your thing, the Nikon Z5IIC is loaded with Nikon’s Picture Controls. Think Fujifilm Film Simulations, but not as good fresh from the box. Thankfully, Picture Controls can be edited so you can come up with your own ‘recipes’, and you can even download examples from other creators. Film Grain isn’t simply overlaid onto your images; it’s rendered each time differently (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) A fairly recent update that debuted on the Nikon Zf is Film Grain. This complements Picture Controls by adding retro film grain to images. Not only does it look the part, but the grain isn’t uniform, so each application is different. I tested this myself and can confirm that it does indeed hold up to scrutiny. You can customize the grain by choosing from three different sizes and seven different intensities. I wouldn’t recommend using everything maxed out, but the default settings do look very convincing. Another feature that really lives up to the Nikon Z5IIC’s ‘Casual’ moniker is the presence of Scene Modes. The Z5IIC is the first full-frame Nikon camera to feature Scene Modes, and while that might not seem like a big deal, I think it’s a great addition. These modes are a great way for novice photographers to exercise a little creative agency beyond the one-size-fits-all Auto Mode. There are 15 Scene Modes in total, allowing you to adapt quickly to a variety of shooting situations. For example, I photographed my dog using the Pet Portraits Scene Mode. The camera instantly opened up the aperture and switched to Animal-Detection AF, so all I had to do was compose my image and fire the shutter. Think of Scene Modes as genre-specific automatic settings (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Similarly, I tried out Night Landscape and Autumn Colors; the camera instantly adapted to both scenarios, raising the ISO and opening the aperture in low light, and warming the image and boosting the saturation when capturing autumnal foliage. Picture Controls and Scene modes aren’t for everyone, but I think they fit the Z5IIC’s intended demographic and are definite selling points for the right photographer. When it comes to autofocus, the Nikon Z5IIC performs very well. Sure, it can get a little stuck or confused at times, like any AF system, but provided you take the time to learn Nikon’s various modes, you’ll be well rewarded. I enjoy using 3D tracking, Wide-Area AF, and Single-Point AF, swapping between modes depending on the subject or scene at hand. I own a Nikon Z8, and while the Z8 will certainly perform better in a side-by-side comparison, I didn’t find myself bemoaning the Z5IIC’s performance, which is high praise indeed. And of course, the Nikon Z5IIC has an autofocus mod con that currently no other Nikon camera has – not even the flagship Nikon Z9 – and that’s fish subject-detection. The Pet Portraits Scene Mode instantly switched the camera to Animal-Detection AF (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Now, I initially found this quite the novelty, but in a world of ever-expanding AF algorithms, why not? I actually used to know a professional photographer who photographed fish for fish-keeping publications, and I’m sure he’d be very happy indeed with this development. It’s exciting news for underwater photographers, too, because put a camera with fish AF in an underwater housing and you’re golden. Speaking of gold, I did my due diligence and found myself a fitting subject to test out this new autofocus mode. Thomas is a rescued fairground goldfish who resides in a local art studio owned by incredibly talented wildlife artist Jacqueline Byrne ( @jacquelinebyrne.art ). Jackie kindly allowed me to use Thomas as a model and I was pleased to find that the camera not only detected the goldfish’s body, but also locked onto his eyes. It did struggle at times, but the conditions were challenging. Reflections and scratches on the tank glass, not to mention underwater foliage, and my need to shoot wide open in low light, all contributed. But fish AF works and isn’t quite the joke addition it may at first seem. Fish AF isn’t the novelty you might think (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) The Nikon Z5IIC’s form factor certainly lends itself to videography, and just like the Nikon Z5 II it boasts some decent specs. Arguably the biggest selling point is internal 4K 30p full-width RAW video. And while it’s nice to have, I always thought it was a little out of place on the Nikon Z5II, and I still think it’s a little out of place on the Nikon Z5IIC. A lot of pro videographers don’t shoot RAW video. After all, it fills up storage as a pastime, creates increased internal heat, and is power-hungry in the edit. That said, it’s nice to have as an option. Although, a word of warning: make sure you’re using a capable SD card. The Nikon Z5IIC will only record RAW video on a memory card that’s over 32GB. And if your memory card isn’t fast enough, it’ll stop recording before time. When it comes to overheating, ambient temperature and camera usage will always affect the outcome, but I shot 13 minutes of uninterrupted RAW footage in real-world testing without issue. The Nikon ZR is proof that Nikon knows how to build a camera that’s very hard to overheat, and while I cannot comment on long-term video usage due to my very short time with the camera, I don’t have any immediate concerns. I also shot some 4K video. As you’d expect, the autofocus performed well; just be aware that 4K 60p enforces a 1.5x (DX) crop. (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Another video boon is in-body image stabilization. It’s not surprising given that the Nikon Z5II also has it, but it was a crucial inclusion because the Z5IIC’s direct competitors also have IBIS. What they don’t have is 7.5 stops of stabilization, with the camera beating the Panasonic Lumix S9’s 6.5 stops and the Sony A7C II’s seven stops. This is a great feature for photographers, too. I’d argue it’s essential for the Z5IIC given its viewfinderless design, because you’re not holding the camera up to your eye, which is the most stable shooting position. While the lower-resolution LCD screen didn’t really bother me when shooting stills, I do think it matters more for video. Metering is such an important part of videography, and while you’ve got aids such as zebras and histograms, every little helps if you’re not resorting to an external monitor. One thing I would suggest that any Nikon Z5IIC owner does is head into Menu>Setup>Monitor Brightness and set the latter to its maximum setting. This will reduce battery efficiency, but you’ll get a brighter and more visible screen. As a photographer, I lament the flip-out screen craze, much preferring a tilting screen, but the Nikon Z5IIC is a camera built to adapt to both worlds, and a flip-out screen is definitely preferable for video. 22.68 21.78 20.46 23.24 Resolution: It’s not surprising that the Sony A7C II comfortably beats the other full-frame cameras thanks to its 33-MP sensor, with the Panasonic Lumix S9 bringing up the rear with its 24.2-MP sensor. The bigger surprise is the Nikon Z5IIC’s performance in relation to the Nikon Z5 II, exhibiting sharper images between ISO3200 and ISO12,800. However, this could simply be a variation in optics, and in a real-world scenario, the difference is going to be negligible. Dynamic Range: Each camera boasts impressive dynamic range and despite differences in resolution, there really isn’t much to separate them. The Sony A7C II just about wins, as to be expected, but the Nikon Z5IIC more than holds its own, performing better than both the Nikon Z5 II and Panasonic Lumix S9. Again, the race is so tight, you’re unlikely to notice much difference in a real-world scenario. Signal to noise ratio: The lower-resolution sensors come out on top here, with the Sony A7C II’s higher resolution proving its undoing, although it doesn’t lag far behind. When it comes to the two Nikons and the Panasonic Lumix S9, you’d have to defer to a photo finish to work out who’s pipped who to the post, but it does look like the Nikon Z5IIC has outperformed the Nikon Z5 II once again. Nikon Z5IIC: Verdict The Nikon Z5IIC is a tale of two halves. On the one hand, it has a slightly awkward design. On the other, its performance punches above its weight. I’m no stickler for always looking through the viewfinder, but the biggest benefit of viewfinderless cameras is their increased portability. And yet, losing the viewfinder doesn’t impact the size and weight of the Z5IIC enough; it’s still a big lump. The upside of this is that it’s built like a tank and feels like a premium, weather-sealed product. I’m not saying the heft is a dealbreaker; just make sure you try it on for size before you buy. Under the hood is where the camera really gains some ground. It’s a fantastic all-around performer, with great autofocus, gorgeous stills, solid video specs, and impressive in-body image stabilization. Plus, you get the rather unusual (if superfluous) bonus of RAW video. Scene Modes is an unlikely standout for me. It really lives up to the Z5IIC’s ‘casual’ moniker and allows anybody to get creative with the camera from the offset. Picture Modes and Film Grain serve as the next step in creative agency, allowing you to apply ready-made or custom presets to your images in real time. Finally, the Nikon Z5IIC is competitively priced. At $1399.95 / £1,349, it sits between the Sony A7C II and Panasonic Lumix S9. It’s not a cheap camera by any means, and I do wonder how appealing that price point is to its ‘casual’ target audience. But it’s got the specs of a more expensive camera. Overall, I was ready to hate on the Nikon Z5IIC when it was announced, but I’ve been pleasantly surprised by how much I’ve enjoyed my limited time with the camera. That said, I wonder if its size and weight could be its undoing. It’s too big to be an everyday carry, and I fear it may be too intimidating for its ‘casual’ target audience. I hope I’m proved wrong, because this is a well-built, exceedingly capable full-frame camera. Just like its blueprint, the Nikon Z5 II. Design ★★★☆☆ I’m not sold on a viewfinderless design for a camera that’s this big and heavy, and the low-res LCD and lack of a joystick are disappointing. But it’s weather-sealed, very solidly built and comes with a nice deep grip. Photo Performance ★★★★☆ Gorgeous Nikon RAW files and accurate AF. The inclusion of Scene Modes makes it more accessible for newcomers, while Picture Controls and Film Grain are great ways to personalize images in-camera. Video Performance ★★★★☆ No open gate, but internal RAW video is impressive (if a little unnecessary). IBIS, 4K 60p (albeit cropped), reliable AF, a flip-out rear screen, and a riggable form factor are all solid video features. Value ★★★★☆ Sits between its closest rivals and will likely soon become the cheapest full-frame camera in Nikon’s mirrorless lineup. It’s not a cheap camera, but it’s competitively priced. Overall ★★★★☆ Nikon Z5IIC: Alternatives This little full-frame mirrorless camera arguably embodies the viewfinderless ethos better than the Nikon Z5IIC in that it’s noticeably smaller and lighter. The Panasonic Lumix S9 won’t beat the Nikon when it comes to stills, but it does boast some seriously good video specs, maxing out at 6K 30p open gate . The Sony A7C II is a few years old, but still a popular choice for those looking for a capable mirrorless camera with a more compact form factor. This camera’s genius is that it manages to squeeze in a rangefinder-style EVF. You also get a 33-MP sensor, but it does occupy a higher price bracket than either the Nikon Z5IIC or Panasonic Lumix S9. Check out our guide to the best mirrorless cameras , and our rundown of the best Nikon Z lenses

items.title: DJI is giving new life to lots of its older drones with unexpected firmware updates –is this a bonus with Americans in mind?
items.summary_what: DJI is giving new life to lots of its older drones with unexpected firmware updates –is this a bonus with Americans in mind?: DJI has delivered new firmware for several popular older models including the Mini 3 Pro, the Mini 2, and the Mavic Air 2 even though many thought these drones had reached...
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Backup existing camera profiles and format media before applying firmware from the official support site.
items.raw_content: DJI has delivered new firmware for several popular older models including the Mini 3 Pro, the Mini 2, and the Mavic Air 2 even though many thought these drones had reached the end of their lives. It's good news for owners, proving that DJI has not abandoned these models even though some are several generations behind (there is a Mini 5 Pro now, for example), and shows the company is still serving the needs of American consumers, who are unable to buy the latest DJI drone models. Official details of new firmware for oldest drones below DJI Fly updates available from DJI downloads The Neo and the Mini 4K have both had recent firmware updates (Image credit: Future) Also on the list of drones with an update is the DJI Mini 2 , which was released back in 2020 and hadn't seen a software update in well over three years. Many might think of that as the end of life for a relatively inexpensive device (not many of us still have phones that old if we use the camera on them). The DJI Mini 2 was the first cheap, light 4K drone (and has had several successors, including the Mini 2 SE , Mini 4K and Lito 1 ) (Image credit: Adam Juniper/Digital Camera World) While the Mini 2 was impressive in its day, delivering 4K video and RAW photos to the 249g highly portable market, as well as reliable video at a (theoretical) 10km transmission range. The 12MP sensor isn't where DJI stopped, though. DJI's Mini drones now stretch to the Mini 5 Pro, which has a 50MP camera, and much larger 1-inch sensor, slow-motion 4K, AI subject tracking, and obstacle sensing and avoidance tech. DJI Mavic Air 2 in flight (Image credit: Adam Juniper/Digital Camera World) The Mavic Air 2 last saw any firmware change in 2023, and the Air 2S in 2024, and both models have been superseded. So why the changes? Well there might well be some issues, and there may be some necessities to keep working with newer phone operating systems (DJI Fly is also getting newer versions on both iOS and Android). It's also very good news for both the American market, where the very latest DJI models are not allowed past customs at the moment, and for those looking for a good resale value. With fresh firmware, confidence in buying a used DJI Mini 2 will stay high and you can see that reflected in relatively high used prices. It's not clear, of course, what has been changed. In the past DJI has added new features by firmware (8K video to the Osmo, vertical video to the Neo). Known issues usually just means software patches (DJI hasn't said "App and OS compatibility" though you can bet that compatibility with the latest phones and apps will have been dealt with). Either way uploading the firmware takes a few minutes before a device restart. Personal tip: do it at home, in the warm, where you've got a good internet connection. Far too often I've literally done it in a field! It will be offered automatically by your DJI Fly app. It's not just older drones getting newer firmware The delivery of firmware is especially interesting for older drones, but DJI has also been delivering for more recent devices, including the Mini 5 Pro , Air 3S , and Mavic 4 Pro . These are arguably the most high-end consumer drones, and again all it's about is "Fixing known issues." DJI is delivering the updates around the world, including the USA, where some of these drones are under threat of being taken from the shelves because the tech is too good (LiDAR collision sensors are being reviewed as 'military' by the FCC ). DJI's firmware rollout isn't just about drones DJI has been delivering a batch of updates for other tech too. Three of the company's remote controls with built-in screens (DJI RC, RC 2, and RC Pro 2) have all seen updates in recent days too. The updates Model New Version Reason Mini 3 Pro v01.00.1000 Fixed some known issues Mini 2 v01.07.0300 Fixed some known issues Mavic Air 2 v01.01.18.00 Fixed some known issues Air 2S v02.04.28.00 Bug fixes You might also like I've been flying drones a lot of my life, and have reviewed all of these DJI drones and a good deal more. You'll find my current favorites in the best camera drones and best beginners drones guides.

items.title: The Death Of The Button: Why The Best Interface Is No Interface
items.summary_what: The Death Of The Button: Why The Best Interface Is No Interface: Ever since the commercialisation of the Graphical User Interface pioneered by systems like the Xerox Star and popularised by the original Apple Macintosh , software has relied heavily on point-and-click interactions.
items.summary_why: Influences typography, UI/UX prototyping speed, and vector design production assets.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: Ever since the commercialisation of the Graphical User Interface pioneered by systems like the Xerox Star and popularised by the original Apple Macintosh , software has relied heavily on point-and-click interactions. If you wanted to book a trip, buy a pair of shoes, or research a health symptom, you were expected to navigate a labyrinth of user interfaces. You click menus, adjust range sliders, fill out multi-step forms, deal with cookie pop-ups, and open dozens of browser tabs just to cross-reference basic information. We have become accustomed to spending more time managing the software rather than actually achieving our goals. That contract is officially changing. Driven by advances in artificial intelligence and large language models, a new generation of web tools is pioneering a radical philosophy: Intent-Driven Design . Rather than expecting our users to learn complex menus and click through elaborate sales funnels, these platforms operate by capturing high-level human goals and silently executing the grunt work in the background. This vision builds on long-standing HCI concepts like Golden Krishna’s “The Best Interface Is No Interface” and Don Norman’s principles of human-centered design . The ultimate goal of modern web design is no longer to build prettier buttons or flashy animations; it is to eliminate the interface entirely. Well, at least what we understand based on our current experience. It is essential for UX designers to understand the changes we’re witnessing and even re-evaluate our role , shifting our focus from designing visible interfaces to guiding transparent, intent-driven AI experiences . The Death Of The “10-click” Process To understand where web design is going, we first have to look at the friction we have accepted as “normal” for decades. Consider the traditional workflow of buying a flight online. The user experience is intentionally hyper-interactive: Navigate to a travel aggregator or airline website. Select “Round Trip” from a dropdown menu. Type the origin city and wait for auto-complete. Type the destination city and wait for auto-complete. Click a calendar modal, toggle through months, and select departure and return dates. Choose the number of passengers and cabin class. Click “Search” and wait for the results page to load. Filter by price, layover duration, departure time, and airline. Sort the results and scan through dozens of individual options. Click through a three-page checkout funnel dodging upsells for rental cars and travel insurance. This is a classic point-and-click UI paradigm . The computer acts as a passive container of data, and the human acts as the orchestrator, manually inputting parameters, interpreting raw outputs, and executing each micro-step along the way. Intent-driven design flips this dynamic entirely. Instead of forcing you to navigate the mechanical steps of how to find a flight, the interface asks a simple question: What are you trying to accomplish? When you express a goal, such as “Find me a non-stop flight to Chicago next weekend under $300 that arrives before 5 PM” , the software reads your intent, executes the multi-step search query behind the scenes, compares the options, and presents a single actionable resolution. The ten clicks dissolve into one clear intent outcome. Three Web Platform Examples Replacing Buttons With Intent This shift isn’t a theoretical vision of the distant future. Some of the world’s most accessible websites allow you to experience intent-capturing systems already. 1. Perplexity AI: Search Without The Open Tabs Traditional search engines like Google were built as directories. You typed a keyword, and the interface rewarded you with ten blue links. The actual work of opening five tabs, skimming long articles, dodging ads, and manually assembling an answer was left to you. Although this is now changing, with AI content appearing first when you search on Google. Perplexity AI allows anyone to perform instant intent-based searches. Instead of forcing you to click into multiple tabs, the interface synthesises the perfect result for your context. The interaction: You ask a complex question in plain English: “Compare the top three budget laptops for a computer science student, focusing on battery life and keyboard quality.” The invisible work: In under two seconds, the platform searches the web, reads dozens of articles, evaluates hardware specifications, and cross-references user reviews. The result: (See screen above) Instead of throwing web pages at you, Perplexity dynamically generates a single custom answer complete with formatted comparison tables, pros and cons lists, and concise inline citations. You get the outcome of thirty clicks in just one. 2. Vercel v0: Web Design Without Dragging And Dropping For years, creating a website meant using visual builders like Figma or drag-and-drop web editors. As designers, we spent hours manually drawing rectangles, picking hexadecimal colour codes, adjusting padding values, and sometimes writing CSS code. Vercel v0 lets anyone test its generative interface builder right from the home page without signing in. The Interaction: A user types a descriptive goal into the input prompt: “Create a modern dark-mode dashboard for a subscription SaaS app showing monthly revenue, active users, and a customer churn chart.” The invisible work: The underlying AI understands layout principles, accessibility guidelines, UI component libraries, and responsiveness. It writes clean HTML, Tailwind CSS, and React code in real time. The result: Rather than spending an afternoon manipulating elements, the user receives a fully functional, pixel-perfect user interface in seconds! The traditional visual design tool disappears, replaced by raw human intent. 3. Goblin.tools: Breaking Down Overwhelming Tasks Many traditional productivity tools require you to manually construct task lists, drag items across Kanban boards, and assign micro-deadlines. Goblin.tools is a free, single-page suite of single-task AI tools designed specifically for neurodivergent users or anyone feeling overwhelmed, requiring zero sign-ups or configuration. The interaction: You enter a vague, intimidating goal into the Magic Todo tool, such as “Prepare for a job interview” . The invisible work: Instead of forcing you to plan every step, the system analyses the cognitive load of the goal and automatically breaks it down into small, actionable sub-tasks adjusted to your preferred level of detail. The result: The interface eliminates the stressful task-planning phase and presents a clean checklist tailored to your exact goal. The Core Pillars Of Intent-driven Web Design When you remove traditional menus, sidebars, and forms, how do you keep a website usable? Designers pioneering this space rely on three core pillars: Pillar Traditional UX approach Intent-driven UX approach User input Micro-actions (Clicks, dropdowns, toggles) 1. High-level goals (Natural language, context, habits) Interface state Static layouts (Everyone sees the same page) 2. Generative UI (Layouts created dynamically on the fly) Task execution Manual execution by the user 3. Autonomous execution by background AI agents 1. High-level Goals An invisible interface doesn’t always wait for you to type a command — it leverages context to anticipate user needs. Guided by industry standards like Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines on Contextual & Ambient Design , modern systems read environmental metadata, such as device state, location, and past interaction patterns, to trigger proactive actions. For example: Time and location: A food delivery web app prioritising your saved home address and dinner items automatically at 6:30 PM on a weekday. Cross-app history: A calendar application noticing an email about an upcoming appointment and surfacing a one-click “Add to Schedule” card without forcing you to copy and paste event details manually. 2. Generative UI In traditional web design, every user sees the exact same layout. An e-commerce store shows the same navigation bar whether you are a first-time visitor looking for customer support or a returning customer tracking a package. As highlighted in the Nielsen Norman Group’s analysis on AI as a new UX paradigm , computing is shifting from command-based interaction to outcome-specification. This enables Generative UI , where interfaces are rendered dynamically on the fly based on what you are trying to do in that exact moment. For example, platforms like Vercel v0 demonstrate how raw intent can instantly render functional code components without manual layout building. If you express a desire to compute complex financial data, the interface generates a dynamic calculator widget on demand, receding once your goal is completed. 3. Execution by AI Agents Traditional interfaces are obsessed with prevention, constantly peppering users with confirmation pop-ups ( “Are you sure you want to delete this file?” ). Intent-driven interfaces adapt Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics on User Control and Error Recovery by shifting the safety net from prevention to easy reversibility . Because autonomous agents take actions on your behalf, products prioritise frictionless rollback mechanisms. A prominent “Undo” button, simple revision prompts ( “Make this summary shorter” ), and transparent audit logs replace intrusive warning modals. The Hidden Risks While removing interface friction is liberating, stripping away visual controls introduces significant product design challenges. When software acts on inferred intent rather than direct point-and-click commands, designers must navigate critical ethical and technical pitfalls. The Illusion Of Control When a website makes decisions for you, it can quickly feel patronising or invasive. As explored by the Stanford Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) Group , automation must maintain clear boundaries to prevent user frustration. Furthermore, ethical frameworks from the Center for Humane Technology emphasise that product designers must guard against manipulative defaults. Designers must strike a delicate balance: automate routine execution, but explicitly prompt the user for high-stakes confirmations (such as financial transactions, publishing public content, or altering privacy settings). The Black Box Problem In a traditional UI, if you get an unexpected result, you can usually diagnose the issue — perhaps you checked the wrong filter box or selected an incorrect date. With an intent-driven interface, troubleshooting becomes harder. To address this “black box” challenge, the Google PAIR (People + AI Research) Guidebook advocates for transparent feedback loops. The system must explicitly state its interpretation ( “Searching for non-stop flights to Chicago under $300...” ) so users can calibrate trust and correct misinterpretations instantly. From A UX Perspective As a UX designer, always being curious to understand how our design approach is changing in the world of AI, I find it essential that we re-evaluate the foundational elements of our craft. Rather than designing static buttons and rigid forms, we need to learn to map and present dynamic, generative UI components that adapt on the fly to user intent. By mastering these evolving patterns, like ambient feedback, inline prompts, and transparent AI status indicators, we can ensure that screenless, agent-driven tools remain intuitive, ethical, and deeply human-centered. Conclusion The ultimate goal: The best design is no design. For decades, the digital industry has evaluated software success through engagement metrics like time spent in app , click-through rates , and page views per session . Websites were deliberately engineered to maximise visual engagement and interaction volume. The philosophy behind Golden Krishna’s seminal book The Best Interface Is No Interface , aligned with the broader Center for Humane Technology’s Time Well Spent movement , turns these metrics on their head. The ultimate test of a modern digital product is no longer how visually captivating its buttons are, but rather: How effectively did this software solve the problem and get out of the user’s way? , We are entering an era where web applications will no longer be measured by the beauty of their interfaces, but by their ability to render those complex interfaces completely obsolete. The future of the web isn’t more interaction — it is seamless, invisible completion .

items.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 and iMac M6 Announced – 2nm Chip, ProRes RAW Media Engine, Up to 32GB Memory
items.summary_what: Apple MacBook Pro M6 and iMac M6 Announced – 2nm Chip, ProRes RAW Media Engine, Up to 32GB Memory: Apple has brought its 2nm M6 chip to the 14-inch MacBook Pro and the 24-inch iMac.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Test new release on a backup or non-critical test project before upgrading active production timelines.
items.raw_content: Apple has brought its 2nm M6 chip to the 14-inch MacBook Pro and the 24-inch iMac. Both machines get two more CPU and GPU cores than before, Neural Accelerators in every GPU core, Wi-Fi 7 and a Media Engine with hardware ProRes and ProRes RAW support. For editors, the more important details sit further down the spec sheet: memory stops at 32GB, and the ports stay at Thunderbolt 4. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $1,999 and the iMac with M6 at $1,499. Pre-orders open tomorrow, October 28, and deliveries start on Friday, November 6. Both use the M6 chip that debuted in the Mac mini in August, which we covered in our Mac Studio and Mac mini launch article . In its full version, the M6 has a 12-core CPU (2 super cores, 4 performance cores and 6 efficiency cores), a 12-core GPU with a Neural Accelerator in each core, third-generation ray tracing, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine and up to 170GB/s of memory bandwidth. Unified memory starts at 16GB and goes up to 32GB. The Media Engine has one video decode engine, one video encode engine, one ProRes encode and decode engine and AV1 decode, with hardware acceleration for H.264, HEVC, ProRes and ProRes RAW. The entry-level iMac uses a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU version of the chip. Apple just released the new MacBook Pro 14-inch and iMac with its new M6 chip. Image credit: Apple The M6 chip and video work Apple’s performance claims for the MacBook Pro compare it with the 14-inch M5 model: up to 30 percent faster graphics, up to 25 percent faster AI workloads such as LLM prompt processing, and a Neural Engine that is up to 1.9x faster. The application examples in the press release are Blender ray tracing (up to 1.3x faster than M5), Affinity image processing (up to 1.2x) and Xcode builds (up to 1.3x). For the iMac, Apple compares against the M4 generation and quotes up to 2x faster graphics and up to 5x faster on-device AI prompt processing in LM Studio. Apple also claims the M6 has the world’s fastest CPU core. None of the figures Apple published for these two machines involves a video editing or grading application, so for filmmakers the Media Engine and memory configuration say more than the percentages. The Media Engine layout is the same as in the M5 Pro: one encoder, one decoder and one ProRes engine. The M5 Max doubles the encode and ProRes blocks. In practice, the M6 machines get hardware decoding for the formats most cameras record (H.264, HEVC, ProRes and ProRes RAW), but parallel exports, for example deliverables and proxies at the same time, share a single encoder. Formats outside that list, such as BRAW, R3D or ARRIRAW, rely on the CPU and GPU instead. After Effects on the new MacBook Pro 14-inch. Image credit: Apple Memory is the more obvious ceiling. Both machines top out at 32GB, and on the MacBook Pro the 16GB base configuration runs at 153GB/s; the full 170GB/s needs 24GB or 32GB. For 4K timelines in Final Cut Pro, Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve, 32GB is workable. Heavy noise reduction, Fusion compositions or 8K material are where the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro (up to 64GB at 307GB/s) or M5 Max becomes the more realistic option. We covered those models in our MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max launch article . MacBook Pro M6: XDR display, Thunderbolt 4 The 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display carries over: 3024 x 1964 pixels at 254ppi, up to 1,000 nits sustained full-screen, 1,600 nits peak for HDR content, a 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio, P3 wide color and ProMotion up to 120Hz. For editors, the fixed refresh rates of 47.95, 48, 50, 59.94 and 60Hz match playback to the project frame rate, and the reference modes include HDR Video (P3-ST 2084). A nano-texture version of the display is optional. Apple MacBook M6 14-inch, port situation. Image credit: Apple On the ports side, the M6 model has three Thunderbolt 4 ports at up to 40Gb/s, plus HDMI, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe 3 and a headphone jack. The M5 Pro and M5 Max models have three Thunderbolt 5 ports at up to 120Gb/s instead. The M6 drives up to two external displays at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz, or one display at 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz. Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 are new. Apple rates the 72.4Wh battery at up to 24 hours of video streaming and up to 16 hours of wireless web use, and says performance is the same on battery and on mains power. The laptop ships with a 70W USB-C adapter; with a 96W or higher adapter, it charges to 50 percent in 30 minutes. It measures 31.26 x 22.12 x 1.55cm / 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61in and weighs 1.55kg / 3.4lb. Storage options are 1TB, 2TB or 4TB, and the colors are space black and silver. iMac M6: two models, two different port layouts The iMac comes in two versions, and the differences matter more for media work than the two extra cores suggest. The 10-core model has two Thunderbolt/USB 4 ports, supports one external display (up to 6K/60Hz), takes up to 24GB of memory and up to 1TB of storage, and has 2.5Gb Ethernet only as an option. The 12-core model has four Thunderbolt 4 ports, 2.5Gb Ethernet as standard, up to 32GB of memory, up to 2TB of storage, support for two external 6K displays (or one 8K/60Hz display) and an optional nano-texture glass. Both start with 16GB of memory and a 256GB SSD, which Apple says is up to 2x faster than in the M4 iMac. With 256GB, media has to live on external storage from day one. The iMac comes in whopping 7 color options. Still no return of the 27 inch version in sight, though. Image credit: Apple The 24-inch (23.5-inch viewable) 4.5K Retina display has a resolution of 4480 x 2520 pixels at 218ppi, 500 nits of brightness and P3 wide color with support for 1 billion colors. It has no XDR or HDR mode and no ProMotion, so the iMac is an SDR editing screen. The iMac also has a 12MP Center Stage camera, a six-speaker system with Spatial Audio and Dolby Atmos support, and a three-mic array. It comes in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver, measures 54.7 x 46.1cm / 21.5 x 18.1in and weighs 4.42kg / 9.7lb (10-core) or 4.44kg / 9.8lb (12-core). The new iMac M6 in use. Image credit: Apple Both ship with macOS 27 Both computers ship with macOS 27 Golden Gate, which includes Siri AI and new Apple Intelligence features. For edit systems, the more relevant point is software support. In our macOS 27 article for video editors , Adobe and Apple had confirmed support, while Blackmagic Design and Avid had not listed macOS 27 as qualified. New Macs generally cannot run a macOS version older than the one they ship with, so anyone buying one of these machines for client work should check their NLE, plugins and I/O drivers first. Where they fit The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is the entry point to Apple’s pro laptop line. It suits editors and shooters who cut 4K H.264, HEVC or ProRes, offload cards on location with the SDXC slot, and want an XDR display for HDR review away from the suite. Projects that need more than 32GB of memory, fast Thunderbolt 5 RAIDs or three external displays point to the M5 Pro version. The iMac is an all-in-one for SDR work: proxy editing, assistant editor stations, social and YouTube production, and offices that need a clean setup. For that work, the 12-core model is the better fit, as it adds the two extra Thunderbolt ports, the second external display and Ethernet as standard. Price and availability The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $1,999 ($1,899 for education) with 16GB of memory and a 1TB SSD. In Germany, Apple lists it from €2,299 including VAT. The iMac with M6 starts at $1,499 for the 10-core model and $1,699 for the 12-core model ($1,449 and $1,599 for education), and at €1,799 and €1,999 including VAT in Germany. Pre-orders open on October 28 in 35 countries and regions, and deliveries and in-store availability start on November 6. B&H and CVP do not list the new models yet. More details are in Apple’s announcements for the MacBook Pro and the iMac , and on the MacBook Pro and iMac tech specs pages. Would an M6 MacBook Pro or iMac cover your editing work, or do 32GB and Thunderbolt 4 push you to the M5 Pro? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below !
