items.title: Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions
items.summary_what: Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions: In organisations today, data has never been more available.
items.summary_why: Dashboards and performance decks exist for almost every function — sales, product, marketing, operations — and the tools to build them have never been more accessible.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: In organisations today, data has never been more available. Dashboards and performance decks exist for almost every function — sales, product, marketing, operations — and the tools to build them have never been more accessible. And yet, in weekly standups and quarterly reviews, the same thing happens constantly: someone shares the numbers, the room nods, and the meeting ends without a decision or clear direction . When that happens, the data usually takes the blame. The numbers weren’t granular enough, the dataset wasn’t complete, we need more information before we can act. But the data is almost never the problem. The reality is that nobody designed it to deliver insights. The chart was built from what was available, not from the question that needed answering. The audience was assumed rather than understood, and what should actually change as a result of seeing this data — that question — was never asked at all. Data visualisation and UX are solving the same underlying problem: both are trying to move the right information to the right person in a way that changes something. The vocabulary is different, but the underlying challenge is identical, and the moment you start treating them as complementary disciplines is the moment dashboards stop being a passive collection of charts and start doing something functional . For designers who work with data, analysts who present to non-technical audiences, and marketers who need their numbers to do more than sit in a slide, this read is for you. The Chart Was Never The Whole Story In 1973, the statistician Francis Anscombe (PDF) published a paper that made a quiet but clarifying point. He constructed four datasets that are statistically identical: same mean, same variance, same correlation coefficient, and same regression line. Run the numbers on any of them, and they are identical. Plot them, and they could not be more different. Anscombe’s lesson to statisticians was about diagnosis: visualisation reveals the operational truth that raw numbers conceal . But visualisation isn’t just diagnostic; it is also communicative . The form you choose is where understanding either emerges or gets lost in the noise. Does your audience walk away with numbers, or with a story they’ll quote and talk about? One of the most striking examples is Visual Capitalist’s History of Pandemics . Instead of burying the reader in a massive data table of casualty counts, it maps the death toll of major historical pandemics using a proportional bubble layout on a single timeline. Before your brain reads a single number, your visual system grasps the sheer scale of the Black Death relative to everything else on the page. The right visualisation does not just plot the data but makes the story impossible to miss. Edward Tufte codified a foundational principle for the craft with his data-ink ratio : every mark on a chart should serve the data, not decorate it. It remains a widely used framework in data visualisation, anchored in the assumption that clarity and visual hygiene are the goal. For a chart in isolation, that holds. But a chart is never read in isolation: it’s read by a person, in a specific context , under specific pressure . Strip a chart down to its cleanest form, and you might be removing the exact layer of context a decision-maker needs. Simplicity isn’t the goal in itself; appropriate complexity is. Data is a message, and the right amount of signal depends entirely on who’s receiving it. Which leads to the core principle of data UX: roughly 80% of the work that determines whether a dashboard succeeds happens before you ever draw a chart. That dependency is the thread the rest of this piece pulls on. The 80% That Happens Before The Chart The high-leverage 80% almost never happens on screen. It happens upstream: before a tool is opened, before a dataset is pulled, before a single design choice is made. It comes down to three questions, and once they become habitual, they change what you notice, what you ask, and what you push back on at the outset of every project. Context: What are we trying to show with this data? This is where you define what the visualisations actually need to serve before you touch any raw data. Writing down the precise operational questions, specifically enough to determine what gets pulled and what gets filtered, is what produces a dashboard that helps with decision-making. Audience: Who is this for, and how do they think? This is the empathy step. Knowing who’s in the room, what they’re accountable for, and how they engage with data determines how much complexity the visualisation can carry, and how it should be presented. Insight: What should change once this data lands? A decision, a new direction, a shift in understanding. If the intended strategic outcome isn’t clear during the design phase, it will remain invisible once the dashboard goes live. Context: What Are We Trying To Show With This Data? Most data-heavy projects start backward: teams pull whatever metrics their internal analytics tools already track and build visualisations around them, while the question the data was supposed to answer either gets assumed or never gets asked. This happens simply because we anchor on the data in front of us as the boundary of what’s possible. Defining a goal first sounds obvious, but in practice, it rarely happens with the necessary clarity. “Show me how the product is performing” is not a goal; “Identify which features drive retention among users who signed up in Q1” is, as it includes three things the first doesn’t: a metric , a population , and an implied action . That specificity is what converts an open-ended exploration into a constrained, answerable design problem. Which one you start from determines everything that follows: what you include, what comparisons matter, and what you leave out entirely. Starting with available data produces a dashboard that answers no particular question, because it was never built for one — every number is present, none of them pointed anywhere. Starting with the operational question does the reverse: every element on the screen earns its place, because each one is there to help answer it. For example, consider a UX team trying to fix a leaky checkout flow for an e-commerce website. A data-first approach pulls everything available, from clicks to scroll depth and device types, yielding a massive dashboard that leaves everyone asking, “Okay, but what do we actually change?” A context-first approach starts with a constraint: “At which step of the checkout do users drop off?” By filtering out 90% of the noise, the team builds a simple funnel chart, instantly spots a bottleneck on the payment screen, and knows exactly what to redesign. Audience: Who Is This For, And How Do They Think? Designing for an audience comes down to two things: accountability and familiarity. Familiarity is about data literacy. Do they read charts instinctively, or does a complex visualisation create friction? Handing a dense, multi-layered dashboard to a Head of Sales and a senior analyst is like giving the same map to someone who navigates by landmarks and someone who reads grid coordinates. The data is accurate, but it is only functional for one of them. Accountability dictates how that complexity must be presented. A chart showing a 12% decline carries vastly different weight for the executive responsible for that number versus the analyst simply reporting it. Understanding your audience means grasping this relationship; data is never processed neutrally when your performance is on the line. Together, familiarity and accountability decide one practical thing: how much you can put in front of someone. In data visualisation, simplicity is not a fixed virtue — the right level of it is contingent on who is reading, and what they need to do. An analyst relies on a high-density environment to conduct diagnostic discovery. By isolating individual behaviour nodes and mapping out raw user flows, they interrogate the data at its atomic level to uncover the hidden insights and underperforming spend that will shape future campaigns. An executive, by contrast, requires a highly synthesised translation of that data to immediately identify what is driving commercial growth. Tailoring a dashboard to your audience means adjusting the density dial, delivering maximum signal with appropriate complexity for the specific brain in the room. Insight: What Should Change Once This Data Lands? Most data projects operate on the comfortable assumption that if a chart is accurate and clear, the insight will take care of itself. In reality, information and insight are entirely different states. Information is what the data shows, whereas insight is the specific decision , shift in understanding, or course correction someone makes as a result of seeing it. If the intended business change isn’t defined before the design begins, a dashboard will default to passive reporting rather than driving action. Marketing and engineering teams experience the danger of this gap whenever a core business metric suddenly plummets. A dashboard built for information simply sounds the alarm, showing a chart that tracks a sharp 15% drop in booking rates. Because the data lacks depth, leadership defaults to panic: they immediately call the UX design team, assuming the app is broken or the checkout flow is flawed. Because the data doesn’t pinpoint the core of the problem, it triggers a costly, misplaced fire drill. A dashboard built for insight isolates the variables required to make an informed decision. Instead of a single, flat booking metric, the visualisation maps the drop against traffic sources and campaign launches — instantly revealing that while app performance and core user conversion are perfectly stable, the sitewide rate was artificially diluted by a massive influx of low-intent click traffic from a newly scaled campaign. The team doesn’t waste time redesigning a functioning app; they get the exact insight needed to pause the underperforming marketing campaign and adjust their acquisition strategy. Every visualisation implies a next step, even if that step is “nothing needs to change right now.” The question is whether the design makes that implication clear enough for the viewer to recognise it. From Questions To Dashboard: A Project Walk-through My aha moment in data visualisation happened during a project for a client-facing B2B SaaS platform focused on enterprise talent management and competency tracking in Pegasystems skills. The platform captured a massive footprint of daily telemetry, and the brief arrived open-ended: “We have an immense archive of user activity, now we need to present it to enterprise teams.” We could very easily have charted everything that was captured, but we wouldn’t be doing end users any favours if they just ended up looking at a data graveyard. My responsibility immediately moved beyond pure interface craftsmanship; it became about architecting a highly practical tool for real people who would open this dashboard routinely and need it to tell them an honest, immediate story about their workflows. Here is how the project actually went. Context The client believed this massive pool of data could help their users perform better, and wanted an interface that finally enabled that growth. Translating that broad ambition into tangible visualisations required defining the practical mechanics of performance. What variables indicate advancement vs passive usage? What does “perform better” actually mean? How do you measure it? An obvious candidate was time spent by product. Every platform tracks it. It is easy to show, and it feels meaningful. But time spent is a proxy; it tells you someone was there, not whether they got anything out of it. The more meaningful signals were competency scores by area, certification completion rates, and historical performance trajectories. Integrating time-spent data alongside these performance metrics added a useful layer of interpretation, helping us surface which modules users were underutilising and whether that directly correlated with lagging scores. Time spent became a supporting signal in the larger story. The second question was about the appropriate level of granularity . An identical metric carries completely different weight depending on who is looking at it. An individual contributor tracking their own completion rate needs to know if they are pacing correctly, whereas a manager reviewing a team aggregate needs to know precisely who requires immediate support. This distinction shaped every subsequent data-exposure and filtering decision. Defining that structural story early determined exactly what to show, and to whom. Audience The most straightforward approach to this design would have been predictable: use the same charts, but offer an individual view and an aggregated team view. Far too many dashboards rely on this shortcut, subtly tweaking the scale of identical data visualisations and labelling it “personalisation.” An authentic analysis of the audience reveals a much deeper rift. Frontline team leads and individual contributors required distinct narrative structures and design principles. Having used e-learning platforms myself, I remember the frustration of opening a tool without a clear sense of my current standing, core strengths, or slipping metrics. That personal experience directly guided the individual contributor workspace; it needed to act as a highly tailored, self-directed mirror that was granular, honest, and personal. Conversely, the manager’s interface had to bypass individual milestones initially to provide a macro pulse check on team vulnerabilities. It was designed around a different operational reality: how is the group progressing, and where are the consistent gaps? The view prioritised the aggregate picture first, while retaining an intuitive path to drill down into tactical day-to-day coordination when needed. Insight Our insight strategy was locked in during the early conceptual phase, long before wireframing a single chart. We intentionally abandoned the idea of building a dense, passive data log and focused on pacing the narrative arc. For individual contributors, the core value was self-direction, ensuring they could glance at the interface on a Monday morning and immediately derive a clear priority list for the week ahead. For managers, the goal was to fundamentally shift the timing of operational conversations, providing them with the necessary baseline to intervene before a skill gap evolved into a critical project failure. The visualisations needed to surface the exact moments when a human check-in would be useful, shifting their workflow from reactive post-mortems to proactive guidance. The comparison tool was the highlight nobody had asked for. A manager dashboard and an individual dashboard are easy to anticipate. What is harder to land is: what if a manager wants to compare two specific team members against the same metrics, side by side? That view came from a design assumption, and it turned out to be the feature that resonated most. The decisions that mattered most in this project weren’t in the initial brief — capturing data they hadn’t thought to request, and structuring it to answer questions they had not previously known how to articulate, which is the core differentiator of a user-centric data strategy. Designing The Mental Model Early The choice of visualisation layout must follow the geometric nature of the data itself. For this project, the core design problem was enabling an individual user to answer a specific question at a single glance: across eight distinct competency areas, where are my relative strengths and gaps? To solve this, we mapped the data using a radar chart. By organising multiple variables across axes radiating from a central point using polar coordinates, the interface connects the data points to form a single, unified shape. An even, balanced polygon instantly signals well-rounded proficiency, while a sharply skewed shape draws the eye immediately to an outlier area. While a traditional linear bar chart would have forced the viewer to scan eight individual bars and mentally calculate the variance, a concentric, radial layout segments the data layers to make progress tracking and skill gaps immediately readable. When all dimensions share an identical scale and scoring method, the radar chart is not an unconventional aesthetic choice — it is the most functional tool for multi-dimensional analysis. The colour system was the other decision made early, and I mean early. During the branding exercise, each of the three products was assigned a colour. That colour did not stay in the brand guidelines. It was built into the data model from the beginning, running consistently across every chart, every filter, every breakdown. By the time a user landed on the dashboard for the first time, the mental model was already in place. They had not been taught the language. They already knew it. What Changed The shift from passive information to active insight showed up first in how the dashboard was actually used. Following the deployment of the personalised dashboards and side-by-side team comparison tools, weekly active engagement on the platform’s analytics features rose noticeably, per internally reported figures. Managers were no longer opening the tool once a month to pull static reports. They were using it every Monday morning to actively plan their week. Revenue and user growth also moved in the right direction over the following two quarters, though — as with most single-project outcomes — it’s hard to isolate the dashboard’s exact contribution from everything else that changed at the same time. The client reported churn across the platform falling to one of its lowest points on record. The clearest evidence of impact came from qualitative feedback. Managers reported that instead of using data to dissect a ‘bad’ month after the fact, the visualisations allowed them to instantly spot slipping performance and schedule a quick supportive catch-up before it turned into a real gap. Closing Data design reaches its full potential when visual presentation is treated as an upstream architectural choice rather than a downstream formatting step. Bringing structured UX thinking to data turns visualisations into active decision-making engines, ensuring every chart, report, and metric directly serves a human purpose: Upstream framing: Grounding every visual choice in a specific operational question rather than defaulting to available metrics. Calibrated density: Tuning the level of complexity directly to the literacy and accountability of the specific reader. Decision-driven insight: Structuring data to reveal strategic outcomes rather than isolated stats, turning visual signals into immediate operational momentum. The next time you are tasked with creating a data visualisation — whether it is an enterprise dashboard, an executive report, or a public-facing infographic — step away from the design canvas and BI tools. Focus your initial effort on the human decisions behind the screen. Only then will your data stop being a passive log of the past and start driving the direction of the future.

Here’s what you need to know about the AI and non-AI selling points for this new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6. Apple’s New MacBook Pro with M6 Now powered by the M6 chip, this new line of Apple MacBook Pros is set to deliver a strong mix of performance, powerful on-device AI, faster connectivity, improved battery life, and other specs. “The 14-inch MacBook Pro is the pro laptop of choice for a wide range of users — from college students, to business professionals across every industry, to multidisciplinary creators doing it all on one device. With the powerful M6 chip, we’re taking performance to the next level, with a boost in CPU speed and graphics and even more powerful capabilities for on-device AI. With its amazing battery life, remarkable Liquid Retina XDR display, and even faster connectivity, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 delivers a fantastic combination of performance, capability, and value.” - Shelly Goldberg, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering This latest MacBook Pro model is being targeted more for a wider range of users who might be most interested in using AI workflows for their work and research, as Apple multiple times seems to be focusing its exploits on college students and business professionals, and less on its usual bread and butter of industry creatives. How’s It Stack Up for Film and Video So, there have traditionally been many reasons filmmakers and video professionals might want to invest in the latest generation of Apple MacBook Pro for their film and video work. You've got people who use laptops for video editing. Whether that's for their home station or for those looking to edit on location or on the go. Some also work in pre-pro or management and want a top-of-the-line laptop for handling emails, scripts, storyboards, etc., on set or while managing complex shoots. Regardless of your needs, though, this new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 should hit some new highs as, alongside its AI powers of 11x faster graphics and 13x faster AI performance, it will also still feature the latest from Apple with its Liquid Retina XDR display with a nano-texture option, a 12MP Center Stage camera, an immersive six-speaker sound system, and a wide array of ports. Price and Availability Overall, we’ll leave it to you to decide how you want to work, or not work, with these next-generation laptops and computers from Apple and its competition, all of which, for better or worse, are gearing up for AI workflows. This new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is powered for AI, but it can still do all its usual tricks, plus offer boosted battery life and other improvements with the latest macOS. If you’d like to find out more, here are the full specs and purchase options. Apple M6 12-Core Chip 16GB Unified RAM | 1TB SSD 14" 3024 x 1964 Liquid Retina XDR Screen 12-Core GPU | Neural Accelerators Dual 16-Core Neural Engine Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) | Bluetooth 6 Thunderbolt 4 | HDMI | MagSafe 3 SDXC Slot | 12MP Center Stage Camera Magic Keyboard | FT Trackpad | Touch ID macOS with Apple Intelligence Apple 14" MacBook Pro Now with the M6 chip, the Apple 14" MacBook Pro delivers even more performance, powerful on-device AI capabilities, and faster connectivity for college students, business professionals, creators, and more. items.title: Photographers are vibe coding 20-year-old DSLR cameras to look and shoot more like film
items.summary_what: Photographers are vibe coding 20-year-old DSLR cameras to look and shoot more like film: I’ve started to notice an unusual trend popping up in my social media feed: Photographers are giving new life to decades-old DSLRs by adding custom firmware that gives the old cameras different film stocks to...
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Backup existing camera profiles and format media before applying firmware from the official support site.
items.raw_content: I’ve started to notice an unusual trend popping up in my social media feed: Photographers are giving new life to decades-old DSLRs by adding custom firmware that gives the old cameras different film stocks to choose from. Photographers using custom firmware for cameras isn’t particularly new – firmware hacks date back well over a decade to mods like the Canon Hack Development Kit and the reverse-engineered Magic Lantern software for Canon DSLRs. But lately, across Instagram and Reddit, photographers have been sharing “hacked” DSLRs loaded with new software that gives the old cameras the option to choose from different film-inspired looks directly on the camera. In many cases, the custom firmware is vibe-coded, built with coding assistance from artificial intelligence. Using AI to make photos look like film feels both like an oxymoron and like the most 2026 thing ever. And yet, as a collector of old cameras and someone who bought my current camera (a Fujifilm) specifically for the film simulations, the idea of bringing new life to an old DSLR is intriguing. Custom firmware carries the risk of potentially bricking the camera and, in many cases, could void the warranty on a newer camera. Which is likely why the vibe coding trend seems to be drawn to older cameras, like the 2005 Canon EOS 5D – bricking an old DSLR that doesn’t cost much and is already well out of warranty comes with less of a risk. That and, with the custom firmware designed for an old-school look, using an older camera just makes sense. One photographer on Reddit shared a beta vibe-coded hack called Soup Engine for the Canon EOS 5D that builds on Magic Lantern to give the camera 13 different looks inspired by film stocks. The looks are applied to JPEGs, while the RAW file is untouched. In another hack, software company Latent Studios is working on firmware that puts the company’s film-inspired desktop RAW photo editor into the Canon EOS 5D and 5D Mark II . But beyond the look of the photos themselves, the software also locks photographers into a “roll” for that look. A post shared by Habib Saleh (@habibsfoto) A photo posted by Photographer Florin Kirtescu developed a similar hack for the Canon EOS 6D , built from Magic Lantern , that adds film-inspired looks, including color and lab-like adjustments for pushing and pulling and correcting for light sources. The firmware, called Film Roll, also limits photographers to rolls of 12, 24, or 36 shots. The software lives on the SD card, so photographers can theoretically pull the card out and use a different one (or format the card) for the camera to function normally again. While those hacks use Canon DSLRs, other photographers on Reddit have reported trying hacked firmware with other camera brands. The Phoblographer's Chris Gampat hacked an old Sony A7 to bring back the PlayMemories App support. A post shared by Massimo 🫧 (@mv.nyc) A photo posted by Locking the camera into a color preset for the length of a typical roll of film reminds me of another trend: the screen-free camera . Some screen-free cameras have similar tools that are designed with the limitations of film. The Fujifilm X Half’s film mode , for example, won’t show creators the files or allow for swapping the film simulation until after a roll is finished and “developed.” Truly screenless cameras like the Flashback One35 V2 are also based around the concept of digital “rolls.” The Fujifilm X Half has a film mode that locks photographers into a "roll" with one silm simulation (Image credit: Future / Gareth Bevan) Beyond the older CCD sensors and look of older DSLRs, the creators behind some of the hacks are also drawn to 21-year-old DSLRs because the slower performance of much older tech feels closer to film than modern cameras. Personally, I wouldn’t even consider a firmware update that wasn’t sanctioned by the manufacturer itself on a modern camera. But on a camera that was otherwise sitting on a shelf and not getting any use? The idea is far more intriguing. You may also like Explore the best DSLRs , or take a look at the best screen-free cameras .

items.title: Feiyu Pocket 4 Announced – 1/1.55-Inch Sensor, 4K60, 111GB Built-In Storage
items.summary_what: Feiyu Pocket 4 Announced – 1/1.55-Inch Sensor, 4K60, 111GB Built-In Storage: FeiyuTech has launched the Feiyu Pocket 4, its new three-axis gimbal camera and the first update to the line since the Pocket 3.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Backup existing camera profiles and format media before applying firmware from the official support site.
items.raw_content: FeiyuTech has launched the Feiyu Pocket 4, its new three-axis gimbal camera and the first update to the line since the Pocket 3. The camera gets a much larger sensor than its predecessor, a 2.64-inch touchscreen that slides down to start shooting and up to cover the lens, and 111GB of internal storage. At $299, it costs a lot less than DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4, but the spec sheet also shows where the money was saved. The Feiyu Pocket 4 uses a 1/1.55-inch CMOS sensor with 50 megapixels behind a fixed-focus 110° lens at f/2.2. It records UHD 4K up to 60fps, 2.7K up to 60fps, and 1080p up to 120fps as H.264 or HEVC in an MP4 container, with a maximum bitrate of 80 Mbps. Stills go up to 8192 x 6144 pixels. A three-axis mechanical gimbal with up to 450° of pan travel stabilizes the image, and AI face and subject tracking work together with gesture control. The camera has 128GB of eMMC storage (about 111GB available to the user) and no microSD slot, and it weighs about 205g / 7.2oz. FeiyuTech sells the camera directly for $299, or $379 in a Creator Kit. We last covered FeiyuTech’s pocket cameras when the company introduced the Pocket 2 and Pocket 2S in 2021. Since then, this category has changed a lot. DJI released the Osmo Pocket 4 in April and the dual-lens Osmo Pocket 4P in July, and pocket gimbal cameras are now a major part of the market. Our analysis of how DJI and Insta360 now ship more cameras than the mirrorless industry gives the context. The Pocket 4 is FeiyuTech’s attempt to compete in this segment on price. Credit: FeiyuTech A sliding screen in place of a lens cap The most unusual part of the Pocket 4 is its mechanical design. The 2.64-inch touchscreen (480 x 480 pixels) sits on a sliding frame. Slide it down, and the camera powers on and is ready to shoot. According to FeiyuTech’s launch blog post , magnetic sensing detects the movement. Slide it up one step, and the gimbal motors lock. A second step extends a wraparound cover that encloses the camera head, so no separate case or clamp is necessary for transport. The square screen is also how FeiyuTech handles framing. The camera natively shoots 4:3, and the user can select 16:9 or vertical 9:16 on the touchscreen without physically turning the camera. According to the manual, vertical video goes up to 3K. The user can also rotate the camera 90° to enter the vertical mode. The body is made of aluminum-magnesium alloy and plastic, and it measures 140.5 x 52 x 31.7mm / 5.53 x 2.05 x 1.25in when folded. The Pocket 4 is not waterproof. Credit: FeiyuTech Sensor, lens and recording formats On paper, the 1/1.55-inch sensor is a large improvement over the Feiyu Pocket 3, which has a 1/2.3-inch, 12-megapixel sensor. It is still smaller than the 1-inch sensor in DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4. The 110° lens is wide for a vlogging camera, and the specifications list it as fixed focus. FeiyuTech’s FAQ states plainly that the Pocket 4 does not support autofocus. Thus, close-up product shots or face-to-camera recording at arm’s length can depend on the depth of field of the small sensor, not on a focus system. Video options include 4K at 24, 25, 30, 48, 50, and 60fps, 2.7K (2720 x 1520) at the same frame rates, and 1080p at up to 120fps. A separate slow-motion mode records at 2x or 4x in HD or Full HD. Time-lapse (static, dynamic, and motion), panorama, and a night mode are also available. ISO goes from 100 to 3200, and the electronic shutter goes from 16 seconds to 1/8000s. Users can switch between auto and manual exposure, select average or spot metering, and set flicker reduction to 50Hz or 60Hz. FeiyuTech does not list a log profile, a 10-bit mode, or an HDR mode on the product page or in the manual. The camera menu has a color option, but the company does not say what it includes. Photos are saved as JPG, and the product page also lists JPG+DNG. The maximum video bitrate of 80 Mbps is less than half of the 180 Mbps that DJI specifies for the Osmo Pocket 4. Tracking, gestures and gimbal control The mechanical ranges of the three-axis gimbal are −100° to +350° on pan, −185° to +134.5° on tilt, and −90° to +229.5° on roll, with a maximum controllable speed of 180° per second. The follow modes are: all follow, pan and tilt follow, and pan follow, and users can set the pan speed to slow, default, or quick. A five-way joystick controls the pan and tilt axes, and a double-tap switches it to digital zoom. Face tracking and subject tracking run on the camera itself; the user taps the subject on the touchscreen to select it. On the Pocket 3, tracking required the Feiyu Cam app. Gesture control has four commands: an OK sign starts or stops tracking, an open palm takes a photo or starts recording, a double L shape sets a custom composition, and a double thumbs-up switches gesture control off. The Feiyu Cam app ( iOS 13 or later, Android 6.0 or later) connects over 5GHz Wi-Fi and gives remote control, live preview, file transfer, and gimbal control through the phone’s motion sensors. Credit: FeiyuTech Storage, battery and connectivity The 111GB of user storage replaces the memory card completely. FeiyuTech says this holds approximately 875 minutes of Full HD video. At the maximum bitrate of 80 Mbps, the same storage holds roughly three hours of 4K footage. Users who shoot a full day of 4K must offload during the day. Files transfer over USB-C to a computer, directly to some phones over USB-C, or over Wi-Fi to the app. The Pocket 4 also works as a UVC webcam over USB-C. Power comes from an internal 1300mAh, 7.4V lithium-ion battery. FeiyuTech gives recording times of up to 2.5 hours at 1080p30, 1.8 hours at 4K30, and 1.5 hours at 4K60, measured at 25°C. Audio comes from the built-in microphone as 48kHz AAC. In FeiyuTech’s comparison table, it lists an external microphone as not supported for the Pocket 4, while the Pocket 3 supports one with a dedicated adapter. The Creator Kit includes a “Microphone & Battery Handle”, but FeiyuTech has not yet published specifications for this accessory. The camera also has a 1/4-inch thread on the base. How it compares with the DJI Osmo Pocket 4 The DJI Osmo Pocket 4 has a 1-inch sensor, 4K at up to 240fps, 10-bit D-Log ( a later firmware update extended it to slow motion), autofocus, 107GB internal storage plus a microSD slot, direct DJI Mic pairing, and timecode. It weighs 190.5g. In Europe, it started at €479 at launch. The Feiyu Pocket 4 is heavier and has no log profile, autofocus, external audio input, or card slot. Its advantages are the larger screen, the integrated lens cover, the larger internal storage, and the lower price. For readers who use a pocket gimbal camera as a B-camera in a professional production, the missing log profile and fixed focus are the main limitations. For travel and vlogging users who shoot mostly 8-bit footage for social media, the Feiyu Pocket 4 is a less expensive choice. Price and availability The Feiyu Pocket 4 is available now from the FeiyuTech online store . The Standard Kit costs $299 and includes the camera, a carrying bag, a USB-C to USB-C cable, a USB-A to USB-C adapter, a wrist strap, and the manual. The Creator Kit costs $379 and adds the Microphone & Battery Handle and a tripod. A portable bag ($49) and an adjustable extension pole ($39) are available separately. FeiyuTech ships from local warehouses in the US, Canada, the UK, and Germany, with free shipping to these regions. At the time of writing, B&H does not list the Pocket 4, and FeiyuTech has not published a euro price. Is the Feiyu Pocket 4’s sliding cover and large internal storage enough to choose it over a DJI Osmo Pocket 4, or are log recording and autofocus necessary for you? Let us know in the comments below!

items.title: Who Was Under the Mask? Who Played Ghostface in the Original 'Scream'?
items.summary_what: Who Was Under the Mask? Who Played Ghostface in the Original 'Scream'?. Everyone knows the movie reveal.
items.summary_why: Provides practical business, lighting, or cinematography guidance for commercial freelancers.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: Yeah, yeah. Everyone knows the movie reveal. Billy and Stu are both mad killers, and the mystery is solved—there were two Ghostfaces all along. But that's only the story answer. The production answer is more interesting. Scream turns 30 this December. It opened on December 20, 1996. Horror icon Matthew Lillard took the original on the road in September, hosting screenings and fan Q&As in Dallas, Houston, and Austin, and Paramount announced a re-release of the original Scream in select theaters on October 30. For the plot and the production, Ghostface was a team effort. It required two characters, a couple of stunt performers, a voice actor hidden on set, and a store-bought mask. We'll walk through who did what, and what filmmakers can learn from a villain built in bits. - YouTube www.youtube.com The Story Answer: Billy and Stu Inside the movie, the killers are Skeet Ulrich's Billy Loomis and Lillard's Stu Macher, a couple of crazy kids. A year before the movie starts, they killed Sidney's mother, Maureen, whose affair with Billy's father had split up his parents. The twist depends on Ghostface being two ordinary teenagers, not a supernatural force. That's also what let the production spread the physical role across multiple people without anyone noticing. We love having an in-world story reason for any inconsistencies, not that they're noticeable. The Bodies Under the Robe: The Stunt Performers In most slashers, the person under the mask isn't the actor you see when it comes off. Most of the time, the slasher is engaging in a lot of stunts, and in a film a stunt can mean almost anything—a fall, a jump, etc. So if the face isn't seen, it's easier to go with stunt safety and specialized movement via a stunt performer rather than Ulrich or Lillard. That keeps the cast's schedules free, too. IMDb's full credits list Lee Waddell as Ghostface and Dane Farwell as a Ghostface stunt performer, both uncredited on screen. Anthony Cecere is listed as stunt coordinator and also as a Ghostface performer. Deep Focus Review gives Farwell the lion's share of the on-screen Ghostface work and even says Wes Craven put on the costume himself for parts of the opening. According to Halloween Daily News , Waddell was the first in the costume. Waddell told the outlet: "I was like, ‘Wes, tell me about this character,’ because I have wardrobe on, I have the mask on, and we’re getting ready to start shooting. And he goes, ‘He moves like a phantom. Very swift with how he moves, and he moves with authority.’" Unfortunately, the mask left him with almost no sight while he chased Drew Barrymore over soaked grass. Craven filmed the chase at a higher frame rate, so it would play back in slow motion and drag out the suspense. - YouTube www.youtube.com The Voice: Roger L. Jackson The most famous Ghostface performance belongs to someone the audience never sees. He wasn't seen by the cast, either, although he was on set. That person is voice actor Roger Jackson. Jackson told The Hollywood Reporter : "It was an open casting. I heard some people saying, 'My agent told me they’re looking for the new Freddy Krueger,' and I read the sides and I said, 'This doesn’t feel like Freddy Krueger.' This is somebody who has to be interesting and kind of flirty and keep her on the phone, make her interested. I subsequently found out that this was to play the scene with Drew Barrymore because she didn’t want the script person just feeding her lines. So they cast in the Bay Area for that and then they were going to dub it later in Los Angeles. But Wes Craven liked what I was doing and they decided to keep me. Jackson spoke his lines in real time from a separate room, and the production deliberately kept him out of the actors' sight. Editor Patrick Lussier recalled that none of the calls were added in post. Jackson delivered every one during takes. "All those phone calls were done live," Lussier told The Hollywood Reporter. "They were tapped into a phone, but Drew and none of the actors could see him. They didn't know what he looked like." Even in the opening, Jackson was hiding outside. Which means the voice of the killer was literally lurking outside the house, watching the victim. It's a perfect image for how Craven blurred performance and menace. "I remember hearing that they had somebody reading for Drew off camera," Ulrich told the outlet. "There were talks that he was hidden away, but it never really crossed our minds. Afterward, it's really wild to realize what Wes did and how great a decision that was. To have the wherewithal to give her something visceral to react to was very smart." Lussier told Bloody Disgusting that Craven auditioned a second voice late in the edit as a gut check, and Jackson's won out. 'Scream' Credit: Dimension Films The Face: A Halloween Mask Nobody Wanted at First The final "performer" is the mask itself, which is of course iconic. Deep Focus Review explains that Fun World was already selling the mask before the movie existed. Designer Brigitte Sleiertin modeled it on a cartoon ghost from a 1933 Betty Boop short (rather than on Edvard Munch's painting The Scream , despite what many think). The company signed off on the license, betting the film would boost sales. Producer Marianne Maddalena told Fangoria : "Well, it's just a thrill to me because I knew when I first laid eyes on that mask that it was special and magical. I'm fascinated with the origins and if you go to my website you can see some of the earliest designs of what would become the mask and it's still a mystery to uncover just who exactly came up with the original design and how it ultimately ended up being used in Scream and became this cultural icon." In Maddalena's telling, Craven originally turned the mask down because he wanted an original design. The team went back for it weeks later, after nothing else clicked. Filmmakers, you don't need a famous face behind the mask. You need a clear note on how the killer moves, a voice that gets under your actors' skin, and a design that reads instantly in silhouette.

items.title: Sigma 50mm F1.4 CL DG Contemporary Announced – 375g All-Metal Prime, New RDD Autofocus, Intentional Softness
items.summary_what: Sigma 50mm F1.4 CL DG Contemporary Announced – 375g All-Metal Prime, New RDD Autofocus, Intentional Softness: Sigma has announced the 50mm F1.4 CL DG | Contemporary, a compact full-frame prime that deliberately does not chase maximum sharpness.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Backup existing camera profiles and format media before applying firmware from the official support site.
items.raw_content: Sigma has announced the 50mm F1.4 CL DG | Contemporary, a compact full-frame prime that deliberately does not chase maximum sharpness. Its aberrations are tuned by simulation for a gentle softness in the focal plane, and a newly developed ring-shaped autofocus motor keeps the all-metal barrel short. It also starts a new “CL” lineage inside Sigma’s I series. But is a lens built for character also a good match for video? The Sigma 50mm F1.4 CL DG | Contemporary is a full-frame mirrorless lens for L-Mount and Sony E-mount. It uses 9 elements in 6 groups (one FLD and three aspherical elements), a 14-blade rounded diaphragm and a new RDD (Rotary Direct Drive) autofocus actuator. The lens measures ø64.7 x 54.0mm / ø2.5 x 2.1in on L-Mount and ø64.7 x 56.0mm / ø2.5 x 2.2in on Sony E, weighs 375g / 13.2oz on both mounts and takes 52mm filters. It has an aperture ring, a distance scale with a depth-of-field scale, and a dust- and splash-resistant build. Sigma plans to launch the lens in early spring 2027. Pricing has not been announced yet. A new branch of the I series Sigma introduced the I series of “Premium Compact Primes” in late 2020, when three new Contemporary primes for L-Mount and Sony E joined the 45mm F2.8. The line grew over the following years, including the 50mm F2 DG DN Contemporary in 2023 . All of these lenses share the all-metal body, knurled rings, aperture ring and magnetic metal lens cap. The CL keeps those elements and adds a second, faster 50mm to the series. The CL is not a smaller version of the 50mm F1.4 DG DN | Art . The Art lens is designed for maximum resolution and weighs 670g / 23.6oz on L-Mount. The CL weighs 375g / 13.2oz and, according to Sigma, has a different design goal: its aberrations are “intentionally controlled” to give a soft rendering of texture in the in-focus plane, smooth bokeh, and a background that separates the subject. Sigma says the lens shows its best bokeh and three-dimensionality wide open at F1.4, and it names portraits and snapshots as the main uses. The MTF charts on Sigma’s product page are for the lens wide open. Sigma also says that the placement of the aspherical elements suppresses ghosting, which it calls difficult to avoid in small, light lenses. The Sigma 50mm F1.4 CL DG Contemporary lens. Image credit: Sigma The RDD autofocus actuator To keep the barrel short, Sigma uses whole-lens extension focusing instead of an inner focus design. This means that the motor must move a heavier focus group. For this, Sigma developed the RDD actuator. It uses the same coil-and-magnet principle as the company’s HLA (High-response Linear Actuator), but arranges the coils and magnets in a circle around the barrel. According to Sigma, this gives high torque without a large increase in lens diameter. Because RDD drives the optics directly, the lens changes to manual focus temporarily when you turn the focus ring during autofocus operation. There is no AF/MF switch. The focus ring turns in direct sync with the focus movement, and the distance scale runs from the minimum focusing distance of 45cm / 17.8in to infinity. Maximum magnification is 1:6.8, and the minimum aperture is F16. The new RDD autofocus actuator arranges coils and magnets in a ring around the barrel, keeping the lens slim. Image credit: Sigma What it means for video shooters Sigma presents the CL as a photo lens, and its marketing does not mention video. The B&H listing states that autofocus performance is slower than an STM or HLA system and that the lens is less suited to the demands of video autofocus. Sigma does not give data on focus breathing, and it does not say whether the front of the lens moves during focusing. For manual focus work, the lens has more to offer. A focus ring with a printed distance scale that rotates in sync with the focus position gives repeatable marks for simple focus pulls. The 14-blade diaphragm keeps out-of-focus highlights round when stopped down. Sigma confirms an aperture ring, but it does not mention a de-click option. The soft rendering at F1.4 can also be a look for narrative and documentary work on small cameras, where a modern 50mm can be too clinical. Anyone who plans to use it on a gimbal or with continuous autofocus should first check how the focus mechanism behaves on their own camera. For L-Mount filmmakers, the obvious pairing is Sigma’s own Sigma FP2 , which was also just announced with 6K open gate and internal ProRes RAW. Sigma shot the official sample images for the CL on the 61MP Sigma fp L . Build, mounts and accessories The barrel, knurled hood, focus ring and aperture ring are made of metal. The lens has a dust- and splash-resistant structure, and the front element has a water- and oil-repellent coating. Sigma says that the lens is not waterproof. The L-Mount version comes in black and silver. The Sony E-mount version is listed in black only. The box contains a pouch, the LH520-04B or LH520-04S lens hood (to match the finish), a LCF-52 IV front cap, a LCF52-02 MB or MS magnetic metal lens cap and a LCR III rear cap. The lens supports Sigma’s Mount Conversion Service, and the L-Mount version works with the Sigma USB Dock UD-11 (sold separately) for firmware updates. Like all Sigma lenses, it is made in Aizu, Japan. Price and availability Sigma has not announced a price for the 50mm F1.4 CL DG | Contemporary. The company plans to launch the lens in early spring 2027 for L-Mount and Sony E-mount, and Sigma America lists it as “In Development – Pricing and Availability TBD”. B&H already has a product page for the lens, with no price yet. CVP does not list the lens at the time of writing. For more information, visit the Sigma website . Would you pick a 50mm that is designed to be soft wide open over a clinically sharp one, and would you use it for video? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

items.title: Accsoon CineView Master 4K II Introduced – DCI 4K60 Transmission, USB-C Output on Both Ends, Camera Control
items.summary_what: Accsoon CineView Master 4K II Introduced – DCI 4K60 Transmission, USB-C Output on Both Ends, Camera Control: Accsoon has introduced the CineView Master 4K II, the second generation of its tri-band 4K60 wireless video system.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Backup existing camera profiles and format media before applying firmware from the official support site.
items.raw_content: Accsoon has introduced the CineView Master 4K II, the second generation of its tri-band 4K60 wireless video system. The core transmission platform stays the same, but the receiver now gets its own USB-C video output, and the transmitter adds a dedicated port for camera control from a phone or tablet. Let’s take a look at what has changed. The CineView Master 4K II transmits DCI 4K and UHD at up to 60fps with H.265 encoding, and it operates on the 2.4GHz, 5GHz and 6GHz bands at the same time through Accsoon’s proprietary RTMS 4.0 protocol. Accsoon specifies a latency below 25ms at 1080p60 and below 35ms at 4K60 (camera latency excluded), and a range of up to 2.5km (1.55mi). Both the transmitter and the receiver now have a USB-C video output for wired monitoring on a phone or tablet, and up to 10 devices can monitor the feed at the same time. A new USB-C camera-control port on the transmitter lets crews start and stop recording and change exposure settings through the Accsoon SEE app. The transmitter-and-receiver kit costs $899. We first saw the original CineView Master 4K at IBC 2024 ( see our first look ), and we later published a full review of the CineView Master 4K . At IBC 2025, a free firmware update added full H.265 encoding up to 4K60 and raised the receiver limit from four to ten, as we reported in our article on Accsoon’s updates to the SEE app, CineView Master 4K and CineView M7 series . Accsoon positions the new model for directors, cinematographers, camera assistants and production crews who need the camera feed, and some camera controls, at different positions on set. Credit: Accsoon Camera control through the transmitter The largest functional change is camera control. A supported camera connects to a dedicated USB-C camera-control port on the transmitter, and a phone or tablet running the Accsoon SEE app then controls it. According to Accsoon, the available functions include record start/stop, touch focus, ISO, aperture, white balance, and shutter speed. Accsoon sees this as a solution for cameras on cranes, car rigs or other positions that are difficult to reach, and for operators who need to change settings without walking back to the camera. There is one restriction: camera control works only when the mobile device connects to the transmitter over Wi-Fi. It is not available through the receiver’s wired USB-C monitoring connection. Which cameras and which functions are supported depends on the model, and Accsoon keeps the current list on its camera control compatibility page . Camera control is not new in the CineView family. Accsoon added it to the lower-cost line with the CineView SE 4K and to its monitor-receivers with firmware for the CineView M7 Pro . The Master 4K II now brings the function to the top of the range. CineView Master 4K – Image credit: Accsoon The transmission platform carries over Accsoon describes the 4K60 workflow, the tri-band transmission and the RTMS 4.0 protocol as the base that the second generation keeps from the first. On paper, the transmission figures are the same as those of the original model. DCI 4K and UHD are supported up to 60fps, and H.265 encoding keeps the bitrate down. The latency and range figures come with conditions. According to Accsoon, the sub-25ms and sub-35ms latency values were measured with 1080p60 and 4K60 video respectively, both at low bitrates and without camera latency. The 2.5km range was measured with 1080p60 video at a low bitrate, in FCC-compliant operation, in an unobstructed environment with no interference. On a real set, with walls, people and other radio traffic, the range will be shorter. The press text does not list the video connections of the new model. The first-generation CineView Master 4K has HDMI and 3G-SDI inputs on the transmitter, with 4K only over HDMI and SDI limited to 1080p. Early UK retailer listings for the II show the same layout. Credit: Accsoon USB-C monitoring at both ends On the original CineView Master 4K, only the transmitter had a USB-C video output for wired monitoring on a mobile device. The CineView Master 4K II adds a USB-C video output to the receiver too. A crew can now connect a compatible phone or tablet at the camera and at the receiving station, without a separate wireless link for each device. A typical setup could be an operator with a phone as a camera-side display, and a director or client at the receiver with a tablet on a USB-C cable. Accsoon says that compatible mobile devices also charge while connected, which helps on long shooting days. Up to 10 devices can monitor the feed at the same time. Accsoon leaves the mix to the production: dedicated receivers at fixed monitoring stations, mobile devices for crew who move around the location, or a combination of both. Ecosystem, Frame.io and power The CineView Master 4K II supports Frame.io Camera to Cloud through a compatible mobile workflow. Accsoon lists compatibility with the CineView Master 4K, CineView Master 4K Lite, CineView SE 4K, CineView M7 Pro and CineView M7H Pro. Owners of first-generation receivers or Accsoon monitor-receivers can thus integrate the new transmitter into their current setup. Our article on the CineView M7 series updates has more information on the monitor side. The transmitter weighs approximately 322g (11.4oz) and the receiver approximately 320g (11.3oz), both without antennas. Power comes from NP-F batteries or an external DC input from 7.4V to 16.8V. Accsoon also offers optional V-Mount and Gold-Mount battery adapters, which are sold separately. We covered the earlier Accsoon V-Lock adapter for the CineView Master 4K when it came out. Current limitations Camera control is available only over the Wi-Fi connection to the transmitter, so the wired receiver-side connection cannot be used to change camera settings. The list of supported cameras and functions is set by Accsoon and depends on the camera model. All latency and range values are manufacturer figures measured at low bitrates under ideal conditions. Battery adapters for V-Mount and Gold-Mount are extra. Price and availability The Accsoon CineView Master 4K II transmitter-and-receiver kit costs $899. For comparison, the first-generation kit launched at $849. Accsoon has not announced an availability date or EUR pricing in the press text. At the time of writing, we did not find the CineView Master 4K II at B&H, and the CVP listings were not available to link to. For more information, please visit the Accsoon website .

items.title: GoPro Close-Up Filters for MISSION 1 Announced – PolarPro Diopters from +0.5 to +2
items.summary_what: GoPro Close-Up Filters for MISSION 1 Announced – PolarPro Diopters from +0.5 to +2: GoPro has released two close-up filter options for the MISSION 1 and MISSION 1 PRO, made by PolarPro.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: GoPro has released two close-up filter options for the MISSION 1 and MISSION 1 PRO, made by PolarPro. The diopters slide over the camera’s fixed lens and give a closer focus range with a shallower depth of field. A single +0.5 filter costs $49.99, and a set of three strengths costs $99.99. But what do these filters change on a camera with a fixed 14mm lens? The new GoPro Close-Up Filter is a single PolarPro +0.5 diopter. The Close-Up Filter Set adds +1 and +2 diopters and a travel case. According to GoPro, the filters use optical-grade, multi-coated glass and slide over the MISSION 1 or MISSION 1 PRO lens, or over an ND filter that is already on the camera. Focus is static, so there is no adjustment to make. Each strength has a fixed focus range: 50 to 150cm / 19.6 to 59in for the +0.5, 45 to 90cm / 17.7 to 35.4in for the +1, and 30 to 50cm / 11.8 to 19.6in for the +2. Both products are available now from GoPro.com. The MISSION 1 series is GoPro’s line of large-sensor action cameras with a 1-inch 50MP sensor. We covered the MISSION 1 series announcement and, more recently, the free update with a zero-lag shutter and anamorphic support . This year, GoPro was sold to Starman Optical for $285 million , and Nick Woodman wrote after the merger that the cameras are staying . New accessories for the MISSION 1 line are one sign that this is the case. GoPro Close-Up Filters for MISSION 1. Image credit: GoPro Three strengths, three working distances A diopter is a close-up lens: it moves the focus range of the camera nearer. On a fixed-lens camera with a 14mm lens, the subject must be close to get visible background blur. The diopter makes this possible because it moves the plane of focus close to the camera. GoPro positions the +0.5 as an everyday filter for vlogs, lifestyle and travel footage. Its range starts at 50cm and ends at 150cm. GoPro’s footnote says that it limits the far focus distance to 150cm so that the filter can give subject separation. Thus, a background at a large distance stays out of focus, and this is the effect that GoPro wants. The +1 gives a range of 45 to 90cm, and the +2 gives 30 to 50cm. With each step, the depth of field becomes shallower and the working distance becomes shorter. The +2 range of 30 to 50cm is a distance for tabletop shots, product shots and detail shots, not for a person who talks to the camera at arm’s length. Stabilization and limits GoPro gives one warning for the strongest filter. High-vibration activities and quick camera movements can affect video stabilization when the +2 diopter is on the camera. GoPro does not give more detail. A shallow focus range also means that a subject that moves out of the range goes soft, because the camera cannot refocus past the limits of the diopter. The compatibility list names the MISSION 1, the MISSION 1 PRO and the MISSION 1 PRO bundles (Grip Edition, Creator Edition and Ultimate Creator Edition). The press release does not list the MISSION 1 PRO ILS, the model with a Micro Four Thirds mount. At NAB 2026, we gave the MISSION 1 PRO ILS one of our CineD Best of Show awards . GoPro Close-Up Filters for MISSION 1, in three different strengths. Image credit: GoPro Price and availability The GoPro Close-Up Filter (+0.5) costs $49.99, and the GoPro Close-Up Filter Set (+0.5, +1, +2) costs $99.99. Both are available now globally from GoPro.com and are covered by PolarPro’s Adventure Assurance program. GoPro Premium and Premium+ subscribers get 20% off, but according to GoPro, this subscriber price applies only when the subscription renews. The subscription is available only in some countries. At the time of writing, B&H and CVP do not list the filters. GoPro has not published a euro price. Would you use a diopter on a MISSION 1 for vlogs and detail shots, or is the fixed focus range too limiting for you? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

items.raw_content: COMAN just launched the T1 Mini on Kickstarter, a compact carbon fiber travel tripod weighing 1.65kg/3.5 lbs and supporting payloads up to 6kg/13 lbs. It keeps the T1’s one-touch leg system and adds a bolt-style Arca-Swiss quick-release ball head, three leg angles, and a modular center column you can invert or swap. So, let’s take a closer look at it! Founded in 2010, COMAN is a Chinese manufacturer based in Zhongshan that designs and manufactures photo and video support equipment in-house. You might remember the Ulanzi & COMAN Zero Y lightweight travel tripod we talked about at IBC 2022 . The T1 Mini is COMAN’s third crowdfunding campaign, following the COMAN Go! M1 Series one-touch monopod and the COMAN Go! Series T1 tripod. According to the company, T1 users asked for a more compact, travel-friendly version that kept its core features, and the T1 Mini is the answer. The COMAN T1 Mini folded and fully extended. Image credit: COMAN COMAN T1 Mini – specifications The COMAN T1 Mini weighs 1.65kg/3.5 lbs and can take payloads up to 6kg/13 lbs. It reaches a maximum height of 1,595mm/62.8″, or 2,285mm/89.9″ with the optional PH110 Light Stand Shaft. The folded length is 533mm/20.98″, so the T1 Mini should fit in or on the side of most backpacks. The T1 Mini has interchangeable rubbera nd steel spike feet. Image credit: COMAN The T1 Mini features four-section legs, and three preset leg angles allow you to adapt to slopes, stairs, or uneven ground. The tripod also includes interchangeable rubber feet and steel spikes. It is made of 3K, 10-layer carbon fiber, 6-series aluminum alloy, and stainless steel. The panoramic ball head offers 360° pan and uses a bolt-style Arca-Swiss quick release. The T1 Mini features two ARRI-style 1/4″-20 threads at the tripod base for attaching accessories such as a monitor, microphone, light, or magic arm. Image credit: COMAN COMAN T1 Mini – one-touch leg system and center column Unlocking, extending, and locking each leg section of a traditional tripod takes time. To speed things up, the T1 Mini uses the company’s proprietary one-touch leg system: flip open the clamps, let the leg sections slide out to the desired length, and close the clamps to lock everything in place. COMAN claims a setup time of as little as 3 seconds. To keep the tripod as compact as possible when folded, COMAN replaced the traditional round center column with a Y-shaped column with a concave-triangular profile. The three legs nest into its grooves when folded, reducing total storage volume by 30%, according to the company. Image credit: COMAN The center column is also modular and can be configured in several ways: Inverted center shaft: remove the bottom hook, pull out the center shaft, reverse it, and reinstall it for low-angle, ground-level, and macro shots. PH100 Short Center Shaft: included in the box, it replaces the standard center shaft for low-angle shooting. Its 3/8″-16 mounting point also lets you use your favorite photo/video heads. PH110 Light Stand Shaft: sold separately, it extends the tripod height to 2,285mm/89.9″ and turns it into a light stand or 360° camera stand. The COMAN T1 Mini ball head. Image credit: COMAN COMAN T1 Mini – ball head and quick-release system The T1 Mini comes with a panoramic ball head that rotates 360° horizontally for panoramas. COMAN says the head uses a US-patented inverted-bowl design that keeps the folded profile compact while still offering a wide tilt range, in both landscape and portrait orientations. Instead of a traditional knob, the head uses COMAN’s in-house Arca-Swiss quick-release system with a bolt-style side latch. Sliding the latch releases the plate, so you can mount or remove your camera in about one second. The company says the clamp is compatible with 99% of Arca-Swiss plates on the market, including Peak Design-compatible plates. The optional COMAN DP59 Magnetic Arca-Swiss Mount. Image credit: COMAN Last but not least, the optional COMAN DP59 Magnetic Arca-Swiss Mount allows you to attach a smartphone magnetically to the tripod. It can also hold a smartphone next to your camera, for example, to use it as a teleprompter or for live-view monitoring. The T1 Mini is available in black, silver, and olive green. Image credit: COMAN Price and availability The COMAN T1 Mini is now available to preorder on Kickstarter, starting at $279.99 for the Black version and $299.99 for the special-edition Silver and Military Green versions. All three versions share the same specifications. The tripod ships with a soft carrying pouch, an Arca-Swiss quick-release plate, the PH100 Short Center Shaft, a dedicated adjustment wrench, and a user manual. For more information, please visit COMAN’s Kickstarter page here . We are saying this at the end of every crowdfunding-related article: be aware of the risks when backing a project on a crowdfunding platform. Please read the platform’s terms of use, and keep in mind that product delivery can be significantly delayed. Some projects may not be delivered at all. COMAN has a good track record regarding crowdfunding campaigns; their two previous Kickstarter campaigns raised over $216K for the Go! M1 Series and over $174K for the Go! Series T1, and they delivered both to backers on time. What do you think about the COMAN T1 Mini? Have you already used COMAN tripods before? Do you usually travel with a tripod, and is setup speed important to you? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

items.title: Tom Hegen explores the landscapes that are paying an invisible price for clean energy
items.summary_what: Tom Hegen explores the landscapes that are paying an invisible price for clean energy: In his new book The Mineral Age, Tom Hagen takes aerial photographs of the mineral mines essential to our transition to low-carbon living.
items.summary_why: Influences typography, UI/UX prototyping speed, and vector design production assets.
