items.raw_content: In his new book The Mineral Age, Tom Hagen takes aerial photographs of the mineral mines essential to our transition to low-carbon living. Everyone knows about the climate crisis. It's almost impossible to go a day without the news reporting on record-breaking phenomena; or, if you're unlucky, you'll experience the consequences first-hand. We all know we need to do our bit to live more sustainably, whether that's by recycling or using public transport. However, most people may be unaware of the resources enabling the world to transition to a more environmentally friendly lifestyle. These minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel, and copper, are part of a new frontier in humanity's quest to move away from fossil fuels. Because these rare earth elements are required for electric vehicles, batteries, and renewable energy infrastructure, demand is high. Photographer Tom Hegen's latest project, The Mineral Age, explores where these critical minerals come from and the environmental, social, and political consequences of extracting them. Compiled over the past six years, his book reveals the often-overlooked physical footprint of technological progress. Tom's interest in these landscapes began while photographing Germany's vast open-pit coal mines. Through this work, he became increasingly interested in humanity's quest to decarbonise its economies. "As I researched the energy transition more deeply, I realised that moving away from fossil fuels does not mean moving away from resource extraction," he explains. "Instead, we are entering a new era of mineral dependency. Many of these resources are concentrated in just a handful of countries, creating new geopolitical dependencies and vulnerabilities" While these minerals may ultimately lead to cleaner living, Tom reveals that their extraction often comes with significant environmental and social consequences which receive relatively little public attention. "This realisation became the starting point for The Mineral Age." Tom's most striking insight when putting the project together was the geographical imbalance between the consumption of these critical minerals and the impacts of their extraction. "Industrialised countries in the Global North are major consumers of minerals that are often extracted in developing regions of the Global South," he says. "This imbalance is shaped by geology, economic structures, cheaper labour, and weaker environmental regulations." He adds: "In some mining regions, environmental protections are poorly enforced, working conditions are hazardous, and local communities face serious consequences from industrial expansion. Child labour and human rights abuses also remain significant concerns in certain mining sectors." It became increasingly clear to Tom that the environmental and social costs of technological progress are often shouldered by communities which are far removed from those who ultimately benefit from it. "We tend to celebrate the promise of clean technologies without paying much attention to the landscapes being transformed to make them possible," he says. "In many ways, we are shifting part of the environmental burden of our consumption to other regions of the world, keeping the consequences largely out of sight." This isn't to say The Mineral Age argues against the shift away from fossil fuels, though. "Rather, I believe we need to acknowledge that even technologies designed to create a more sustainable future have a substantial material footprint." Tom's photographic practice is strongly research-driven, and The Mineral Age is no exception. Before travelling, he spends considerable time investigating global mineral supply chains, identifying significant mining regions, and studying the industrial processes involved. "Accessing these places is often one of the greatest challenges," he says. "Many mining operations are extremely remote, heavily restricted, or kept out of public view. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, it took me more than two years to arrange access to some of the mining sites. Every photograph in The Mineral Age was taken from an elevated perspective. Tom primarily works with heavy-lift drones carrying a high-resolution medium-format camera. "When drone operations are not possible, I photograph from helicopters or small aircraft. The aerial perspective allows me to reveal the immense scale of these industrial landscapes." The Mineral Age will contain 247 aerial photographs, which Tom believes will spark curiosity, encourage conversations, and make the complex topic of energy transition more accessible. "My intention is not to provide simple answers, but to raise awareness of the often-invisible consequences of our demand for resources," he says. "Ultimately, The Mineral Age is about the landscapes behind our modern lives, and the consequences of building the future."

items.title: Apple Creator Studio Update Announced – MotionVFX in Final Cut Pro, Generate Fill, Cinematic Mode Encoding
items.summary_what: Apple Creator Studio Update Announced – MotionVFX in Final Cut Pro, Generate Fill, Cinematic Mode Encoding: Apple has announced what it calls its most exciting update to Apple Creator Studio since the subscription bundle launched in January.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: Apple has announced what it calls its most exciting update to Apple Creator Studio since the subscription bundle launched in January. Final Cut Pro for Mac now ships with MotionVFX effects and plugins built in, the Content Hub adds stock video, and images move between Final Cut Pro and Pixelmator Pro without reimporting. Let’s take a look at what changes for editors, motion designers and anyone handling sound in post. The update arrives on the App Store in November as a free update for existing subscribers. In Final Cut Pro for Mac, MotionVFX templates, titles, transitions and graphics sit directly inside the app, together with tools for rotoscoping, tracking and color grading. The Content Hub, Apple’s library of curated stock assets, now includes video and is available inside Final Cut Pro. Editors can send any still image from the timeline to Pixelmator Pro and have the edited version update in the project automatically, and Pixelmator Pro adds Generate Fill for prompt-based image edits. Disconnecting clips from the primary storyline to place them anywhere on the timeline, in the latest Final Cut Pro update. Image credit: Apple Final Cut Pro also gets more keyframe easing options, clips that can be disconnected from the primary storyline, and 23 new transcription languages. Motion adds MotionVFX plugins for color grading, 3D camera tracking and one-click selection, plus a new Displacement filter. Compressor can now encode Cinematic mode video from the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. Logic Pro gets a redesigned Browser, a Stem Splitter that separates drums, and an intelligent assistant in beta. A subscription costs $12.99 / €12.99 per month or $129 / €129 per year. We covered the launch of Apple Creator Studio in January, when Apple first bundled Final Cut Pro, Motion, Compressor, Logic Pro, MainStage and Pixelmator Pro into one subscription. In March, Apple acquired MotionVFX , the Polish developer best known for its Final Cut Pro plugins and templates, and this update is the first time that content appears inside Apple’s own apps. It also follows Final Cut Camera 2.4 and Final Cut Pro 12.4 in September, which added aperture control for the iPhone 18 Pro and Cinematic mode refocusing in post. 23 new transcription languages in the latest update of Final Cut Pro. Image credit: Apple MotionVFX content inside Final Cut Pro According to Apple, Final Cut Pro for Mac now gives editors access to “thousands of elements” from MotionVFX. These include themed templates, graphics, titles and transitions, as well as tools for rotoscoping, tracking and color grading. Until now, MotionVFX products were separate purchases from the developer’s own store. Apple does not list which individual MotionVFX plugins are included, and the press release does not say whether the one-time-purchase version of Final Cut Pro also receives this content. Editors can tap into the Content Hub directly within Final Cut Pro and access a library of Apple-curated stock video, photos, and backgrounds to fill gaps, add polish, or spark new ideas without leaving their workflow. Image credit: Apple The Content Hub is now available inside Final Cut Pro as well. It holds Apple-curated stock video, photos and backgrounds that editors can drop into a timeline to fill gaps or build quick mockups. Apple does not give the size of the video library or the license terms in the press release, so anyone planning to use these clips in client work should check the usage conditions first. Final Cut Pro also adds generative image creation from text descriptions inside a project, with quick edits and style adjustments. Apple does not name the model behind it. Workflow changes in the timeline Apart from the new content, three changes concern day-to-day editing. Keyframe easing gets more options for finer control over animation curves. Connected clips can now be disconnected from the primary storyline and placed anywhere on the timeline, which addresses one of the long-standing habits that editors coming from track-based NLEs have had to adapt to in Final Cut Pro. Transcription adds 23 new languages, which extends caption creation and transcript-based search to more productions outside the English-speaking market. Final Cut Pro introduces more keyframe easing options for finer animation control. Image credit: Apple Pixelmator Pro round trip and Generate Fill The round trip between Final Cut Pro and Pixelmator Pro works for any image in the timeline. An editor opens the still in Pixelmator Pro, makes the changes, and the saved version replaces the original in the project with no reimport. Motion gets the same round trip, and Freeform follows in December. Final Cut Pro users can now open any image from their timeline directly in Pixelmator Pro to take advantage of advanced editing tools. Image credit: Apple Generate Fill is Pixelmator Pro’s new prompt-based editing tool. Users circle an area of the image and describe the change they want, or make a more precise selection with the existing Free Selection, Quick Selection and Magnetic Selection tools. According to Apple, Generate Fill matches the lighting, perspective and texture of the surrounding image, and the built-in Super Resolution feature upscales the generated content so it stays sharp at larger sizes. The result can be merged into an existing layer or placed on a new layer with a mask for further refinement. For editors, the obvious uses are cleaning up stills, extending backgrounds for title cards, or adapting a photo to a different aspect ratio. Motion and Compressor Motion receives its own set of built-in MotionVFX plugins, which Apple describes as tools for cinematic color grading, 3D camera tracking and one-click selection for visual effects. It also adds text-to-image generation and editing, the Pixelmator Pro round trip, the new keyframe easing options, a new Displacement filter and an interactive demo project for new users. Generate Fill, known from Adobe Photoshop already as “Generative Fill”, comes as a new tool for editing images based on a user’s description to Pixelmator Pro. Compressor now encodes Cinematic mode video recorded on the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo . Together with the Cinematic mode editing that arrived in Final Cut Pro 12.4, this completes the path from capture to delivery for that footage inside Apple’s apps. Note that Cinematic mode editing in Final Cut Pro 12.4 requires macOS 27 Golden Gate, according to Apple’s release notes. Logic Pro for sound in post Logic Pro is primarily a music app, but several of the new features are relevant for editors who handle their own sound. The Stem Splitter can now isolate, replace or rebalance drum parts without the original multitracks, which helps when a licensed track needs a quieter rhythm section under dialogue. The redesigned Browser on Mac gathers loops, instruments and effect patches in one place. A feature Apple calls music understanding, an on-device audio analysis tool, classifies and tags added sounds automatically, so users can search their own collection or drag in a loop to find matching audio. Apple also includes a Splice library in the new Browser. Logic Pro for Mac and iPad gets an all-new design featuring Liquid Glass, with translucent surfaces and deeper contrast that highlight waveforms and tracks. Image credit: Apple Logic Pro for Mac also gets a new intelligent assistant in beta, built on a combination of Apple’s own models and OpenAI. According to Apple, it can help with production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project. On the iPhone side, Voice Memo Studio Sound reduces room ambience and background noise in recordings made on supported iPhone models, with the option to continue in Logic Pro. Logic Pro also gets a new interface design with Apple’s Liquid Glass look, and a Producer Pack from salsa producer Sergio George. Keynote, Pages, Numbers and Freeform The productivity apps receive an intelligent assistant in beta, also built on Apple models and OpenAI, that works with the content of the open document. Model Context Protocol (MCP) support lets external AI agents read content, make edits and run automated actions in Keynote, Pages and Numbers. Keynote adds the Keynote Interchange Format (.keyx), an open JSON-based file format. Stock video from the Content Hub and new templates and themes come to all three apps. Freeform adds text styles and board background colors. Requirements and limitations Several of the new features have restrictions that matter for a global audience. Both intelligent assistants are available in US English only. The Logic Pro assistant requires macOS 27 Golden Gate on a Mac that supports Apple Intelligence, and MCP support in Keynote, Pages and Numbers also requires macOS 27. We looked at how the major NLEs and plugin makers handle macOS 27 Golden Gate earlier this month. The Creator Studio version of Final Cut Pro for Mac requires macOS 26.6 or later and runs on Intel and Apple silicon Macs, although Apple notes that some features require Apple silicon. Final Cut Pro for iPad requires iPadOS 26.6 or later and an iPad with an A16, A17 Pro or M1 chip or later. Logic Pro for Mac requires macOS 26.1 and Apple silicon. Motion and Compressor require macOS 15.6 or later. For Apple Immersive Video processing in Compressor, Apple specifies 32GB of RAM as the minimum and recommends 64GB with storage read speeds of 2,000MB/s or faster. Price and availability The update will be available on the App Store in November, free for existing subscribers. New subscribers pay $12.99 / €12.99 per month or $129 / €129 per year (euro prices from Apple Germany, including VAT), with a one-month free trial. Buyers of a new Mac or a qualifying iPad can get three months free. University students and educators pay $2.99 / €2.99 per month or $29.99 / €29 per year. Up to six family members can share the subscription through Family Sharing, and it is a universal purchase across Mac, iPad and iPhone. More details are on the Apple Creator Studio page and in Apple’s press release . The one-time-purchase versions remain available on the Mac App Store: Final Cut Pro at $299.99, Logic Pro at $199.99, Pixelmator Pro , Motion and Compressor at $49.99 each, and MainStage at $29.99. The free versions of Keynote , Pages , Numbers and Freeform also continue. Does built-in MotionVFX content change the value of the subscription for you, or will you stay with the one-time purchase of Final Cut Pro? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below !

items.title: Canon Q3 2026 Results: Strong Imaging Sales Driven by Network Cameras
items.summary_what: Canon Q3 2026 Results: Strong Imaging Sales Driven by Network Cameras: has released their Q3 2026 financial results and they look to be a mixed bag for the imaging division.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.

items.raw_content: Canon Inc. has released their Q3 2026 financial results and they look to be a mixed bag for the imaging division. They're making money, which is the point of it all, but there have been challenges. Revenue in the camera and lens business did rise 4% because the average selling price kept climbing, not due to unit sales. Both the EOS R6 V and EOS R6 Mark III have sold well, but they're higher priced cameras which helps with total revenue. Looking at local currencies, overall camera sales dipped 3.6% for the quarter compared to last year. Canon points to the conflict in the Middle East and weaker consumer spending in China as key reasons for the drop. Compact Cameras Canon can't get new PowerShots out fast enough, their compact camera business grew 50% on the back of 8 year old cameras like the PowerShot G7 X Mark III . Canon is going to have a big focus on this segment going forward. Unsurprisingly, a lot of this is being driven by younger and first time buyers of a Canon camera. All is not rosy for compact cameras. Canon says there are still component shortages affecting unit production. AI datacenters aren't just hammering storage and DRAM capacity, there is also high demand for circuit boards, which has a big impact on camera production. Canon EOS R6 Mark III Full-Frame 32.5MP 40FPS 7K60P 32.5MP Full-Frame CMOS Sensor 7K 60p 12-Bit Internal RAW Light Video Open Gate 7K 30p, High-Speed 4K 120p Dual Pixel CMOS AF II & Movie Servo AF Up to 40 fps & Pre-Continuous Shoot Mode 8.5-Stop 5-Axis Image Stabilization $2,799 €2,699 · £2,799 Shop Now → Canon EOS R6 V Full-Frame 32.5MP 40FPS 7K60P 32.5MP Full-Frame CMOS Sensor 7K 60p 12-Bit Internal RAW Light Video Open Gate 7K 30p, High-Speed 4K 120p Dual Pixel CMOS AF II & Movie Servo AF Up to 40 fps & Pre-Continuous Shoot Mode 8.5-Stop 5-Axis Image Stabilization $2,499 €2,499 · £2,399 Shop Now → Canon EOS R8 Mark II Full-Frame 24MP 40FPS 4K60P 24.2MP Full-Frame CMOS Sensor 4K60p 10-Bit Internal Video, Canon Log 3 40 fps Electronic Shutter, Pre-Capture 5-Axis In-Body Image Stabilization Dual Pixel CMOS AF II with Tracking 2.36m-Dot OLED Electronic Viewfinder $1,899 €1,799 · £1,729 Shop Now → Affiliate links Network Cameras Back in 2015, Canon acquired AXIS Communications for $2.8B and it looks like that acquisition has paid off in spades. Network cameras saw a 30% year-over-year increase in sales. We're not sure if PTZ cameras are included in Network Cameras, but they don't really fit the EOS R system. Research & Development As most of you will know, Canon is always one of the global leaders in the number of patents they're awarded for any year, and it's been that way for a long time. R&D in the imaging division rose 32% year-over-year so far in 2026, which is quite a jump and tells us Canon is investing a lot in new technology and wants to remain the king of camera and lens marketshare. Canon Q3 2026 results Imaging business: the numbers Q3 sales ¥294.9bn +16.3% Y/Y Q3 operating profit ¥46.8bn +22.7% Y/Y Q3 margin 15.9% +0.9 pts (15.0%) Q3 2025 Q3 2026 ¥ billions Imaging sales (total) +16.3% 2025 253.6 2026 294.9 Cameras +4.0% 2025 152.7 2026 158.8 Network cameras & others +34.9% 2025 100.9 2026 136.1 Operating profit +22.7% 2025 38.1 2026 46.8 January–September 2026 Imaging sales ¥847.6bn vs ¥726.4bn · +16.7% Operating profit ¥144.4bn vs ¥108.4bn · +33.2% Operating margin 17.0% vs 14.9% · +2.1 pts R&D spending ¥103.3bn vs ¥78.3bn · +32.0% In local currency, Q3 camera sales fell 3.6%; the weaker yen turned that into the +4.0% shown. “Network cameras & others” also includes cinema, broadcast and MR products. Source: Canon Inc. Q3 2026 results, October 27, 2026. Imaging Business 2026 Forecast Canon has lowered their 2026 forecast for both network and consumer cameras. Canon has reduced the forecast for revenue by ¥22.1B ($141M USD) for the EOS R system, but a total increase in revenue of 8.1%. As far as the booming network camera business, the forecast has been raised by ¥11.3 ($72M USD) and could still see an impressive 19.9% increase in revenue compared to 2025. Sales of interchangeable-lens cameras cut to 2.75M units, down 5% on last year and below Canon's earlier 2.8M target. Canon is saying the total global interchangeable will ship 6.3M units. That would put Canon at about 44% marketshare if we do the math from those forecasts. The imaging division forecasts a 12.9% in sales and 10.8% in operating profit for the year. That seems pretty solid to us. Canon appears to be navigating the current global fun well all things considered. Canon FY2026 outlook Cameras trimmed, network cameras raised FY imaging sales ¥1,190.7bn +12.9% · cut ¥10.8bn FY operating profit ¥191.6bn +10.8% · unchanged ILC camera units 2.75M −5% · was 2.80M FY2025 actual FY2026 forecast Previous forecast ¥ billions Imaging sales (total) +12.9% −10.8 vs prev. 2025 1,054.9 2026F 1,190.7 Cameras +8.1% −22.1 vs prev. 2025 625.5 2026F 675.9 Network cameras & others +19.9% +11.3 vs prev. 2025 429.4 2026F 514.8 Operating profit +10.8% +0.1 vs prev. 2025 172.9 2026F 191.6 Behind the forecast Operating margin 16.1% forecast vs 16.4% in 2025 ILC unit market 6.3M units; Canon forecasts 2.75M (~44%) Local-currency growth Cameras +1.5% (was +5.4%) · NWC +13.1% (was +11.3%) Implied Q4 profit ≈¥47bn vs ¥64.5bn in Q4 2025 (derived) Camera forecast cut for the Middle East conflict, weak demand in China and component shortages limiting compact camera output. Network camera growth target raised to about 20%. Implied Q4 = full-year forecast minus January–September actual. Source: Canon Inc. Q3 2026 results, October 27, 2026. Conclusion Overall, Canon’s imaging division delivered a pretty solid quarter, even if it’s a bit surprising to see network cameras leading the charge. While global challenges in China and the Middle East led to lower forecasts, imaging remains a key growth engine for Canon overall.

items.raw_content: From an industrial slab named after a hardness scale to a display face woven from memories of lace, this October brings a bumper crop of new typefaces. Is it that time already? The clocks have gone back, the weather is getting colder and wetter, and the countdown to 25 December has begun in earnest. But for designers looking for exciting new fonts, it might feel like Christmas has come a couple of months early. October has delivered one of the most eclectic typographic hauls of the year. We're talking a variable font five years in the making, a humanist sans designed for dyslexic readers, a display typeface assembled from clay impressions of gravestones, and a geometric stencil that can switch between sharp and rounded at the pull of a variable axis. Elsewhere there's elegance in a new revival of a 1921 Garamond interpretation, a sense of solidity in an eight-weight industrial slab named after a metallurgical hardness test, and outright quirkiness in a type system that deliberately sits "at the threshold between reading and looking". In short, while it's easy to feel design and creativity are being taken over by AI, the fresh typefaces we've collected below remain very much hand-crafted. That thought alone should keep you warm and cosy as the nights draw in. 1. Twista Sans by Viktor Nübel Twista Sans is something different: a uniwidth typeface. That's not the same as being monospaced: Twista Sans keeps characters proportional. But all its glyphs share the same horizontal width, so you can switch weights without your layout reflowing, opening up new possibilities for hover effects and UI animations. Designed as a sans companion to Nübel's display face Twista, Twista Sans could work well for packaging, branding and editorial. 2. Corsario by Felix Braden Cologne-based Felix Braden, the designer behind Floodfonts, has channelled five years of work into Corsario. Inspired by the British transitional style, it features sharp, prominent serifs that make text stand out. With 54 styles, this variable font family lets you set both elegant headlines and legible captions from a single font file. 3. Triode by MuirMcNeil MuirMcNeil's work sits somewhere between typeface design and visual art, and Triode is a prime example. This new geometric type system explores what happens at the crossroads between language and pattern. Its precisely calibrated components can be combined, layered, and offset to create transitions and collisions between language, image, pattern, and texture. To mark the release, MuirMcNeil has published an edition of 40 unique colour posters, each measuring 50 × 70 cm. 4. Kellarie by Laura Worthington When you need a script with real warmth that feels hand-drawn, Laura Worthington is usually worth checking out. Compact lowercase forms, buoyant rhythm, and a lively forward slant give words the momentum of hand lettering, while sweeping capitals, generous loops, and curling flourishes add personality. This font works well on packaging, stationery, and editorial headers. 5. Thorn Serif by Type Forward Type Forward has an interesting catalogue, and Thorn Serif is a confident new addition. It's inspired by the raw, distinctive lettering on ancient Roman coins. The family takes the compact proportions, heavy serifs, and low-contrast construction of these historical forms and translates them into a contemporary type system. 6. Bw Ubica by Branding with Type Branding with Type is known for sans-serifs that are clean without being anonymous, and Bw Ubica continues in that tradition. Its sharp geometry and balanced anatomy provide impact, while its balanced x-height and slightly condensed proportions are optimised for high legibility without losing a single hint of its character. Available in 12 styles, this font gives brands a unified voice across editorial layouts, user interfaces, and physical product sleeves. 7. Hyperspace Cargo by Swell Type Hyperspace Cargo looks exactly like its name. Derived from the earlier Hyperspace Race, it's an all-caps, stencil typeface available in a range of weights from Light to Heavy. Horizontal-line Stylistic Alternates add further variety, and it also supports Cyrillic, Greek and Vietnamese. The variable version offers Weight and Roundness axes for extra flexibility. 8. Mourn by Nina Type Mexican type designer Ubaldo Ortiz spent two years building this display face around the structural logic of bobbin lace, painstakingly constructing each character letter by letter before weaving lace patterns around them. Mourn is the launch typeface for his new studio Nina Type, which also offers the sharp serif Osé and everyday workhorse Nina Sans. 9. Pen by DDOTT × Morula What happens when a pen pauses on paper? Those small drops of ink at the moment of hesitation, correction, or interruption form the core concept of Pen, a new typeface from DDOTT, developed in collaboration with Morula. Designer Dominik Thieme launched the project with a live plotting performance in Barcelona, and the release includes a thoughtful essay tracing the history of automated drawing and writing. 10. CoFo Cinema1909 by Contrast Foundry Cinema1909 began as a custom typeface for one of the world's oldest cinemas, inspired by metro-station lettering, before being released as a retail typeface. This month, Contrast Foundry published a significant update, adding lowercase letters, ordinals and expanded language support. Combining elegance and decorative details with a refined feel, it works particularly well in tight, compact headlines. 11. WTF Hammer by W Type Foundry W Type Foundry built Hammer around a single premise: what can you do with proportion alone? The answer seems to be: well, quite a lot, actually. This contemporary grotesk superfamily features 12 width variants, plus matching italics. Moving between styles creates rhythm and contrast, making headlines and layouts feel dynamic, not static. 12. GS Merca by GS Type Gerard Sierra has spent a lot of time with the ornate lettering on the façade of the 1920s Art Nouveau market in the Spanish city of Tarragona. The font this inspired carries its source material's character while adding a stencil-like, rebellious feel. The lowercase expands this language, creating a typeface with enough identity to shift between the vernacular and sharper, more contemporary contexts. 13. Altus Grotesk by Type Innovations Alex Kaczun, former principal type designer at Linotype-Hell, helped shape the Adobe PostScript Font Library, and his solo foundry, Type Innovations, continues to build on that legacy. Altus Grotesk is a high-impact geometric display font that combines sharp-cornered, highly stylised capitals with clean circular forms and generous proportions. A strong choice for logos, posters, and headline branding work where you need both presence and clarity. 14. IvyMazarin Big by Ivy Foundry IvyMazarin demonstrates the difference between reviving a historical typeface and simply reproducing it. Designer Jan Maack took Astrée, a 1921 Garamond interpretation commissioned for the Imprimerie Nationale in Paris, and drew out a display version with precision and sensitivity. Think dramatic contrast, generous proportions and a sense of grandeur. 15. Thalo by Signal Type Foundry Thalo began as a commission from a state transportation agency: a humanist sans designed to meet accessibility requirements for signage and timetables. Max Phillips at Signal Type Foundry in Dublin has kept contrast low, with generous letterspacing and open counters and apertures throughout. Letters such as b, d, p, and q have been carefully drawn to minimise confusion for dyslexic readers, while I, l, 1, and i are as distinct as possible. This clarity means Thalo can create impact in branding and editorial, as well as signage. 16. Shuffle by Local Type Originally designed for a children's healthcare centre in Brazil, Shuffle is a two-axis variable display font (weight and bounce) that ranges from bold and exuberant to lighter and sharper, with 12 static styles too. It's the first release from Local Type, João Luiz Wittkowski's new foundry based in Valencia, Spain, and one style is free for personal and commercial use. 17. Blubird by Rajesh Kumar Blubird is a contemporary narrow sans-serif with nine weights, 36 styles, and two optical sizes (Display and Text) for genuine range. With dedicated italics, this font strikes a strong balance between visual impact and typographic refinement. 18. Vestige by Claire Wilde Vestige takes the idea of a handmade typeface into new, unusual territory. Designer Claire Wilde developed this uppercase display typeface from physical clay impressions of lettering found on gravestones, while retaining the irregularities and weathered character of the original impressions. Her documentation of the process has reached 147k views. 19. Puerile Grotesque by Applied Systems Design Studio Alister Shapley at Applied Systems Design Studio has been thinking about what "play" actually means in typography, and Puerile Grotesque is his answer. While his earlier font, Puerile Display, explored ornament and expressive forms, Puerile Grotesque questions the underlying structure of letterforms. Together, they form a complementary, convention-busting family. 20. Magmæ by Arillatype Pedro Arilla and Cristina Villellas at Arillatype named their new industrial typeface after the molten rock beneath the Earth's crust. It's a design of opposites: fluid, organic curves contrast with a mechanical digital skeleton; soft outer contours meet structured, squared counters. Engineered for high functionality and precise performance, this font has a raw energy that makes it a strong choice for packaging, industrial branding, and architecture-based projects. 21. Scooch by Fred Wiltshire Scooch is a large serif family that pairs gaiety with typographic rigour – no mean feat. The swash capitals, influenced by 19th-century display typefaces, add flourish; the lowercase is tamed by comparison, with a simplified "t" that runs through the family as a visual thread. One of those rare display families that can function as text when needed. 22. Clamp by Daniel Iglesias Clamp is a type system that builds multiple personalities directly into a single typeface, rather than creating separate styles. Designers can adapt it to different contexts by changing its character through OpenType alternates. 23. Brinell by Latinotype Latinotype named its new slab serif after the Brinell hardness scale, a 1900 engineering test that measures a material's resistance to deformation. The team drew on classic industrial slabs like Rockwell and updated the proportions and details by removing some serifs, flattening contrast, and creating a cleaner overall look. Its intentional inconsistencies (the terminal on the /a, the slightly off-rule details) give it a warmth that precise, corrected type often lacks.

items.title: Why the Horror Thriller 'Cruel Hands' Was Largely Shot Like a Western
items.summary_what: Why the Horror Thriller 'Cruel Hands' Was Largely Shot Like a Western: What happens when a horror thriller borrows the visual language of a western?
items.summary_why: Provides practical business, lighting, or cinematography guidance for commercial freelancers.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: What happens when a horror thriller borrows the visual language of a western? A feature like Dark Sky Films’ Cruel Hands is born. The synopsis for the film reads: Amid the worst bushfires in Australia’s history, Maria (Mavournee Hazel) and her son Dai (Diesel La Torraca) escape a violent and abusive husband and make their way to an abandoned farmhouse. While hiding, Maria tries to create a new home for Dai as Jason (Josh McConville), the police, and the fires close in. In a climactic battle, two damaged, traumatized parents fight over Dai's fate, with deadly consequences. For Cruel Hands , DP Charlie Cole used bold compositions, locked-off frames, and deliberate dolly movements to give the film a Western-inspired aesthetic, heightening the tension as a man hunts down his estranged wife and child. The result is a striking visual contrast between the film’s suspenseful pursuit and the more intimate, emotionally grounded moments at its center. In the interview below, Cole breaks down the cinematography behind Cruel Hands and discusses his collaboration with longtime friend and director Al Kalyk. Cruel Hands is available to rent or buy on Prime Video . It is also available on Plex . - YouTube www.youtube.com No Film School: How did you first discover your passion for cinematography? Was there a particular film whose visual style or cinematography made you realize this was the path you wanted to pursue? Charlie Cole: I fell in love with cinematography through a handful of films that I saw within a year. At the time, I was a Drawing major at Pratt Institute, and my roommate and I watched Enter the Void and Antichrist . A few months later, I watched Requiem For A Dream - those 3 films together shook me out of wanting to be a fine artist, and pulled me into the life of filmmaking. All of them shared a similar approach to me: If you have a challenging (hard to watch) script, shoot it beautifully - this will make the audience engage with the poetry of the visuals and open their hearts more to what the film is saying. If people are prepared for a jump scare, they are guarded. These three films impacted me so deeply, and I think a large part of that is due to the cinematography being quite poetic in each case. I watched them unguarded, and therefore the films affected me deeply. NFS: How did you become involved with Cruel Hands and what did pre-production look like for you? CC: The director, Al Kalyk, and I attended the American Film Institute together and had worked on several projects. He has become one of my best friends, and it just felt right that I would shoot his first feature. We had been talking about it on and off for a few years before it got wings and financing. Pre-pro was 6 weeks in Australia. We shot the film in January. (Australian summer), so we did about a month of solid prep on the Gold Coast (where the film was shot), then 2 weeks of Al and me prepping over Christmas and New Year's while in Sydney. It was a pretty magical experience. One I hope to get to experience again. DP Charlie Cole on 'Cruel Hands' Credit: ProjectionPR NFS: Can you talk about the collaboration between you and Cruel Hands director Al Kalyk? How did you align your artistic visions for this project? CC: Our collaboration was very friendly and trusting. Al and I are like brothers. My initial thoughts for the visuals on the film were far more brooding and muddy compared to where we landed. I had sent Al a fairly extensive lookbook, which served as my initial take on the script before seeing any of his ref images. Immediately, Al let me know I was wrong (in a loving way). He had this wonderful idea to shoot this film in part like an old western film. Ultimately, the film lends itself to both styles, I feel: There’s a duality between bold-angled, western locked-off or dolly shots when we’re in the thriller parts of the film where Jason is hunting down his ‘escaped’ wife and child, and a more delicate sensibility when we are sitting with Dai and Maria, a mother and son trying to emotionally survive this new chapter in their lives and hopefully get closer along the way. Visually, Al and I are quite in tune stylistically. We’ve never really had issues syncing up with how we both feel about images. Al brings a lot of paintings as references, while I bring a lot of cinematic references. During prep, I put together a Visual Bible of the film, which is every scene broken down into Tone, Lighting, and Framing. I make sure that Al approves of every image, and it’s built very much based on our conversations about the film and how the visuals push the story forward. After about a month or so of putting that document together, the film’s visual language is very fine-tuned. Now it’s just a matter of making it. NFS: Walk us through your camera, lens, and filtration choices, and how they supported the tone of Cruel Hands ? CC: Right off the bat, my instinct was to shoot this film in Large Format. We were going to be dealing with small rural spaces that we wanted to feel Cinematic. LF was our choice to capture that, but we were naturally concerned with the lens choices available, especially since we were locked into a rental house in rural Australia that our Producer had set up an excellent bargain with. Luckily for us, the rental house (Cine 2481) had everything we needed! After 2 days of testing, we ended up selecting the following combination: CAM: Mini LF (4.5k Open Gate) LENSES: Leica R FILTRATION: Low Con // Black Satin One of our main references for the look of the film was Phantom Thread . We wanted to create a softness and delicacy in the lenses that counteracted the boldness of the western style (dolly push-ins / tense angles, dark lighting). I’m very happy with where we ended up. NFS: Looking back on Cruel Hands , is there a creative or technical achievement you are especially proud of that viewers may not realize while watching the finished film? CC: The film takes place during the wildfires of 2019, so we knew we would have to build that look into the world. The air gets choked with smoke, and all the light turns a deep orange. So, in the third act of the film, when the fires have started (further away from our character, but slowly impeding), we build the intensity of smoke and color. To achieve this, we had to instill a strict ‘no direct sun’ rule for shooting any scene that took place in the third act. This meant only shooting exteriors at dusk, dawn, or overcast moments (rare in Australia’s summer). Then we had an amazing, helpful team of art department / PA’s / grips who would help control the 2 household hazers and 1 fogger; we had to spread out the smoke as best we could. I’m really happy with the effect of feeling like you’re surrounded by wildfires. So much of what you see in the film is all practical. Color (done by Al Kalyk), of course, helps a ton with the feeling of burnt skies, along with additional smoke effects added in post by our VFX team for the final scenes. 'Cruel Hands' BTS Credit: ProjectionPR NFS: You also had a film, Corpus , recently premiering at the Fantasia International Film Festival. Can you tell us about the look of that film? CC: Oof, that is a fun film. The film takes place in the early 2000s NYC and is an erotic body horror thriller. The film is a mix of the NYC club scene, dingy apartments, and a remote mansion in upstate NYC. The look of the film ranges within those worlds; director Corrin Evans and I maintained deep colors and sensual tones. The film is meant to feel hot and sweaty, full of shadows. It is for sure a summer movie- we shot on the Super Baltars for a rich, warm, human feeling. Production Designer Sadra Tehrani brought so much of this world to life, and we collaborated in incorporating so much of the lighting into practicals. The whole film is shot with Tungsten and HMI lighting for a heavier, more period-honest look. The majority of the shots and setups were oner-focused, letting the handheld camera roam around the characters, with little to no marks and a guided sense of where we needed the emotions to come out in the scenes. The actors were amazing, very game for all of it, extremely consistent and dedicated. Focus Puller / 1st AC Julia Crytser made so many of the moves possible. We were almost always shooting wide open on a 100mm with no marks, just flowing. Corpus also just won Best Cinematography at Brooklyn Horror Fest! I just found out this morning, as I’m writing this. NFS: Both Cruel Hands and Corpus fall into the horror genre. Why do you think you've found such a strong creative home in the genre, and what keeps you returning to it? CC: I love the horror genre! I like when it’s mixed in with other genres. Horror - thriller /drama/romance. Horror tends to bring a tension in the tension. There is inevitably some duality, deceit, mystery, and intrigue. All of these lend themselves to interesting images and approaches. In horror, you can go so many visual routes. It can be clean and disturbing ( Backroom, Midsommar, The Substance ) or gritty and dark ( Blair Witch ). Underneath it all, with both Cruel Hands and Corpus , it’s a story of longing for those you love, and how you’ll do anything to be closer to them. NFS: What sequence in both Corpus and Cruel Hands required the most planning, and how did you and your team execute it? Cruel Hands has a big, fiery, violent climax (sorry, spoiler!) That was a difficult sequence to pull off; we had a large wide, stunts, weapons, fire, smoke, and of course it took place at dusk. We also needed a very specific terrain (a clearing within a forest) and a fallen tree that one of the characters hides behind (this tree ended up being dragged in through the forest on a forklift - Australians will get the job done, let me tell ya). We pulled this off with elaborate planning and several scouts. The fire effect was kind of simple when you break it down. Large sources far away, and hidden behind tree lines, hills, bushes. Then blast them with smoke so we get a huge backlight. The smoke helped us light because it carries the light everywhere. Supplement with a few lights and voila — fiery climax smoke battle! Corpus had a few challenging scenes. The climax is (surprise surprise) also violent. This scene has a bunch of stunts and prosthetics involved, and took 2.5 days to shoot. The scene is in a large room with tons of windows. Of course, the first day was sunny, the second was raining, and the third was partially cloudy. The lighting continuity credit goes to Gaffer Claire Halloran and Sophia Williams, who kept us on track and kept the look consistent while we shot in nearly every direction over those days. I would be remiss not to mention the large opening scene of Corpus that takes place in a huge club called Red Light Dharma. We had about 200 extras and had to light a massive warehouse. No particular trick to it, except that we knew we needed to have 360-degree visibility in the scene, so PD Sadra Tehrani and I worked to make all the lights we needed practical. The teams pulled it off so well - we were able to see everything in the frame, and only used lights that would have existed at the time, and in those venues, for more authenticity. Corrin Evans (director) was so good about fighting for that throughout the film. 'Cruel Hands' Credit: ProjectionPR NFS: How would you describe your visual style, and how do you adapt it across films like Cruel Hands and Corpus ? My visual style lies in intimacy and intrigue. I love a curious camera. My background is in fine arts; I went to school for drawing. And a lesson that always stuck with me was when a professor reminded us all - everyone here knows how to draw - what makes your drawing special. I try to keep that lesson alive with cinematography. Another drawing professor (that school clearly had a big impact on me ;) - thank you, Pratt Institute!) said that when you bring a piece up to show to the class, you should feel nervous. You should feel vulnerable. As a cinematographer, we are so protected by the camera; we risk nothing. The actors and directors are analyzed/criticized. I try to use that safe privilege to try and show as much of what I’m feeling as possible. And hopefully it comes across in the images.

items.title: SmallRig Cage and L-Shaped Plate for Sigma FP2 Introduced – Wooden Grip, HawkLock NATO Rail, Arca-Swiss Base
items.summary_what: SmallRig Cage and L-Shaped Plate for Sigma FP2 Introduced – Wooden Grip, HawkLock NATO Rail, Arca-Swiss Base: Although the Sigma FP2 hasn’t started shipping yet, SmallRig has its first accessories ready: a full cage with a built-in wooden grip and a lighter L-shaped mount plate.

items.raw_content: Although the Sigma FP2 hasn’t started shipping yet, SmallRig has its first accessories ready: a full cage with a built-in wooden grip and a lighter L-shaped mount plate. Both match the look of SmallRig’s original Sigma FP cage and are now available for pre-order. The new Sigma FP2 keeps the modular brick concept of the original fp: no built-in grip, no viewfinder, and accessories added as the job demands. That makes a cage almost mandatory for many video users. When the first fp arrived, SmallRig was quick with a cage for it as well, and the new FP2 cage follows the same recipe with a wooden handle on the right side. Credit: SmallRig The cage SmallRig’s Cage for Sigma FP2 (item 6505) attaches with a three-point lock, combining a bottom screw, a locating pin and a side screw. According to SmallRig, this keeps the cage from twisting, while cutouts leave all buttons, ports and Sigma’s own accessories accessible. Credit: SmallRig For expansion, the cage has a built-in HawkLock NATO rail, 1/4″-20 threads and ARRI locating holes for magic arms, monitors and top handles. A modular cold shoe can be removed so that the cage stays compatible with Sigma’s original EVF. The base has an integrated Arca-type quick release plate, which SmallRig says mounts directly on Arca tripod heads and DJI RS 2, RS 3, RS 4 and RS 5 gimbals. An HDMI cable clamp is included to protect the camera’s port when an external monitor is connected, and a magnetic wrench is stored in the cage for tool-free adjustments. The cage is made from aluminum alloy and stainless steel, with a wooden grip and silicone parts. It measures 127.8 x 53.0 x 89.6mm / 5.0 x 2.1 x 3.5in and weighs 174g / 6.1oz. In the box are the cage, the HDMI cable clamp, a cold shoe mount and a user manual. Credit: SmallRig The L-shaped mount plate For users who want less bulk, SmallRig also offers an L-Shaped Mount Plate with Wooden Handle for Sigma FP2 . It mounts with a 1/4″-20 screw and an anti-twist locating block, and protects the bottom and right side of the camera. A threaded hole on the back supports Sigma’s original optical viewfinder, and the bottom has 1/4″-20 threads and locating holes for Arca-type quick release plates. A magnetic wrench is integrated here as well. There is no NATO rail, cold shoe or HDMI clamp on the plate. It measures 125.0 × 56.7 × 79.0mm / 4.9 × 2.2 × 3.1in, and weighs 129.0 g / 4.6oz. Price and availability The SmallRig Cage for Sigma FP2 (6505) is listed at $79.99, and the L-Shaped Mount Plate at $49.99. Both are available for pre-order from SmallRig, with a 2-year warranty. The cage is expected to ship shortly before the camera, which Sigma will release on November 11, 2026 at $2,199 / €2,199 for the body. For more information, please visit the SmallRig website . Are you planning to rig up the Sigma FP2, and would you go for the full cage or the lighter L-plate? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

items.raw_content: Canon has released new firmware for the EOS C50, EOS C80 and EOS C400. The update fixes some bugs in the cameras. We generally recommend waiting on firmware updates, check out usergroups for these cameras and see if there is discussion about issues that may have arisen. We hate saying it, but Canon has a bit of a track record in regards to new firmware bringing new bugs to the cameras. Canon Cinema EOS C400 Firmware v1.0.8.1 Fixes & enhancements Enhanced security for IP streaming Corrected display problems in some language environments Download Firmware Shop Now → Affiliate link Canon Cinema EOS C50 Firmware v1.0.6.1 Fixes & enhancements Enhanced security for IP streaming Fixed display problems in some language environments Fixes an issue where image recording to the card may not complete in Photo mode Download Firmware Shop Now → Affiliate link Canon Cinema EOS C80 Firmware v1.0.8.1 Fixes & enhancements Enhanced security for IP streaming Corrected display problems in some language environments Download Firmware Shop Now → Affiliate link Affiliate links In Closing The firmware is nice, but it’s strange to see that Canon really only has 3 Cinema EOS cameras. We suspect a camera or two above the C400 are coming, but we have no idea when. It feels like we’ve been waiting forever, but we think Canon is going to re-imagine the higher end level of cameras. Sony is the big player, and it seems the higher budget filmmakers simply don’t look at Canon and roll with Sony and ARRI.

items.title: How Mother Design turned a séance into a new identity for Purple Garden
items.summary_what: How Mother Design turned a séance into a new identity for Purple Garden: The London studio began rebranding the psychic services platform with a chakra reading and a little charcoal, and the result is a rich, purple-hued brand world that feels alive.
items.summary_why: Influences typography, UI/UX prototyping speed, and vector design production assets.
items.summary_action: Review the full source announcement for technical requirements and deployment details.
items.raw_content: The London studio began rebranding the psychic services platform with a chakra reading and a little charcoal, and the result is a rich, purple-hued brand world that feels alive. It's almost Halloween, so forgive me if, on discovering that a branding project began with a séance, I immediately thought of that brilliant 'Day-O' dinner party scene in Beetlejuice. You know, the one with the late great Catherine O'Hara? I presume no one at Mother Design was forced into an impromptu calypso number, but it's a wonderful mental image. What actually happened involved way less dancing and uncontrolled lip syncing. The independent design studio, part of the Mother Family, has crafted a new identity for Purple Garden, the mobile and online psychic services platform. Fittingly, the team decided to lean into a more spiritual approach to get there. The brief was to "bring the feeling of spiritual practice into the digital world", which was no easy task. The spiritual services industry is worth around $2.3 billion, and apps and online platforms are opening up new ways for people to connect with guidance. But things can get lost in translation on screen: the atmosphere, ritual, and energy – it's hard to replicate online when you're not in the room. Mother Design's job was to fix that. The new brand therefore reframes Purple Garden from somewhere you visit for a one-off reading into a home for ongoing spiritual practice. It's built on a rather lovely insight: some questions keep returning no matter how much life changes. The audience, which Mother calls 'Believers of the Bigger Picture', are "seasoned seekers" looking for growth and meaning. So the creative idea, 'A Living Practice', moves from passive advice to active clarity through repetition and growth. How did Mother Design figure all this out? They staged a séance and a chakra reading, alongside an automatic drawing and writing workshop led by one of Purple Garden's holistic practitioners. It's what we've come to expect from the studio, as it encourages its team to experiment with unfamiliar disciplines. Armed with paper and charcoal, they worked instinctively, trying to ignore and bypass conscious thought. The forms and feelings that emerged from the session then became the foundation of the identity. "So much of spiritual practice is about things you feel rather than things you can see – energy, intuition, connection and those moments when you feel altered somehow," says Joanna Tulej, creative director at Mother Design. "The challenge was how you translate that into a brand experience without falling back on the visual clichés of the category. "We realised that if we wanted the identity to feel spontaneous and alive, we needed to allow some of that spontaneity into the way we designed it too. Starting with the séance and automatic drawing session gave us permission to step away from the screen and the rational design process. Some of the textures, energy and unexpectedness that came out of that experience found their way into the final identity." I absolutely love this. Whatever you make of spirituality, it's nice to remember that the best work comes from being experimental and having fun. I think we need that now more than ever. I was also fascinated to learn that the approach was partly inspired by the Swedish artist Hilma af Klint and The Five, the collective of brilliant women who experimented with trance-like states and automatic drawing to ignore conscious thought and let images and words emerge freely. (If you've not heard of her, look her up! Her paintings are considered to be among the first major abstract works in Western art history.) But the inventiveness didn't stop at charcoal. During development, Mother Design moved back and forth between traditional design software and AI tools, iterating constantly to generate unexpected visuals and add more unpredictability to the process. Looking at the outcome, I'll start with the typography because you can see all this play spilling through. The wordmark itself balances modern with whimsical. Elongated serifs and curved corners seem to grow outward. A "digital-first", crystal-like glyph acts as a symbol of guidance and forms the basis of the entire icon system for navigating the platform's many services. Literatura Present and ABC Social complete the type system. Literatura's flowing descenders and serifs add to that sense of growth, and ABC Social does the functional, sensible stuff so things are easy to read on screen. I really love the "living type" detail, inspired by cymatic patterns. That's the shape sound makes when it vibrates through a surface, if you didn't know. The subtle message is that Purple Garden helps you to grow, too. Colour-wise, purple clearly takes the lead. But Mother Design has developed a palette of six warmer purples, deliberately moving away from the cool, blue-toned purples so common in this category. The imagery feels more intimate and tactile, while the motion reinforces the idea of growth. The project follows Mother Design's recent rebrand of Keen , another spiritual guidance brand within the Ingenio portfolio. While Keen targeted a more mainstream, "spiritually curious" audience, Purple Garden is for those already seasoned in this space: two brands, two different jobs. "Purple Garden is for people who already have a deep connection with spirituality and see it as an active part of how they navigate their lives," says Ariana Hellebuyck, CMO at Ingenio. "We wanted the brand to reflect the depth of the experiences our guides provide and make that connection feel just as powerful in a digital environment. "Mother Design has created something that feels distinctive to Purple Garden and true to our audience, while giving us a richer and more immersive platform for the next stage of the brand." The new identity is now being rolled out across Purple Garden's website, app, advertising, and social channels over the coming weeks. It's got me thinking about how I love to switch off. Admittedly, my rituals are less mystical and don't involve any summoning. I find ironing, getting out on my bike, or spending time in the garden helps me zone out. Not as exciting, but the principle is the same. Just like Hilma, this project reminds us to play and try new things. Don't be afraid to experiment. And let creativity flow. You never know what will come out the other side.

items.title: Modern camera lenses are becoming increasingly perfect. Sigma’s upcoming lens boldly takes a different approach. Are softer optics the missing piece to the retro camera trend?
items.summary_what: Modern camera lenses are becoming increasingly perfect. Sigma’s upcoming lens boldly takes a different approach. Are softer optics the missing piece to the retro camera trend?: Retro camera designs are a longstanding trend in photography.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.

items.raw_content: Retro camera designs are a longstanding trend in photography. But while photographers have multiple options for retro-inspired digital cameras, a retro-inspired lens is arguably much harder to find. That’s what grabbed my attention when Sigma announced a new “CL” lens series last week, which will debut in 2027 with the L-Mount and E-Mount Sigma 50mm f/1.4 CL DG Contemporary . The upcoming 50mm lens looks quite retro with its metal exterior and focal distance scale. But Sigma seems to hint that the new CL lens isn’t just about a retro look to the lens itself, but to the image that it creates too. (Image credit: Sigma) Sigma describes the images coming from the lens as a “gentle softness within the in-focus plane” and a “soft rendering of texture that helps the subject stand out.” Sigma has so far only announced the development of the lens for a Spring 2027 launch, but Australian photographer Mitch Lally tested an early sample at a portrait shoot and described it this way : “The subject remains sharp and detailed, but the transition into the out-of-focus areas has a softer, less clinical quality. Wide open at F1.4, the backgrounds have a softness and character that adds to the overall feel of the image.” Image shot with the Sigma 50mm f/1.4 CL DG Contemporary (Image credit: Sigma / Mitch Lally) That “less clinical quality” grabbed my attention. Retro cameras and photographs that look like they were shot on film are trending – but the lens is half the equation to getting that look and often forgotten. Modern camera lenses have made significant strides forward in creating tack-sharp subjects and fighting off flare and ghosting with modern coatings. But at what point does a lens become too technically perfect? Sigma / Mitch Lally Sigma / Mitch Lally Sigma / Mitch Lally Sigma / Mitch Lally I want a reasonably sharp subject, but not so sharp that I can count the pores in my portraits. This feels particularly true lately: toss an overly sharp, “perfect” image on the internet today, and watch the AI accusations roll in. I’ve even started toning down the skin edits in my portraits. Skin without texture isn’t human. And then, there’s lens flare. Many modern lenses brag about using coatings to prevent lens flare, but I actually love lens flare most of the time. Yes, there are scenarios when I want full clarity in challenging backlight, but most of the time, I’d rather have streaky golden light. I’ve adapted old film lenses to my modern mirrorless camera in order to really try to get a more film-like look on digital. But I want to have my cake and eat it too – I want lenses that have both character and modern features. I’ve taken to using a warm diffusion filter on a majority of my portraits so I can get warm tones and glowing light, but on a modern autofocus lens. Looking at the sample images from the Sigma 50mm f/1.4 CL DG Contemporary, I’m drawn to the soft colors and smooth bokeh. The subject still looks sharp, but not overly so, and there’s a nice fall-off to that soft background. While Sigma has already shared a full set of technical specifications, the development announcement lacks a key detail: Price. The upcoming CL will be smaller and lighter than Sigma’s 50mm f/1.4 Art . I think if it’s also more affordable, it may draw a lot of photographers who prefer a softer, more retro style. You may also like Take a look at the best nifty fifty lenses or the best retro cameras .

items.title: What does the Nikon ZR price get you? A full-frame RED-powered cinema camera for less than you might think
items.summary_what: What does the Nikon ZR price get you? A full-frame RED-powered cinema camera for less than you might think: The compact cinema camera market has become increasingly competitive in recent years, with manufacturers finding new ways to squeeze professional filmmaking features into smaller, lighter,...

items.raw_content: The compact cinema camera market has become increasingly competitive in recent years, with manufacturers finding new ways to squeeze professional filmmaking features into smaller, lighter, and more affordable bodies. However, one camera that continues to catch my attention is the Nikon ZR. Priced at $2,199.95 in the US at Adorama , or B&H , and currently available for just £1,999 in the UK from Wex , or Park Cameras , down from £2,199, Nikon's first cinema camera developed with RED represents a particularly interesting proposition. We're talking about a full-frame cinema camera with some genuinely impressive filmmaking credentials, yet it costs considerably less than many of the established professional alternatives. For independent filmmakers, content creators, and even photographers looking to explore filmmaking, I think that's a pretty compelling starting point. But what exactly are you getting for your money? Well, underneath that rather understated exterior sits a 24.5MP partially stacked full-frame sensor capable of recording 6K video at up to 60fps, including internal 12-bit RAW recording using Nikon's R3D NE format, developed with RED. That's a pretty serious specification for a camera at this price point, especially when you consider the RED color science, dual-base ISO settings of 800 and 6400, and Nikon's claimed dynamic range of more than 15 stops. There's also support for N-RAW and ProRes RAW, giving filmmakers considerable flexibility when it comes to editing and color grading. To me, this is arguably the ZR's biggest selling point. You're getting access to a genuinely sophisticated RAW video workflow without having to invest in a much larger, more expensive cinema system. However, it's not just the image quality that makes the Nikon ZR interesting. Nikon has clearly understood that modern filmmakers want equipment that works just as well when shooting independently as it does on a professional production. The ZR features a large 4-inch vari-angle touchscreen, in-body image stabilization, intelligent subject-detection autofocus, and perhaps one of its most impressive features, internal 32-bit float audio recording. Being able to capture high-quality audio directly into the camera, with greater flexibility to adjust levels in post-production, is a huge advantage for anyone recording interviews, documentaries, or spontaneous content. Better still, the entire body weighs approximately 540g, making it incredibly portable and ideal for handheld shooting or mounting on a compact gimbal. For someone who appreciates smaller cameras that don't compromise on their creative potential, there's a lot here to get excited about. Of course, Nikon isn't operating in an empty market. Cameras such as the Sony FX3 , Sony FX30 , Canon EOS C50 , and Blackmagic Cinema Camera 6K have already demonstrated just how much demand there is for compact filmmaking systems. Yet I think Nikon has approached things slightly differently with the ZR, combining the familiarity and versatility of its Z-mount mirrorless ecosystem with the filmmaking heritage of RED. It isn't perfect, of course. There's no built-in electronic viewfinder, no internal ND filters, and the inclusion of micro HDMI rather than a full-size connection might frustrate filmmakers who rely on external monitoring equipment. You also only get one CFexpress Type B slot alongside a slower microSD slot, which limits your options for redundant high-bitrate recording. Nevertheless, these are compromises I can understand when you consider the camera's size, price, and overall capabilities. So, is the Nikon ZR worth its asking price? Personally, I think it's one of the more interesting compact cinema cameras currently available, particularly when you consider what Nikon has managed to offer for around $2,200 or less than £2,000. Naturally, you'll still need to factor in lenses, memory cards, and potentially some additional accessories, but the foundations of a remarkably capable filmmaking setup are already there. What excites me most, however, is what the ZR represents for the wider camera industry. Professional filmmaking technology is becoming increasingly accessible, and cameras like this are challenging the idea that you need to spend thousands more to produce genuinely cinematic results. The market might be crowded, but if Nikon can continue delivering this level of performance at such competitive prices, I have a feeling the ZR could be just the beginning of something much bigger.

items.title: Is this the future of Micro Four Thirds? New sensor technology could deliver more than 17 stops of dynamic range
items.summary_what: Is this the future of Micro Four Thirds? New sensor technology could deliver more than 17 stops of dynamic range: For years, Micro Four Thirds cameras have been fighting an uphill battle against larger full-frame and APS-C sensors, particularly when it comes to dynamic range and low-light perform...
items.summary_why: (Image credit: Rednote) The technology in question is known as LOFIC, short for Lateral Overflow Integration Capacitor, and it could represent one of the most significant developments in digital sensor technology in years.

items.raw_content: For years, Micro Four Thirds cameras have been fighting an uphill battle against larger full-frame and APS-C sensors, particularly when it comes to dynamic range and low-light performance. But what if the next big leap in image quality has nothing to do with increasing sensor size? According to a fascinating new rumor, the future of Micro Four Thirds could be about to get considerably brighter, with an entirely new generation of sensors reportedly being developed using LOFIC technology. If the claims prove accurate, we could see Four Thirds sensors capable of delivering more than 17 stops of dynamic range, potentially transforming what photographers and filmmakers can achieve with smaller cameras. (Image credit: Rednote) The technology in question is known as LOFIC, short for Lateral Overflow Integration Capacitor, and it could represent one of the most significant developments in digital sensor technology in years. Unlike conventional sensors, which can struggle to retain information in extremely bright areas of an image, Lofic uses additional capacitors to capture excess electrical charge that would otherwise be lost when a pixel reaches its capacity. In simple terms, this means a sensor can preserve considerably more highlight detail without sacrificing the information captured in darker areas. For photographers, that could mean greater flexibility when editing RAW files, while filmmakers could benefit from an enormous increase in exposure latitude when recording challenging, high-contrast scenes. According to 43 Rumors , information originating from a Chinese source suggests that new Four Thirds sensors incorporating this technology could arrive between 2027 and 2028. The source claims, "New domestic M43 sensors featuring LOFIC technology are on the horizon, promising even greater dynamic range and faster readout speeds compared to their predecessors." More interestingly, the rumored sensors could combine dual conversion gain technology with LOFIC to achieve 14-bit sampling at 60fps, more than 17 stops of dynamic range, and a claimed exposure recovery range extending from +9 to -4 EV. The report also suggests the next generation could be based on a larger Four Thirds-format version of OmniVision's OV50X sensor, although none of these developments or performance figures have been officially confirmed. Waveform from CineD's testing of the DJI Osmo Pocket 4P showing the incredible dynamic range of its 1-inch LOFIC sensor (Image credit: CineD) What makes this rumor particularly exciting is that Lofic isn't simply theoretical technology waiting to be proven. We have already seen what it can achieve in the DJI Osmo Pocket 4P, which features a 1-inch sensor incorporating the technology. Independent testing by CineD measured an astonishing 16 stops of dynamic range at a signal-to-noise ratio of 2, increasing to 17.2 stops at a ratio of 1. Those are remarkable figures from such a small sensor, and they demonstrate why this technology is attracting so much attention. If similar performance could be achieved in a larger Four Thirds sensor, it could fundamentally change expectations of what compact camera systems are capable of, particularly for photographers who want exceptional image quality without the size and weight associated with larger formats. (Image credit: James Artaius) Of course, there is still a considerable difference between a promising sensor rumor and seeing that technology inside the next OM System or Panasonic Lumix camera. The suggestion is that DJI products could receive these sensors first, with no guarantee that traditional Micro Four Thirds manufacturers would have access to them. Nevertheless, I find the possibilities incredibly exciting. Micro Four Thirds has always offered a compelling balance of portability, lens reach, and performance, but imagine combining those advantages with dynamic range that could rival, or potentially surpass, what we currently expect from much larger sensors. Sensor size will still influence noise, depth of field, and overall image quality, but Lofic could help remove one of the format's most persistent disadvantages. If these rumors become reality, perhaps the future of Micro Four Thirds isn't about trying to compete with full-frame cameras by becoming something bigger, but by proving just how much more a smaller sensor can achieve. items.title: Thypoch Simera-C 100mm T1.9 Announced – Telephoto Prime Completes Seven-Lens Cine Set
items.summary_what: Thypoch Simera-C 100mm T1.9 Announced – Telephoto Prime Completes Seven-Lens Cine Set: Thypoch has added a 100mm T1.9 to its compact Simera-C cine prime series, the seventh and final focal length in the full-frame set.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.

items.raw_content: Thypoch has added a 100mm T1.9 to its compact Simera-C cine prime series, the seventh and final focal length in the full-frame set. The new lens takes the line beyond 75mm for the first time and targets close-ups, reaction shots , and narrative details. It keeps the familiar Simera-C formula of a 16-blade iris, 210° focus throw and native Sony E or Leica M mounts, at a price that stays well below traditional cinema glass. The Thypoch Simera-C 100mm T1.9 covers the full-frame image circle (43.2mm) and uses an optical design of 11 elements in 8 groups. Its horizontal field of view on full frame is 21.4°, and the minimum focusing distance is 0.85m / 2ft 10in, measured from the sensor plane. The aperture runs from T1.9 to T16 through a 16-blade iris. Focus rotation is 210°, and both the focus and iris rings carry 0.8 MOD gears. The front diameter is 72mm / 2.83in, with an M67x0.75 filter thread. In Sony E mount, the lens measures 86.4mm / 3.4in and weighs 477g / 1.05lb; the Leica M version is 76.6mm / 3.02in long and weighs 451g / 0.99lb. We first covered the series when the original four Simera-C cine lenses (28, 35, 50 and 75mm) arrived in 2024. Thypoch later added the 21mm T1.5 and, in May 2026, the 16mm T1.9 together with a six-lens kit. With the 100mm, the Simera-C family now spans 16, 21, 28, 35, 50, 75 and 100mm. Thypoch Simera-C 100mm. Credit: Thypoch Optics and rendering According to Thypoch, the 100mm is tuned for defined subject detail combined with soft, natural bokeh and smooth transitions into the out-of-focus areas. The company also highlights chromatic aberration control as a priority of the optical design. Like the 16mm, the 100mm opens to T1.9, while the five focal lengths in between stay at T1.5. On a long lens with a 0.85m close focus, T1.9 already produces a very thin focus plane, and the lens has no electronic contacts, so focus pulling remains fully manual. Credit: Thypoch Matching the rest of the set The 100mm shares its barrel length (86.4mm in E-mount) and its 67mm filter thread with the 75mm, and it is only 24g heavier. Gear positions are consistent across the series, so follow focus motors and screw-on filters can move between the two longest lenses without readjustment. Gimbal users get the same advantage: swapping between the 75mm and 100mm requires little or no rebalancing. For standard 80mm matte boxes, the 67-80mm adapter ring Thypoch recommends for the 75mm also fits the 100mm. Thypoch Simera-C 100mm E-Mount. Credit: Thypoch Mount options The lens is available in black with a native Sony E or Leica M mount. With Thypoch’s positive-lock adapters, part of what the company calls its “M TO ALL” approach, the Leica M version can be used on compatible cameras from Sony, Canon, Fujifilm, Panasonic Lumix, and DJI. Each lens ships with front and rear caps, back-focus adjustment shims, a mount tool kit, and a warranty card. Credit: Thypoch Price and availability Thypoch says shipping starts in late October 2026. The suggested retail price is $879 / €799 in Sony E-mount and $959 / €869 in Leica M mount (euro prices include VAT). Is the 100mm the focal length that makes the Simera-C set complete for you, or would you rather see a longer lens or a zoom? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!
