items.title: Apple's New iPad mini Is Thinner, Lighter, and Maybe More Useful for Filmmakers Now?
items.summary_what: Apple's New iPad mini Is Thinner, Lighter, and Maybe More Useful for Filmmakers Now?. If it’s not beefing up its computers and smartphones, the company is slimming things down and making them more portable.
items.summary_why: It will also be faster, more powerful, and more resistant to water and dust.
items.summary_action: Test new release on a backup or non-critical test project before upgrading active production timelines.
items.raw_content: As always, Apple will do its thing. If it’s not beefing up its computers and smartphones, the company is slimming things down and making them more portable. Often, Apple does both at the same time. And that’s what appears to be the case with this new iPad mini, which has gotten perhaps its biggest update ever, as it will feature a new OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design. It will also be faster, more powerful, and more resistant to water and dust. But will it be more helpful for filmmakers and their pre-pro and on-set management needs? Or even in the edit? Let’s take a look at what the new iPad mini offers. The New Apple iPad Mini is Here Set to deliver, as the company claims, a huge leap in performance with its A20 Pro chip and durability, the iPad mini's larger 8.5-inch OLED display will deliver higher contrast and more than 2x higher peak brightness than the previous-generation iPad mini. “iPad mini is beloved for its fantastic portability, performance, and display by a wide range of users, from creators and small business owners to doctors, field service workers, and gamers. With a remarkably thinner and lighter design, a stunning new OLED display, the incredibly powerful A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance, the new iPad mini is a huge leap forward for users who love having the full iPad experience in the palm of their hand.” - Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. The A20 Pro will supercharge AI usability with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core and a dual 16-core Neural Engine. This latest iPad mini model will also feature a 12MP Center Stage front camera on the landscape edge, perfect for video calls or recording film and content, plus an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience. The iPad mini will also feature faster wireless and cellular connectivity, fast-charge support, and seems designed specifically to add portability and ease of use. Could it be Helpful for Filmmakers? While we’d all love an extra tablet for day-to-day life, whether the iPad mini could serve filmmakers, videographers, or content creators today depends on the creative holding it. Of course, any camera, whether that's an ARRI ALEXA or an iPhone (or, in this case, an iPad mini), can be used for the right video projects. But if we’re being honest, most of the appeal of a more affordable, more versatile iPad mini is in pre-pro and on-set management. Several apps can turn iPads into monitors , and it should be even more useful on location and for stressful doc work thanks to its battery and brightness improvements. Price and Availability Whether it be for pre-pro, management, as a backup monitor, or as a remote video editing station using Final Cut Pro for iPad , if this new model seems appealing to you for any of the above, then that might be the answer for you. If you’d like to find out more about the full package, including pricing for different storage and connectivity options, here are the full specs and purchase options. Apple A20 Pro Chip 8.5" OLED Super Retina XDR Display 2316 x 1512 Resolution (326 ppi) 128GB Storage Wi-Fi 7 | Bluetooth 6 Front 12MP Center Stage Camera Rear 12MP Wide Camera Supports Apple Pencil Pro & Pencil Acoustic Display | IP67 Rating iPadOS Apple 8.5" iPad mini (OLED, Standard Glass, 128GB, Wi-Fi Only, Midnight) OLED has finally come to the Apple 8.5" iPad mini . Now featuring an 8.5" Super Retina XDR OLED touchscreen, the iPad mini delivers vivid, accurate colors, 1,200 nits of peak HDR brightness, and a near-infinite contrast ratio.

items.title: Is a Partially Stacked Sensor Coming to the Canon EOS R7 Mark II?
items.summary_what: Is a Partially Stacked Sensor Coming to the Canon EOS R7 Mark II?: The Canon EOS R7 Mark II is slated for a Q1 2027 release .
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.

items.raw_content: The Canon EOS R7 Mark II is slated for a Q1 2027 release . We haven’t anything to dispute that as of yet, so that’s what we’re rolling with. Not much has come our way in a month or so letting us know what we can expect, but that changed today when some news from a solid source hit our inbox. EOS R7 Mark II Partially Stacked Sensor? We have been told that the Canon EOS R7 Mark II will have Canon’s first EOS (as far as we know) partially stacked sensor. The source claims that a “stacked sensor” has been talked about for quite some time, but recently that changed to partially stacked. We’re writing about it because it makes a lot of sense. We imagine a partially stacked sensor would cost less to manufacture and give the added bonus of faster readout speed. I think EOS R7 Mark II customers will take the fastest readout speed that Canon can give them. Sensor Resolution We have been told numerous times that the pixel count of the sensor will go up from the EOS R7’s 32-MP pixel count, and the only resolution that we have ever heard is 39MP, or very close to it. This has always made sense to us. An EOS R7 Mark II will be a very popular camera for wildlife, sports parents, and many other uses. We think the cropping potential of a 40MP sensor will be a selling point for a large segment of shooters. Canon EOS R7 Mark II Specifications We don’t have anything to add that we’re confident in about what else to expect from the follow-up to the EOS R7, which is a high-volume camera for Canon. We think it’s safe to say that we can expect some of the features from the EOS R8 Mark II and EOS R6 Mark III will to come to the R7 II. Features like IBIS (the real version), Pre-Shooting, 40fps and it will likely be a capable video camera as well. In Closing We still believe Canon will have one more announcement date before the end of 2026, but there won’t be any new EOS R cameras coming before Q1 of next year. We have also heard a few times that Canon will announce an RF-S lens or two that will be aimed at R7 Mark II customers, aimed at R7 Mark II customers; what those lenses will be, we don’t know. It would be nice to see a super-telephoto zoom for the RF-S series and a good fast prime like the EF-M 32mm f/1.4 STM. Again, we don’t know. It seems every other manufacturer has decided to go with partially stacked sensors outside of flagship products and it’s probably time that Canon does the same thing. We also wouldn’t be surprised to see the all-new sensor make its way into higher-end Powershot cameras, but smaller than APS-C. A lot of people think the sensor in the PowerShot V1 is based on Canon’s 32.5MP APS-C sensor. We don’t have 100% confidence in the information above, but we do think it’s solid enough to write about. More to come soon.

items.raw_content: The Canon EOS R8 Mark II is finally shipping after a long lead time from the September 15, 2026 announcement . Stock levels for the camera are good in every country that we have looked at. We think this camera is going to be a slow burn sales wise with its new ergonomic design and the fact that it’s $1899. The EOS R8 is a beloved camera for shooters that have no interest in $10,000 kits and with the launch price bump for the EOS R8 Mark II, that may keep many with their EOS R8 bodies, or even entice new R8 customers. Canon EOS R6 Mark II Full-Frame 24MP 40FPS 4K60P 24.2MP Full-Frame CMOS Sensor 4K60 10-Bit Internal Video, C-Log 3 External 6K ProRes RAW Recording Dual Pixel CMOS AF II 12 fps Mech. Shutter, 40 fps E. Shutter Sensor-Shift 5-Axis Image Stabilization $1,999 €1,999 · £1,699 Shop Now → Canon EOS R8 Mark II Full-Frame 24MP 40FPS 4K60P 24.2MP Full-Frame CMOS Sensor 4K60p 10-Bit Internal Video, Canon Log 3 40 fps Electronic Shutter, Pre-Capture 5-Axis In-Body Image Stabilization Dual Pixel CMOS AF II with Tracking 2.36m-Dot OLED Electronic Viewfinder $1,899 €1,799 · £1,729 Shop Now → Affiliate links EOS R6 Mark II vs EOS R8 Mark II The Canon EOS R6 Mark II is still a current product and is only $100 more currently and we think there is going to be a lot of cross shopping between the two cameras. On the surface, I’d take the EOS R8 Mark II for what I’d use it for, but for people that want or need a mechanical shutter, the EOS R6 Mark II is going to be the better choice. Features like pre-shooting don’t matter to everyone and there are a lot of other software tricks that may be of no interest to a lot of consumers. The EOS R8 Mark II does not have the same video chops as the EOS R6 Mark II, so that will be a consideration for some. Canon EOS R8 Mark II First Impressions I am not a reviewer and I have zero desire to be one. The zero day reviews for the EOS R8 Mark II all kind of said the same thing. There was a lot of focus on the design language and I think that had a lot of influence in the tone of the reviews. There was also the whole “retro” thing that we started. Canon says it’s retro inspired, and with the EG-E2 ergonomic grip, there is some visual cues that look like a throwback to yesteryear. Zero day reviewers do not have gear for more than a week or two in a lot of cases, even less time sometimes, so they have to get things out there as best as they can. The reviews that are going to come a month or 6 months from now are going to paint a different picture I think. Whether that’s in a positive or negative way, we’ll see. There will also be a demographic of people that hate big change in the way a camera is physically designed, and that’s ok. As for our initial impressions now that we have the camera? I much prefer the new design language over the R8, and the camera feels a bit more premium. The grip material feels a lot better than the EOS R8. Overall the new 8-series camera feels a notch higher than the R8. I also ordered the Canon EG-E2 ergonomic grip and it is really well executed and makes a significant difference for me. Is This Really Going to be Canon’s Entry-Level Full-Frame Camera? At $1,899, the price doesn’t feel entry-level, full-frame or not. I can assure you that this won’t be Canon’s entry-level full-frame camera at some point in time over the next year. For now, we’re calling the coming entry-level camera the EOS R9 . There is going to be hardware they’ll be able to remove from an entry-level camera to bring the price down significantly from $1899. If the price of the EOS R8 Mark II is too steep for you, I think we’re going to see it appear at the Canon USA Refurbished store a bit earlier than most other cameras. This may be a camera worth waiting 6 months to save some money. In-Closing I look forward to putting the EOS R8 Mark II through its paces alongside the EOS R1 this weekend. I’m not a fan of iPhone vs ARRI camera nonsense but I do enjoy seeing what the “normal” consumer buys vs the flagship professional products. Yes, the EOS R1 is going to outperform the EOS R8 Mark II by a large margin when it comes to autofocus and sensor readout speed, but it’ll be interesting to see if the R8 Mark II is better or equal at some other things. I think Canon has done well here.

items.raw_content: In this video, I explain the softmax function and the concept of temperature in the context of language models and neural networks. I start by revisiting the Markov chain coding challenge, then break down how softmax converts raw neural network outputs (logits) into probabilities, and how temperature can be used to adjust those probabilities making outputs more random (higher temperature) or more deterministic (lower temperature). I also briefly cover top-K and top-P sampling. Everything is demonstrated with p5.js sketches and a transformers.js language model running in the browser. items.raw_content: Edward Goldner ACS, cinematographer for the psychological crime thriller ‘Treasure & Dirt’ talks about bringing this six-part TV series to life using 65mm cinematography. Set in a dying opal town in the Outback, this is Australia’s very own ‘Twin Peaks’ full of strange folk and even stranger places. “I wanted the show’s imagery to be classic, shot in a way that would feel epic but also uncomplicated in a sense. We would often try to hold action in wider frames with minimal edits to create a bit of a theater quality. This also fed into the show’s stark, deadpan tone. The URSA Cine 17K 65 really complemented this, allowing the experience to be simultaneously restrained yet connected”. Read the full story at http://bmd.link/tXfFkr

items.summary_why: Affects color grading, Fairlight audio, and cut-page timelines in DaVinci Resolve production pipelines.

items.raw_content: A new live action projection mapping film, ‘Texas Legacy in Lights’, was captured with Blackmagic URSA Cine 12K LF and Blackmagic PYXIS 6K digital film cameras. Director John Franklin Rinehart of Austin Film Crew created the project for the Gonzales Memorial Museum, producing a first of its kind narrative film that’s projected twice a day against the large exteriors of the museum. Rinehart collaborated closely with DP Alex Walker for the project. “When we first conceived ‘Texas Legacy in Lights,’ the world's first live action projection mapping film which covers the Texas Revolution of 1835, there were a lot of technical questions and challenges that came up right off the bat. Alex and I were pioneering something together, solving problems that didn’t yet have answers. There were moments on set where we’d look at the monitor and realize we were capturing something that had never existed before,” explained Rinehart. Read the full story at https://www.blackmagicdesign.com/media/release/20260723-01

items.title: He photographed a Ramone in Queens and blues legends on a floral sofa, but this New York photographer’s real passion is everyday people
items.summary_what: He photographed a Ramone in Queens and blues legends on a floral sofa, but this New York photographer’s real passion is everyday people: In 1983, a line of Aboriginal men in traditional body paint and grass skirts walk across a patch of wasteland in Lower Manhattan, carrying spears.

items.raw_content: In 1983, a line of Aboriginal men in traditional body paint and grass skirts walk across a patch of wasteland in Lower Manhattan, carrying spears. Behind them, one of the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center soared into the sky. It’s very much a Harvey Wang picture. For decades, Wang has been photographing people from every walk of American life. Musicians. Punks. Shopkeepers. Complete strangers. Now his work is the subject of a new exhibition, Wang’s World: Photographs and Films of Harvey Wang , at the Bronx Documentary Center. The show brings together Wang’s photographs with his films, offering “an expansive view of an artist whose career has been rooted in observation”. Origin story Wang first picked up a camera as a teenager in Queens, where he was born and bred. After graduating in 1977, he worked as a photographer for the Village Voice under picture editor Fred W. McDarrah. Since then, his work has spanned documentary photography, portraiture, journalism, commercial work and film. His portraits stand out for their warmth and directness. In one, from 1979, three blues legends (Lightnin’ Hopkins, Clifton Chenier and Honeyboy Edwards) sit side by side on a floral sofa in front of even busier wallpaper: a real visual riot. Lightnin' Hopkins, Clifton Chenier, Honeyboy Edwards, NYC, 1979 (Image credit: Harvey Wang) Aboriginal People in NYC, 1983 (Image credit: Harvey Wang) Ella Baker, Civil Rights Activist, Harlem, 1982 (Image credit: Harvey Wang) In another, shown at the top of this page, rock icon Dee Dee Ramone and his wife Vera pose on a train platforms, all leather, denim and wild hair, yet still evoking the countenance of the bored commuter. Alongside his portraits, Wang has spent a career documenting the Big Apple's changing streets, especially the East Village in the 1970s and 1980s. This was a time of huge social and cultural change. The city was gritty and often broke, but it was also bursting with creative energy. In the words of the organisers, his work captures “a world populated by New Yorkers, Americans, artists, workers, families, strangers, neighborhoods, and fleeting moments”. These are pictures that above all capture everyday moments, although never in a way that's boring. In one, from 1984, a group of marathon runners make an unscheduled stop against a chain-link fence under an overpass; nature, evidently, had called. Marathoners, NYC, 1984 (Image credit: Harvey Wang) Cleveland Place, NYC, 1979 (Image credit: Harvey Wang) Brighton Beach, 1980 (Image credit: Harvey Wang) Another photograph depicts a scene that's more visceral and shocking – a young boy taking a baseball bat to a wrecked car, sending glass flying – although for many residents at the time, that may have seemed mundane too. Wang is also an award-winning filmmaker whose work ranges from documentary to experimental. By showing both types of work side by side, the exhibition explores the links between “the single frame and the passage of time, between portrait and story”. Wang’s World: Photographs and Films of Harvey Wang runs from November 13 to January 2027 at the BDC Annex, 364 E 151st St, Bronx, New York. It’s open Thursday and Friday from 3pm to 7pm, and Saturday from 1pm to 5pm. Admission is free but you need to reserve a spot. There’s an opening reception on Friday, November 13, from 6pm to 9pm.

items.raw_content: I love Italy, which I've visited a few times for both work and pleasure, and the places I've been have been pretty much what you'd expect from the tourist brochures. Gondolas. Vespas. Golden light on terracotta. Well-dressed and immaculately styled people. All present and correct. I admit, though, I've made little effort to visit the other side of the tracks. But that doesn't mean I'm not interested. And so a new show by Miron Zownir, the German-Ukrainian photographer dubbed "the poet of radical photography", definitely piqued my interest. Titled simply Italy , the exhibition takes place at Galerie Bene Taschen in Cologne, Germany. Shot across cities across the north and south of Italy, as well as rural Apulia in the south-east, these images offer a window onto Italy's many and complex social realities. If you know Zownir's work, you'll already have a good idea what that entails. If not, here's a quick primer. AIDS, arrests and a trip to Hell Born in Karlsruhe in southwestern Germany in 1953, Zownir took up photography in the late 1970s, at the height of the punk era. In 1980 he moved to the US, where he spent 15 years living in New York, LA and Pittsburgh, and his moody, expressionistic black-and-white pictures captured gay parties shortly before the AIDS crisis. Along the way he was arrested, censored and threatened more than once. Milan, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) Taranto, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) Florence, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) In 1995 he spent three months in Moscow photographing the homeless, the dying and the dead, an experience he described as "Dante's inferno". Since then his work has hung alongside Goya, Picasso and Cindy Sherman, appeared in Fotomuseum Winterthur's Darkside exhibitions and, in 2023, placed in direct dialogue with Otto Dix at the Deichtorhallen Hamburg. So how can we summarise his Italian photos? I'd say that above all, he's seeking to capture the gap between the image the country is selling and the life its people are actually living. In Milan, a giant Dolce & Gabbana ad of a man in a wide-brimmed hat looms over an almost empty bar, with a lone drinker hunched at the counter. In Venice, a carnival reveller strides past the door of a Parisian jewellery boutique, while another frame shows a canal bridge and its lamps dissolving into fog. In Florence, Zownir shoots the famous statues of the Piazza della Signoria from below, turning Hercules into a muscular black silhouette against the clouds, David reduced to a bystander. In Taranto, he finds a crumbling palazzo with huge eyes staring out from its empty window frames across a deserted square. Venice, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) Venice, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) Milan, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) It's not all grim and negative, though. For instance, a shot of a young woman in Milan, all face piercings and leg tattoos, reflects the fascination with people outside the mainstream he's had since his punk days. Indeed, Zownir himself would bristle at the idea that he's only interested in gloom. "What you might consider dark or grotesque might well be free, uncompromising, strange, tragic, unique, interesting or whatever," he once told Slow Travel Berlin . On this evidence, Italy has plenty of all of the above. Italy runs at Galerie Bene Taschen , Lindenstrasse 19, Cologne, Germany, from Saturday, November 28, 2pm-6pm until Saturday, February 6.

items.title: MotionVFX Content is Coming to Final Cut Pro as Apple Creator Studio Gets Overhaul

items.raw_content: When it was first announced, it sounded like Apple was going after Adobe by introducing its own version of Creative Cloud with Creator Studio. Today, that becomes much clearer as Apple has introduced some major updates to its Creator Studio, highlighted by the announcement that Final Cut Pro for Mac will now include built-in MotionVFX along with Pixelmator Pro. Is Final Cut Pro back, baby? We’ll wait and see for now, but this is a major transformation for Apple Creator Studio and FCP, so here’s what you need to know. A Major Update for Final Cut Pro So, while there’s a lot to explore with Apple Creator Studio getting a transformative overhaul itself, it’s hard to not just really focus on MotionVFX coming to Final Cut Pro, as this should add an expansive collection of visual effects, plugins, transitions, templates, and motion graphics tools to the previously VFX-lackluster NLE. “This is our most exciting update since the launch of Apple Creator Studio. MotionVFX content in Final Cut Pro gives subscribers rapid access to extensive professional video effects and content, bringing incredible value to the suite. Logic Pro’s new Browser allows users to explore and experiment with more sounds than ever as they create music. Pixelmator Pro’s sophisticated fill capabilities now let users completely reimagine any part of an image. And the assistant capabilities in Logic Pro, Keynote, Pages, and Numbers are going to change the game for how people interact with and learn to use these apps.” - Brent Chiu-Watson, Apple’s senior director of Worldwide Product Marketing for Apps and iCloud. The other big news is that Pixelmator Pro will now be available in FCP, and it will also introduce its own Generate Fill feature, which lets editors transform selected areas of an image using natural language. A Big Step Forward for Apple Creator Studio Along with the FCP updates, Apple Creator Studio aims to be much more robust and expansive overall, as it will also add several new features for Logic Pro for Mac, including a new intelligent assistant in beta, an enhanced Stem Splitter that will be able to separate drums, and a completely redesigned Browser that will be able to incorporate all sounds, with music understanding and even a Splice library. Keynote, Pages, and Numbers also get a host of new AI features, as your AI assistants become more empowered to support automated workflows and MCP support. There are also new stock video options in the Content Hub and more themes and templates. Freeform is getting a boost with new text styles for one-step formatting and reuse across boards, custom and preset board background colors, and the ability to edit images directly in Pixelmator Pro and generate editable shapes from text descriptions, which will arrive in December. Price and Availability All these new updates in Apple Creator Studio are set to be available this month, and they will be free for existing subscribers. New subscribers can sign up for plans starting at $12.99 a month or $129 a year. You can find more info about these Apple Creator Studio and Final Cut Pro updates on the company’s website here .

items.title: Take a trip back to Perth’s rave scene in Simon Wright’s design retrospective
items.summary_what: Take a trip back to Perth’s rave scene in Simon Wright’s design retrospective: Drawing on the Future is a two-volume series that documents the Australian city's underground music scene at the turn of the millennium.
items.summary_why: Influences typography, UI/UX prototyping speed, and vector design production assets.

items.raw_content: Drawing on the Future is a two-volume series that documents the Australian city's underground music scene at the turn of the millennium. It may be hard to believe, but it's been 26 years since we entered a new millennium. And while it may feel like yesterday, the late 90s and early 2000s were a wildly different time for technology, dance, and graphic design. Branding specialist and multi-disciplined designer Simon Wright takes a look back at this unique era in his latest book series. Drawing on the Future is a two-volume collection which brings together more than a decade of his design work for Perth's underground rave and electronic music scene. "It explores the typography, print techniques, visual experimentation and DIY culture that shaped the scene before social media existed," Simon tells Creative Boom. Documenting a bygone landscape where design work straddled digital and analogue tools, these collections offer fascinating insight into a lifestyle and work ethic that has long since transformed beyond recognition. Unlike more conventional design retrospectives, Drawing on the Future is filled with Simon's irreverent wit as he tracks his journey from university all the way through to designing flyers, posters, and other promotional ephemera for the underground dance scene. Packed with dozens of drawings and logo mock-ups, its pages are a snapshot of an optimistic future that never quite materialised. For readers of a certain age, the aesthetic will be all too recognisable. Pulpy comic-book illustrations sit alongside sleek, chromatic typography, capped off with overlaid compositions that showcase the Photoshop trends of the time. An explosive concoction, perhaps, but emblematic of the scene's mood. "It took around a year to put together all my old source files, scans and stories about the making of these artworks," says Simon. "It's an historical record of how the scene was at the time, how the flyers and artwork influenced - and were influenced in turn - by the music and the different sub-genres." Given the constraints of computer storage at the time, not to mention the sometimes precarious nature of digital archiving, the volume of work presented here is somewhat miraculous. Drawing on the Future is a group effort, pulling not only from Simon's personal archive, but also the rave community itself. This is even more notable when it comes to the iterations of brandmarks and flyers Simon has carefully presented. It would be so easy for these to be lost to time or the recycle bin, but here readers can learn about how they evolved as the tools and techniques are meticulously explained. Even if you weren't there to witness Perth's rave scene at the time, there's plenty to appreciate from a design perspective. As Simon explains: "I've also included unused concepts, sketches, 'how they were made' anecdotes and a few misremembered tales of those times. "I wanted to create a collection that wasn't just an archive of the many, many flyers," Simon adds. "But also a bit of a historical context and a look into what was going through my brain at the time. How, why, what, when and where!"

items.title: International Assembly 2026: Glasgow's festival returns with a secret stage and a night in a castle
items.summary_what: International Assembly 2026: Glasgow's festival returns with a secret stage and a night in a castle: Here's everything you need to know about the November event.
items.summary_why: Influences typography, UI/UX prototyping speed, and vector design production assets.
items.summary_action: Review the full source announcement for technical requirements and deployment details.
items.raw_content: Here's everything you need to know about the November event. We get it: it's cold, raining, and you just want to stay inside for the next six months. But you know, in your heart of hearts, this only leads to misery. And if you can get to Glasgow this November, there's an event that's purpose-made to blow the cobwebs away and get your blood pumping again. International Assembly , the design and creative festival run by INTL, returns to Britain's third biggest city from 12–22 November, with events at Glasgow Royal Concert Hall and The Pyramid at Anderston. Over those 11 years, the organisers have packed in a tremendous amount, including a one-day conference, weekend workshops, and a two-day Live Project connecting students with industry. And that's not all. This year there's an all-new Secret Stage with undisclosed guests (ooh!). Plus the International Creative Awards return, which this year will be presented in a medieval castle (double ooh!). Throughout the event, you'll also have a chance to check out the International Poster Exhibition, which was my personal highlight of the 2025 event. Not your average event Yes, I was there in person last year to help judge its student competition. And so trust me when I tell you: this isn't your standard sit-in-the-dark-and-take-notes design conference. Yes, there are talks, of course, pretty darned good ones if 2025 was anything to go by. But a lot of the energy comes from people rolling up their sleeves and actually making things together. As co-founder James Gilchrist puts it: "Our goal has always been to create the dream event which we would want to attend." The conference kicks off on Thursday 12 November, bringing together thinkers, makers and innovators working across graphic design, branding, coding, animation, art and advertising. This year's line-up includes Bráulio Amado, COLLINS, Harriet Richardson, FISK, Shamma Buhazza, Vlad Boyko, Coding Systems, Eva Cremers, GF Smith and Readymag, with further names still to be announced. Sounds like a random mix? That's deliberate. "We have a bit of a formula for curation, so we hope there will be somebody who everyone can connect with deeply," explains project manager Mook Attanath. As for the brand-new Secret Stage, which opens for business on Saturday 14 November, four undisclosed special guests will share personal stories, insights and work. Who they are is anyone's guess, which is a fun idea I've never seen at a design conference before. Workshops and projects Beyond the talking, there's lots of doing. Workshops run over the weekend of 14–15 November and cover type design, coding, editorial, illustration, visual language, poster design, and traditional graphic design. As co-founder Beth Wilson explains: "I think it's one of the few festivals where there are not only audience-based events but intensive workshops and projects where you actually produce new work." Here's what's on offer: Signopic with Patryk Hardziej: learn the traditional techniques the old masters used to create logos, symbols, marques and signs. Scavenged Narratives with Vlad Boyko: develop your own visual language and create experimental posters. Flexible Visual Systems Design with Coding Systems (Tim Rodenbröker and Martin Lorenz): starting with an application built in Processing, discover how to combine tech, art and design to produce generative visual work. Daily Disk with FISK: produce your own experimental piece of editorial work and contribute to a collaborative newspaper, printed courtesy of Newspaper Club. Type Playground with Shamma Buhazza: create a custom modular font using patterns, textures, grids and drawing. Alien Assembly with Eva Cremers: design and illustrate your own 3D character, considering personality, emotion and story, then watch it come to life. From contest to ceilidh On 16–17 November, students and recent graduates take part in the Live Project: two days of mentorship from design studios while working on a live competition brief. More than 22 work placements are on offer, along with the chance to present work at the festival and win prizes. Having judged last year's entries, I can vouch that the standard of work is high and the opportunity is valuable. On Monday 16 November, a panel discussion tackles a question many in the sector will recognise, with the blunt title: 'What the f_ck is happening in the Scottish design industry?'. Nowt like getting straight to the point. The International Creative Awards, meanwhile, get a bit of an upgrade this year. For the first time, winners and guests will gather at the medieval Rowallan Castle on Friday 13 November. The evening will feature traditional music, fine dining, and the presentation of handcrafted concrete trophies to this year's winners, plus a ceilidh, a traditional night of Scottish music and dancing. Oh, and if you're new to the city, Readymag is also running walking tours of Glasgow earlier that day so you can get nicely acquainted with this fabulous place. Finally, if you're in Glasgow at any point during the event, I'd urge you to check out the International Poster Exhibition, which, as I said, runs throughout. Featuring 190 contemporary works by more than 200 designers and creatives from around the world, the exhibition opens on Thursday 12 November with music, refreshments and the launch of the new International Poster Book. It closes with a goodbye gathering on Sunday 22 November. What's on when With so much going on, it's worth planning ahead. Here's a quick summary of the main events: Thursday 12 November: Conference; International Poster Exhibition opening Friday 13 November: Glasgow Walking Tours x Readymag; awards ceremony; festival ceilidh Saturday 14 November: Weekend Workshops (day one); Secret Stage Sunday 15 November: Weekend Workshops (day two) Monday 16 November: Live Project (day one); Nitty Gritty panel discussion Tuesday 17 November: Live Project (day two) Sunday 22 November: Goodbye gathering at the International Poster Exhibition I'll leave the last word to James. "If you're looking for a sense of community, a kick up the arse, an excuse to get out of the studio, a reminder of why you do what you do, then get yourself to International Assembly," he says. "You'll be welcome."

items.title: A Practical Guide To Naming Things
items.summary_what: A Practical Guide To Naming Things. The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it.
items.summary_why: That’s why we have so much confusion about colors, icons, UI components, features — and that’s why we struggle to name design tokens, HTML classes, and variables.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: Naming is hard. The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it. That’s why we have so much confusion about colors, icons, UI components, features — and that’s why we struggle to name design tokens, HTML classes, and variables. Sometimes, the names we choose are too generic , so it’s difficult to understand what exactly is meant. And sometimes they are too specific , leaving little room for flexibility and reuse. How do we choose the right names? And which naming conventions work best? Let’s take a closer look. How To Name Things If you’re looking for some inspiration for naming HTML classes, CSS properties, or JavaScript functions, Classnames is a wonderful resource jam-packed with ideas that get you thinking outside the box . The site provides thematically grouped lists of words perfect for naming. You’ll find terms to describe different kinds of behavior, likeness between things, order, grouping, and association, but also themed collections of words that wouldn’t instantly come to one’s mind when it comes to code, among them words from nature, art, theater, music, architecture, fashion, and publishing. How To Name Colors How would you choose the right name for a given color? Fortunately, David Aerne maintains a tremendous repository of color names , currently with 30355 unique color names , sourced from various references and 1000s of user contributions. Of course, the repository comes with a color picker and name search and plenty of other color pickers as well. Tremendous work, which is also a fantastic reference to keep nearby. How To Name Layers and Groups What makes a good name? Javier Cuello summarized a set of naming best practices that help you name your layers, groups, and components in a consistent and scalable way. As Javier points out, a good name has a logical structure, is short, meaningful, known by everyone, and not related to visual properties. He shares do’s and don’ts to illustrate how to achieve that and also takes a closer look at all the fine little details you need to consider when naming sizes, colors, groups, layers, and components. How To Name Design Tokens How to build a flexible design token taxonomy that works across different products? That was the challenge that the team at Intuit faced. The parent company of products such as Mailchimp, QuickBooks, TurboTax, and Mint developed a flexible token system that goes beyond the brand theme to serve as the foundational system for a wide array of products. Nate Baldwin wrote a case study in which he shares valuable insights into the making of Intuit’s design token taxonomy . It dives deeper into the pain points of the old taxonomy system, the criteria they defined for the new system, and how it was created. Lots of takeaways for building your own robust and flexible token taxonomy are guaranteed. Frequent Names For UI Components Looking at what other people call similar things is a great way to start when you’re struggling with naming . And what better source could there be than other design systems? Before you end up in the design system rabbit hole, Iain Bean did the research for you and created the Component Gallery . It’s a collection that includes plenty of examples for more than 50 UI components — from accordion to visually hidden — and also lists other names that the UI components go by. A fantastic resource, and not only with regard to naming. Bonus: Name That UI , a visual dictionary of common UI components. How To Name New Features Features often have low adoption due to poor discoverability . Feature adoption needs time — first the feature must be discovered, then understood, then tried, learned, and eventually built into existing workflow . Erin Gannon has written a helpful practical guide on how to make sure all of it happens. Good names are driven by user needs and problems. They should signal the value or outcome of a feature (the job-to-be-done), and — most importantly! — tap into the user’s own language. So ask people to explain a feature in their own words and then use the words they use. How To Name Variables (Taxonomy Map) A wonderful example of naming guidelines for a complex multi-brand, multi-themed design system comes from the Vodafone UK Design System team. Their Variables Taxonomy Map breaks down the anatomy and categorization of a design token into a well-orchestrated system of collections. The map illustrates four collections required to support the system and connections between tokens — from brand and primitives to semantics and pages . It builds on top of Nathan Curtis’ work on naming design tokens and enables everyone to gather insight about where a token is used and what it represents, just from its name. If you want to explore more approaches to naming design tokens, I’ve put together a list of useful Figma kits and resources that are worth checking out. Design Token Naming Guide + Inventory Romina Kavcic created a helpful little tool for naming design tokens — from learning how they work and how to name them well to configuring your own naming structure with components, categories, states, and roles. Bonus: The Design Token Names Inventory spreadsheet , with a simple structure with four levels to give you a bird’s-eye view of all your design tokens. You can easily add rows, themes, and modes without losing track, and filter your tokens . Naming Products or Services If you are looking for the right name for your product or service, Onym is a fantastic open-source repository that organizes tools and resources for finding names for brainstorming, vetting, guides, sprints, etymologies — all the way to cautionary tales and agencies that name things, as well as useful books to take a look at. Useful Bookmarks for Naming Things A quick-reference list of tools and guides for naming just about... well, anything , in one place: Naming buttons → NN/g on UI copy Naming classes → classnames.paulrobertlloyd.com Naming colors → parrot.color.pizza Naming design tokens → Intuit’s design token taxonomy Naming features → Shopify Polaris naming guide Naming icons → Iconography guide Naming layers → goodpractices.design Naming products → guide.onym.co Naming UI components → component.gallery Naming UI behavior → namethatui.com Naming variables → Vodafone UK Variables Taxonomy Map and naming-cheatsheet on GitHub UI terminology → Moccu’s naming convention framework Wrapping Up The right name is the one that’s well-understood and used by the team and users. So much time is wasted speaking about the very same thing but in different dialects — the designer’s dialect, the developer’s dialect, the product manager’s dialect, and the user’s dialect. That’s what often causes frustration and confusion. So if you see low adoption, it might be merely because of the name. And pay attention to potential naming conflicts and put them in a backlog of things to address later. It’s one of those fine little details that can reduce frustration and confusion and help teams work together better. Editor’s Note We hope you’ll find these wonderful projects useful — put together by wonderful creators. A friendly shout-out to everyone sharing their work with folks to use and learn from! That’s one of the reasons why we truly love the web and people building and designing it. 💚 At Smashing, we love the web . That’s why we publish articles and books, run workshops and events around everything web. We love seeing what we all can do to make the web more accessible and usable. We also love organizing and attending online events — with friendly discounts for large groups (5+ attendees) and schools and students. Interested? Just send us an email and we’ll sort it out! items.title: Stop Treating CSS Container Queries Like Traditional Media Queries

items.raw_content: To be completely honest with you, I missed the news when CSS Container Queries first shipped. And when I finally heard about it, my very first thought was, “Why exactly do I need this when media queries already exist?” I’m not proud of that reaction, knowing what I know now, but it was comforting to know that I wasn’t alone. In fact, there are legions of us out there. What baffles me is that container queries aren’t a new feature, as it currently sits at around 94% browser support . And yet, very few people are actually using it. According to the State of CSS survey, 86% of developers are aware of container queries, but only 41.4% actually use them. Surveys can be biased and not completely representative of our entire field, but this one is certainly the best indicator we’ve got. Kevin Powell also talked about this at SmashingConf Amsterdam 2026: Container Queries adoption has been terrible. And that is so strange to me, knowing that the ability for components to adapt to the size of their outer container has been at the top of so many CSS wishlists over the years. I’m not particularly interested in how many people are using container queries as much as in how they are using them. I can’t account for everyone, but from what I’ve seen — including in my own early attempts — many of us are using them wrong . The bottom line is that incorrect use comes down to the same impression I had when learning about them: they absolutely look just like media queries at first glance . And since they look similar, it’s easy to assume they serve similar purposes and work the same way. They don’t. Note : I should state up front that what I’m focusing on in this article is using container size queries, i.e., a responsive design technique for responding to the size of a particular container. There are also container style queries that respond to a container’s computed styles (and are experimental at the time of this writing). You can catch up on those in Juan Diego’s piece here on Smashing Magazine where he examines their possible use cases. Media Queries Look Outward The viewport is a proxy. It always has been. Media queries are what gave us the illusion that screen width alone is responsible for how responsive apps adapt to their environment. Ask yourself this: When you write @media , what are you asking the browser? @media (min-width: 1024px) { .card { display: flex; } I, like most developers, am asking the browser: How wide is the screen right now? That’s it. Media queries answer that beautifully, but what happens when this .card component is placed in a grid cell that’s 300px wide on a 1920px desktop screen? The media query doesn’t care; it does its job. The viewport is still 1920px , so min-width: 1024px fires and the matched query styles are applied, even though the card only has 300px of space to work with. Eventually, everything in the card deforms, overflows, or cramps up. “Media queries are dumb. Not dumb in terms of the concept, but dumb in that they don’t know very much. In fact, most people assume that they know more than they do.” — Kevin Powell It’s common to think of responsive design purely as a system for updating complete page layouts, like going from two columns on a large screen to a single column on a small screen. Container Queries Look Inward Container queries are smarter than that. They make responsive layouts more reliant on what’s happening inside a component rather than on the outer context that has no insight into a component’s contents. It is more like: “How much space is available for me in this specific spot, right now?” Here is the same card code example we looked at in the last section, but with a container query: .card-wrapper { container-name: card; container-type: inline-size; } @container card (min-width: 450px) { .card { display: flex; flex-direction: row; } } This changes everything. The card isn’t influenced by the viewport; its only concern is whether the .card component’s parent wrapper has at least 450px of inline (i.e., horizontal in a left-to-right writing mode) space. If that condition is true, the component goes horizontal; if not, it goes to its default block display. The logic works like this: When there’s enough room, both items ( .flex-item ) sit side-by-side, each exactly half the parent container’s width. When there is limited space, the second item wraps to the next line. Because flex-grow is active on each item, the wrapped items stretch to fill most of the parent’s width. If the item is a container itself, it detects the sudden width expansion and fires. /* The flex parent */ .flex-layout { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; } /* Register a flex item as a container */ .flex-item { container-type: inline-size; flex: 1 1 390px; /* Grow to fill space, wrap at 390px */ } /* Default Card Styles (narrow / side-by-side) */ .card { display: flex; flex-direction: column; background: #f4f4f4; } /* Once there's enough room for a full row */ @container (min-width: 600px) { .card { flex-direction: row; align-items: center; background: #e2f0d9; } } This works. As the parent size shrinks and the cards wrap to two lines, the card item expands, the container query fires, and applies the necessary styles. Conclusion At the end of the day, the core reason why container queries look incredibly similar to media queries is simply familiarity. They’re not exactly “new”, but they are way less understood and adopted than media queries. But media queries have plenty of their own limitations; otherwise, we wouldn’t need container queries to fill those gaps. What we have is a more effective feature for detecting when a specific component’s context changes and a means for adjusting styles based on its content, as it should be when that component can exist in multiple contexts.

items.title: Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom
items.summary_what: Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom: Sooner or later, a CFO looks at your wireframes and asks what any of it actually does for the bottom line.
items.summary_why: Influences typography, UI/UX prototyping speed, and vector design production assets.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: Sooner or later, a CFO looks at your wireframes and asks what any of it actually does for the bottom line. Storyboards don’t answer that question, and the era when a 5-minute pitch could answer it ended, unfortunately, a while ago. These days, if you want to win budget, buy-in, and backing for UX , the design has to be provably good for the business, not only for the people using it. And proving that takes more than taping a dollar sign to a redesign. You have to understand how your organization defines value in the first place, how it measures that value, and how a credible line gets drawn between a design initiative and an outcome leadership already cares about. Rather than scatter tips, this article follows one worked example the whole way through. Meridian is a mid-size B2B SaaS company, and it is entirely made up — that label matters, so it gets repeated where it counts. Its onboarding redesign carries the same figures from goal-setting through cost accounting , causal testing , and the final ROI number , because a framework only becomes tangible when the numbers connect. Every step is one you can rerun inside your own organization. Why ROI Matters More Than Ever in UX Conversations Companies now want clarity on what every dollar buys, and “delightful user experiences” stopped clearing that bar some time ago. I still remember a former colleague celebrating a $1 million redesign he’d gotten greenlit mostly on the strength of a couple of three.js tricks. Try that pitch in front of a finance team today and see how far the particles get you. Executives don’t hate UX, they just hate vagueness . A pitch built on “users will find it easier” loses, every time, to the department promising 12% more sales in Q3. The difference is the one between a streamlined checkout flow that reduced cart abandonment with completed purchases up 22%, and the same work rewarded with “the QA testers like it.” One of those goes on your resume. The rest of this article is about earning the first version, with Meridian’s numbers doing the work. When Business Goals And KPIs Don’t Exist Yet Most writing about UX ROI makes a convenient assumption: that the organization already owns clean business goals and KPIs for you to hook your work onto. Real companies are messier than that. Plenty run on ambitions like “grow faster” or “ improve the customer journey ” that nobody ever broke into anything measurable, and an ROI case built on that ambiguity sounds impressive right up until somebody scrutinizes it. So the first job is often to help the organization define what success even looks like . Interview stakeholders across departments — what does product consider a good quarter, where does customer success watch users struggle, where do sales deals stall — and listen for the themes that keep resurfacing across conversations, because those recurring themes are the company’s latent business objectives. A useful forcing function is the OKR model (Objectives and Key Results) , which doesn’t tolerate vagueness. At Meridian, the stated ambition was “improve the rate of new users’ adoption of the platform,” which you can neither design toward nor measure against. Interviews turned up the real shape of the problem. Trial users needed a median of 14 days to reach first value, most churned before getting there, and onboarding questions were burying the support queue. Out of that came an OKR with actual edges: reduce median time-to-first-value from 14 days to 7 with the use of a guided setup flow, and lift trial-to-paid conversion from 8% to 9.5%. One warning about formalizing KPIs : Impose them from inside the UX team and leadership will suspect you’ve rigged the field in your own favor, so co-create them with whoever owns the outcome — though never at the price of accepting targets that set your team up for an uncomfortable situation. Meridian’s head of product agreed that setup-completion rate was a fair proxy for onboarding usability, and customer success signed off on time-to-first-value, a number already sitting on their own dashboard. A KPI ladder that ends at a metric somebody already watches buys you credibility before any design work starts. Quantifying The Full Cost Of The Investment ROI has a denominator , and the denominator is where most UX teams go wrong. You can’t calculate a return without strategic financial planning , yet cost usually gets counted as designer salaries or consulting hours and nothing else. A finance team will find the rest whether or not you counted it, so count it first . Direct costs are the visible ones. Meridian’s redesign ran $45,000 in design and research labor plus another $8,000 in tooling and participant incentives. Licenses for Figma , UserTesting, Hotjar, analytics platforms, research incentive spend — all of it belongs in the total, and that’s before the inevitable instances of vendor lock-in every UX team eventually faces. Engineering sits in the same column, because a UX redesign doesn’t stop at the mockup . Building the guided setup took two frontend sprints plus a QA pass, $38,000 worth, and the project generated about $4,000 of coordination overhead along the way in new syncs and shared dashboards. The line item nearly everyone misses, and the one worth stealing from this article if you steal nothing else, is stakeholder time . Workshops, design reviews, and feedback sessions all pull senior people away from their primary work. A VP of Product spending four hours a week in UX reviews is a VP not spending those hours on roadmap planning or partner negotiations. Log the attendance — who came, for how long, at what seniority — and price it at fully loaded cost, meaning salary plus benefits divided by productive hours. A quarter’s worth of workshops, reviews, and interviews at Meridian priced out at $22,000. Add it all up: $45,000 in design labor, $8,000 in tooling, $38,000 in engineering, $22,000 in stakeholder time, $4,000 in coordination. The investment is $117,000. Saying that number out loud beats saying “we spent $45K on design,” precisely because it already includes everything a finance team would have dug up on its own. Proving Causation, Not Just Correlation Most UX ROI pitches die right here. Conversions rose after the redesign, sure — and the CFO wants to know how you ruled out the new pricing, the seasonal traffic bump, and the marketing campaign that shipped the same week. Without a convincing answer, your entire ROI story crumbles . After all these years, the gold standard for proving causation is still A/B testing : run the old experience against the new one on an even traffic split until the sample means something. Onboarding happens to suit a phased rollout, which is why Meridian could do this cleanly. For eight weeks, half of new trial signups received the redesigned guided setup while half stayed on the legacy flow. Control converted to paid at 8.0%. The variant came in at 9.4%. With roughly 6,100 trials inside the window, the difference was statistically significant, but a 1.4-point gap on a single test is still the kind of result that deserves a second look before anyone builds a budget on it, which is one reason the team held back on attribution below. Where a split isn’t feasible — a change too structural, a user base too small — fall back to a time series instead. Measure steadily for weeks before the change, implement, then keep measuring against the baseline you established. Documenting whatever else happens around the same time as your UX change is the unglamorous half of causation. A pricing-page test from Meridian’s marketing team overlapped weeks five through eight of the rollout. The UX team noted it, confirmed it hit both cohorts evenly, and still chose to attribute only 70% of the observed lift to the redesign in the final math. There is no formula that produces that number; treat it as an illustrative assumption for this example. The team asked how much of the lift could plausibly belong to the pricing test if it had helped one cohort slightly more than the other, settled on a ceiling of about a third, and rounded the redesign’s share down to 70%. Your figure will differ. What matters is that it is written down and argued for before the results arrive, not fitted to them afterwards. That restraint is worth money in a skeptical room. “We attribute roughly 70% of the lift to the onboarding change, with the remainder likely influenced by concurrent pricing work” survives cross-examination; claiming everything does not. Cohort analysis then backed the number up, since the lift held across acquisition channels and tenure bands, and at that point the skeptics had very little left to work with. Leading and lagging indicators belong on the same slide, because each covers the other’s weakness. Meridian’s leading indicators moved first — setup completion climbed from 62% to 89%, median time-to-first-value dropped from 14 days to 6.5 — and the lagging trial-to-paid number followed. Mechanism first, business outcome second. Presented together, they form a causal chain that’s harder to poke holes in than either one alone. The ROI Calculation, End to End So what did Meridian actually earn? The company sees about 40,000 trial signups a year. Lifting conversion from 8.0% to 9.4% adds roughly 560 paying customers annually, and at an average of $1,800 in annual recurring revenue per account, those customers represent about $1,008,000 in new ARR. Applying the conservative 70% attribution from the causal work trims the defensible figure to roughly $706,000. Set that against the full $117,000 investment and the first-year ROI lands near 5:1, with payback arriving in roughly two months. There’s a second line, too. Onboarding-related support tickets dropped about 30%, some 3,600 fewer tickets a year, worth another $54,000 annually at $15 per resolved ticket. Keep it as its own line rather than folding it into one swollen headline number. The case reads as more honest that way and loses none of its force. Three assumptions carry that result, and each belongs on the slide next to it. The 40,000 signups and the $1,800 average ARR are the prior year’s actuals held flat, so a growth or pricing change moves the outcome in either direction. The 70% attribution is the illustrative assumption from the causal work, not a measured quantity. And the two-month payback counts new ARR as it lands rather than revenue recognized net of churn, which flatters the timeline; on a net basis the payback stretches to roughly a quarter. State those three plainly and a finance team can adapt the example to its own numbers. Hide them and the whole thing starts to look like marketing math, however careful the experiment was. What persuades in the final presentation is not sophistication. Open with the baseline: what stalled trials and support volume were already costing. Show the delta in terms leadership reads fluently, metrics like conversion rate uplift chief among them. A chart of setup completion climbing from 62% to 89% will beat a paragraph of UX jargon, and a translation like “each abandoned setup costs us 0.3 support tickets” beats the chart. Above all, keep every figure identical from the first slide to the last. A room full of finance people forgives many things, but never numbers that wobble between slides. Tailoring The Case To Whoever Holds The Purse Strings Budget decisions come out of coalitions. A CFO may hold the final say when adding AI to the checkout process , but marketing, product, and customer success all lean on that decision, and each means something different by “value.” A CFO hears cost, revenue, and risk. A CMO hears conversion and acquisition cost, since UX is a lever for increasing marketing ROI . Product counts support tickets; customer success thinks in retention. The underlying numbers never change; only the framing rotates, and a CFO wants a projection, not a moodboard . Meridian’s CFO slide read “the onboarding redesign protects roughly $706,000 in new ARR a year against a $117,000 investment,” while the CMO version led with what a 9.4% trial conversion does to blended acquisition cost. Beyond the Dollar Sign: Qualitative and Non-Financial Metrics Some UX outcomes never translate cleanly into revenue, and pretending they do weakens the parts of your case that are solid. The trick with qualitative evidence is collecting it rigorously enough that nobody can wave it off as anecdote. Scores like Net Promoter Score (NPS) , CSAT, and Customer Effort Score already sit inside most reporting cadences, which makes them cheap to borrow. Tie your work to their movement, and segment wherever the data allows. Meridian could say that NPS among trial users on the redesigned onboarding was 51 against 34 for the legacy flow, which lands far harder than any blended average. Verbatim feedback from surveys, support transcripts, and app store reviews adds the emotional weight the scores lack. Internal tools deserve the same discipline, since employee experience is increasingly recognized as a business driver — a dashboard redesign that hands account managers 45 minutes a day back is a productivity gain, a satisfaction gain, and a retention lever all in one. Brand perception resists direct measurement but leaves tracks in repeat visits, organic referrals, and social sentiment. It carries extra weight in trust-sensitive industries like finance or healthcare , and it forms fast, given that UX design influences the first impressions of a whopping 94% of customers . Whatever you collect, systematize the collecting . Run pre- and post-surveys with consistent question sets, use structured usability testing with task-based scoring, and put the qualitative right next to the quantitative when you present. “Setup completion rose from 62% to 89%, and in post-test interviews 8 of 10 participants called the new flow intuitive, against 3 of 10 for the old one” — a pairing like that is much harder to dismiss than either half on its own. Making the Case Stick UX loses the budget battle unless it’s mapped to company-wide objectives , so phrase the proposal in the words of this year’s board presentation. Nobody at Meridian pitched “simplify the onboarding UI”; the pitch was a redesigned trial experience worth 1.4 points of upgrade rate, roughly $1M in annual recurring revenue before attribution. Bring evidence in both registers, since that is what social proof is for : the case, clearly labeled, plus screenshots, impact graphs, and user quotes. Find internal allies who can repeat the ROI narrative in rooms you’ll never enter, and write the playbook down, because repeatable ROI is what earns recurring investment . Resources for Going Deeper This topic has been explored extensively by researchers, practitioners, and consultancies. Here’s a curated set of resources worth studying if you want to build a stronger ROI practice around UX. “Measuring the User Experience” by Tom Tullis and Bill Albert is the definitive guide to UX metrics. It covers everything from task-based measurements to survey design to statistical analysis, and it’s written for practitioners, not academics. Jared Spool’s “The $300 Million Button” case study is a classic example of how a single UX change (removing a mandatory registration step) generated massive revenue uplift. It’s a story every UX professional should have in their back pocket. Forrester’s research on UX ROI provides enterprise-focused frameworks for building business cases around experience design, including their widely cited finding that every dollar invested in UX returns $100. “UX Strategy” by Jaime Levy bridges the gap between design thinking and business strategy, offering practical tools for aligning UX initiatives with organizational goals and market positioning. The Design Value Index by the Design Management Institute tracks publicly traded companies that invest heavily in design against the S&P 500. The data consistently shows that design-led companies outperform the index by significant margins, and it’s a powerful data point for executive presentations. Google’s HEART framework provides a structured approach to selecting UX metrics at scale. HEART stands for Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, and Task success, and it’s particularly useful for teams that struggle to decide which metrics to track. Conclusion A seat at the table never comes from beauty or novelty. It comes from measurable, defensible impact , which means UX leaders have to trade the artist’s posture for the strategist’s. Speak in outcomes rather than outputs. Connect pixels to profit. When someone challenges the numbers, don’t flinch. Show the controlled experiment, the cohort analysis, and the before-and-after metrics, every figure holding steady from the first slide to the last, the way Meridian’s did, with the customer quotes and the employee-satisfaction data sitting right beside the revenue impact. Prove the work does more than delight users, and be ready to defend the ratio line by line. That’s when the CFO leans in, and that’s when design stops being optional.

I explain Bayes' theorem, demonstrate word frequency analysis, implement Laplacian smoothing, and build a working sentiment classifier that runs entirely in the browser. items.title: Sidney Lumet Reinvented the Walk and Talk in 'The Verdict'
items.summary_what: Sidney Lumet Reinvented the Walk and Talk in 'The Verdict'. Aaron Sorkin’s hallway marches made it a signature move, and we’ve covered how to write one .

items.raw_content: You’ve seen a thousand walk-and-talks. Aaron Sorkin’s hallway marches made it a signature move, and we’ve covered how to write one . They're nice as a shot choice and in writing because they automatically give a scene energy. Characters feel like they have a purpose, like they're going somewhere, instead of just standing or sitting and delivering lines. But they are harder to shoot because of that motion. Usually it means a Steadicam just backpedaling in front of two actors firing off lines, but you also have to light a bigger space and think about coverage from potentially multiple angles. In ye olden days you'd have to get a dolly track involved. A new essay from Moviewise looks at how Sidney Lumet handled the same basic setup in The Verdict without leaning on a tired formula... but still made things difficult. David Mamet adapted the film from Barry Reed's novel. It stars Paul Newman as Frank Galvin , an alcoholic Boston ambulance-chaser. It was nominated for five Academy Awards: Best Picture, Director, Actor (Newman), Supporting Actor (James Mason), and Adapted Screenplay. Check out the video here. You’ll learn why most walk-and-talk scenes feel mechanical and how Lumet used fixed angles to let actors come to him. You’ll also see why the simpler-looking approach demands more planning, and how to bring that freedom to your own dialogue scenes. - YouTube www.youtube.com The Problem with Static Dialogue We already mentioned this, but if you have blocking that's so static that it just has characters sitting or standing, it's maybe realistic but not that interesting to watch. Most dialogue coverage is two people planted on marks, cut as shot/reverse shot. Moviewise says the walk and talk became the default escape hatch. "In our age of stand and deliver, with directors shooting dialogue scenes by sticking actors in place and cutting between them, walk and talk is virtually the only solution most of them can find to make characters move during dialogue." That's not really true if you give your actors blocking and have them do "the business" (or something we like to call "toast" ). But the camera will still need to be moving quite a bit to follow the action, which can be challenging. A walk and talk is a good solution, but it can get stale, too. “The problem is just like any tool, walk and talk can be overdone and used mechanically," Moviewise says. "The question becomes, how do you take an ancient technique nearly as old as cinema itself and make it something new and fresh." The big thing to remember is that movement should be motivated. Lumet Directed Like It Was a Different Decade The Verdict came out in 1982, but Lumet wasn’t going for the slick style of the era. It feels like an older film. "Sidney ditched the trendy tricks in fashion and gave a lesson on how you could still make a classic-type picture in the age of Star Wars ," the video says. He followed several simple principles to get this across in his work. Locations were deliberate and character-appropriate. He didn't put people in places just to make them look cool. Within those spaces, he used harmonious compositions and wide angles that place people in the environment. But at the same time, scenes opened on details before widening. So we get something specific before something broad. The blocking is active, to resist stillness. Any camera movements were understated, and long takes were utilized. Transitions were slow dissolves. The video calls out a close-up insert of a newspaper, a glass of whiskey, and a donut. This shows the character looking through obituaries for funerals to attend. "We’re talking about filmmaking so proficient that even an insert like this overflows with information and personality. You see the character’s past through funerals he’s been to, his future by the next funeral he’s underlining to attend." Inserts are kind of the worst, because you need them, but they eat up a lot of time. This is an example of how worth it they are, just to get these kinds of character details. 'The Verdict' Credit: Credit: 20th Century Studios Let the Actors Come to the Camera The big takeaway on Lumet's filmmaking here is how he shoots the walk and talk in a new way. "Lumet could follow the actors with the camera as everyone does, and as he does for a few seconds," the video says, "but mostly he chooses the correct angle and lets his actors come to him, or he lets his actors get away from him. Let the sound guys do the hard work. Instead of tracking or Steadicamming along, we are given a fixed position and follow frequently from afar by panning." The actors’ movement toward the lens does the work a push-in would do. It's worth pointing out, again, that this creates new challenges. A locked-off pan sounds cheaper than a Steadicam rig. It isn’t necessarily easier. You have to lav these actors or ADR any dialogue you can't hear. Timing is huge—actors have to walk a greater distance and hit a mark at specific beats, all while delivering their lines perfectly. Background actors also have to be timed, too. Someone has to pull focus on characters in motion. The camera is moving too, either in tilts or pans or zooms. Lumet was shooting a lot of these in wides, and for any beats that needed tighter coverage, that would require a totally different setup. Meanwhile, a simple Steadicam walk-and-talk might require just one medium shot, and you could call it good. If you want to try this, remember that wide fixed angles expose your whole set, so budget for background and production design. They also make sound harder. One of our Lumet tips pieces notes he rehearses typically for two weeks, and this kind of staging is why that matters. It's a big dance, but when it works, it's beautiful. Moviewise’s big idea is that Lumet doesn’t treat the walk and talk as one-shot type. It’s a staging toolkit. "If you think about it, Lumet is treating walk and talk with the same freedom as ensemble staging. It’s a means of letting characters interact with each other and the location in multiple ways." For your next dialogue scene , pick the option that serves the beat instead of defaulting to following.

items.raw_content: How do you bring Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility to life for a modern audience while preserving its emotional depth? In this episode of the No Film School Podcast , director Georgia Oakley joins No Film School's GG Hawkins to discuss her new adaptation, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the Dashwood sisters. Oakley shares how she approached the film through the lens of sisterhood, longing, and the timeless tension between women's expectations and societal constraints. She breaks down her filmmaking process, from shooting on 35mm film and using two cameras to capture authentic performances to collaborating with cinematographers Arnaud Potier and Tasha Back on naturalistic visuals. The conversation also explores casting, building chemistry between actors, adapting rehearsal techniques to individual performers, and navigating the pressures of an ambitious location-heavy production. In this episode, we discuss: (02:09) How Oakley landed the directing job on Sense and Sensibility and pitched her vision to Working Title (03:24) Making the relationship between Elinor and Marianne Dashwood the film's central love story (05:28) Why Austen's themes of women's independence, societal expectations, and romantic yearning remain relevant (07:16) How modern hyperconnectivity and busyness have fueled a cultural desire for longing and human connection (09:44) Using nature, stillness, and the passage of time to create intimacy in a period drama (11:22) Oakley's pre-production process, including storyboards, shot lists, and adapting camera setups on location (13:35) Collaborating with two cinematographers and using natural light and environmental details to build the film's visual language (15:04) How shooting with two cameras allowed Oakley to capture simultaneous emotional reactions and spontaneous performances (17:41) The challenges of shooting on 35mm film with limited takes and tailoring rehearsals to each actor's needs (19:55) Filming at London's National Gallery under strict time and lighting constraints (23:24) Building trust with actors through communication, personalized rehearsals, and relationship-focused preparation (27:26) Casting Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles and developing their believable sisterly chemistry (33:15) How Oakley uses intense focus and directorial intuition to recognize authentic performances (35:50) Redirecting actors when a scene isn't working without undermining their confidence (37:59) Sustaining creative energy through a demanding 50-day shoot and relying on a supportive production team (40:15) Working with Old English Sheepdogs and embracing the spontaneity animals bring to a film set Guest: items.title: Why The Full Frontal Male Nudity in 'You Can See Everything' Is Essential To The Story
items.summary_what: Why The Full Frontal Male Nudity in 'You Can See Everything' Is Essential To The Story. I hope so; that was my intent, because I am here to tell you that the penis in this landmark documentary is maybe the most essential part of it; the penis tells the whole story of Elizabeth Holmes.
