items.raw_content: Did the headline pull you in? I hope so; that was my intent, because I am here to tell you that the penis in this landmark documentary is maybe the most essential part of it; the penis tells the whole story of Elizabeth Holmes. If you haven't seen You Can See Everything , go watch it. It's amazing. This article will be all spoilers. If you have, you know that about forty minutes into the movie, judging by my internal clock, we get a workout montage featuring Elizabeth Holmes's husband, Billy Evans. Then, Billy steps into the shower to wash off, and we see him fully naked as he washes himself off. This is literally a tie-in to the title, but this naked sharing of their lives also becomes a metaphor for the story, an emasculation of the directors, and a hubristic trap Evans himself falls into. Yes, the whole theme of the movie is tied up in one penis. Let's dive in. - YouTube www.youtube.com You Can Literally See Everything In most documentaries, you're not getting full-frontal male nudity. In fact, I don't think I have seen many docs with any nudity at all. They're usually pretty scholarly, and even ones about salacious things pick and choose when to show someone naked. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything also makes careful, calculated decisions about what it shows and when it shows it to you. So getting a penis early in the movie is something they decided to do in the edit. They could have left it out, so I want to explore why it's here, why it's so early, and what it means for the characters. This movie is three hours long and split into two parts, with perspective shifts that recontextualize what we have seen, like a magic trick. This is a tale as old as time in docs, first seen in Orson Welles's F is for Fake and later used in docs like The Act of Killing to illustrate a point. Here, Fielder and Oppenheim use that strategy to turn our judgment of Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans. But the only way to do that is to show them, naked, in the first half as the people they claim to be. That it is both literal and metaphorical. One from the living with the subjects sense, and the other from seeing a penis in the shower. Enter: actual nudity from Billy Evans post-workout. At the time, we just think this is a quirky thing from a guy who is proud of his body, a narcissist who is leaning way too slowly into the "We're innocent, we'll show you anything you want and let you examine our lives to any degree to prove it." But as we get deeper into the film, we recontextualize this nudity as narcissism and toxic masculinity. Something planted early on, when we see him yank the omelet away from his wife and tell her she whips the eggs wrong. In both instances, we have plants that pay off later, showing how physical exposure (both penis and egg power) can function as psychological warfare, and how they connect only when you reveal a person's true motive. Since we have the motives early on, as the toxicity shows itself later, we can harken back to both the dick and the omelet as precursors to us hitting that this story would be about a power swing. In this movie, Billy's true motive is seen as control. The big question becomes: how much of that control does Elizabeth cede to avoid charges, and how much is she actually being taken advantage of by a man pushing her around? 'You Can See Everything' Credit: A24 The Power Dynamic Behind the Exposure According to co-director Lance Oppenheim, the nudity moment early in the movie wasn't either director's idea. Evans offered to let the crew film him in the shower, claiming he had zero problems about being seen naked. So, they obliged. To Evans, exposure is leverage. On paper, his bizarre justification for showing his body on camera is that displaying his penis somehow serves as absolute proof of his wife’s innocence. It’s a delusion wrapped in pseudo-logic, but it also exposes that Billy just wants to dominate everyone around him. This guy is showing his penis to use his own body as an instrument of intimidation. It's a way of showing the documentarian he's the alpha in the room, and their cameras can only capture him succeeding. This is Billy Evans's attempt to assert a twisted form of hyper-masculinity, designed to emasculate the directors behind the lens. It's a classic power play, converting raw exposure into a literal flex. And somehow, Fielder and Oppenheim keep their composure enough to include it in the movie, which lets them have all the power later. Billy can't conceive of them having any power, because he doesn't see these two funny directors as guys with power. But he's wrong; beneath the surface, they have all the power, not just in the edit, but in the ability to edit a movie with hindsight. They can harken back to his penis and say...why show us that? Who are you really? Something he's not smart enough to understand. This all makes the penis necessary, and the whole crux of the movie, as they all dance around the Holmes accusations and portray different versions of the same story, allowing the audience to decide her innocence. For directors and editors, the scene offers a brilliant study in how subject agency can reveal character faster than any interview dialogue ever could. Fielder and Oppenheim turn Evans' attempt at emasculation on its head. The moment stops being a display of male dominance and becomes a staggering portrait of self-delusion. It's truly one of the bravest acts of documentary directing and one of the funniest things, to see this blowhard's big penis backfire on him so completely that you walk out of the documentary talking about how dumb this big dicked idiot looks on screen. The Takeaway for Directors Yes, there are lessons in all of this, and the directors set them. When you make a doc, you can find the underlying truth in the edit, and I think in You Can See Everything , they found it later when they saw Billy's true colors. When they set up the movie, you get the nudity early, which jars many viewers; only later do you realize what it's for, and only then do you feel it. So, when your subject tries to hijack your camera to project power, sometimes the most honest choice a filmmaker can make is to let them do it, holding the shot until the performance exposes itself. You have that; you can share it with the world. That's what makes this one of the greatest documentaries of all time, and I think a movie is also a piece of modern art. Let me know what you think in the comments.

items.title: Film Quote of the Day: Walter Koenig’s ‘Star Trek’ Line That Perfectly Captured Chekov’s Humor
items.summary_what: Film Quote of the Day: Walter Koenig’s ‘Star Trek’ Line That Perfectly Captured Chekov’s Humor: I was sad to read about Walter Koenig's passing this morning at age 90, but happy he's among the stars once more.

items.raw_content: I was sad to read about Walter Koenig's passing this morning at age 90, but happy he's among the stars once more. Star Trek fans remember him as Chekhov, the Russian with a lot of wit and old sayings who kept the rest of the Enterprise in good spirits as it journeyed through worlds unknown. Chekov was defined by an unwavering, fiercely patriotic running gag: Russia was responsible for most things in the world, and he applied that to the universe, too. Today, I want to look at one of Chekhov's funnier lines and talk about how it left a mark on Star Trek , and on his character, forever. Let's dive in. The Mysterious Tribble Infestation | Star Trek: The Original Series www.youtube.com The Scene in Question One of the most famous episodes of the original Star Trek series was "The Trouble with Tribbles" (Season 2, Episode 15). It's a hilarious episode in which the Enterprise crew has their minds changed and reshaped by furry little creatures that make them act ridiculous. But before that, the episode has a fun scene where Chief Engineer Montgomery "Scotty" Scott and Chekov grab a drink at the bar. They're taking a break from the station's political tensions and sharing a drink to talk through their problems in the utopian society of the Trek world. Scotty mocks Chekov for ordering vodka, teasingly calling it "soda pop" and asking when he's going to get off his "milk diet." This rubs Chekhov the wrong way, but he says nothing. Scotty proudly declares Scotch to be a "real drink for a man." Without missing a beat, Chekhov finally counters with a classic piece of revisionist history for which his character is known... Scotty: "When are ya gonna get off of that milk diet Laddy? Now Scotch is a real drink for a man." Chekov: "Scotch was invented by a little old lady from Leningrad." - YouTube www.youtube.com What The Quote Means This is a joke. It's Chekhov finding a way to make even the most Scottish thing possible Russian. It's not that deep, as the kids say. It's just this perfect runner that also shows the deep friendship between these guys. Chekhov and Scotty aren't going to back down, but they also won't be friends over these drinking arguments. They tolerate each other and find humor in it. That's the utopia Star Trek brings forward. You can be from a different place and still joke with someone; even if you find their stance ridiculous, you can still drink with them and be their friend. On the surface, it’s a quick throwaway joke, but this single line encapsulates everything fans love about Chekhov’s signature humor. Koenig turns a running gag that could have felt repetitive into a genuinely affectionate character beat, showcasing the effortless chemistry that made the Original Series crew feel like family. It's a life that feels aspirational to us all. Summing It All Up Walter Koenig’s performance as Pavel Chekov brought warmth to a TV show made at the height of the Cold War, shrugged off the animosity, and showed that if we all worked together, we could reach for the stars. This role bridged the gap between the perceptions of two countries and showed us all getting along. It gave us a future to strive for and put a face to the promise of peace and exploration. Long live Chekhov, and rest in peace, Walter Koenig.

items.raw_content: In today’s age of video editing and, well, you know, AI, speed matters more now than ever before. Whether you’re a fan of AI in general or AI tools like Resolve’s IntelliSearch analysis, if you’re using them in your video edit, you’ll want them to work quickly and efficiently. That’s what this latest update for DaVinci Resolve (version 21.1.2) is set to offer: Blackmagic Design has announced up to fourteen times faster IntelliSearch analysis on Apple M6, plus improved timeline editing and faster OGraf playback. Here’s everything you need to know. DaVinci Resolve Update 21.1.2 It’s kind of crazy how often Blackmagic Design pushes out DaVinci Resolve updates. It sure feels like the company gives Resolve a boost every week. Some of them are a bit minor, sure. But often they are significant updates and improvements with new features and boosted tools. This update leans more toward major improvements, as 21.1.2 adds well over a dozen new features and enhancements. The big ones are the aforementioned speed-ups for IntelliSearch analysis on Apple M6 and four times faster OGraf playback. Timeline editing has also improved, and Resolve gets more Linux graphics support and expanded scripting APIs for automated photo and editing tasks. Here’s a full breakdown of everything new in DaVinci Resolve 21.1.2: Select nearest edit point type prioritizes selected edit points. Lasso selecting edit points can now enter dynamic trim automatically. Selecting edit points for gaps now activates trim editor. Timeline view option to display current clip indicator. Option to show loudness meters in the edit mixer. Project settings option to disable DNG lens correction. OGraf clips now use action durations to place stop actions. Up to 4x faster OGraf playback in edit and Fusion pages. Support for OGraf select and multi-select template controls. OGraf responsive templates now adapt to timeline aspect ratio. Support for OGraf and Lottie graphics on Linux. Improved HDR global wheel trackball sensitivity on color panels. Fast Noise option to follow the FX tracker. Addressed double squeezed anamorphic video output in Fusion. Addressed issue with Follower animation using expressions. Addressed overlay issues with SDI and remote monitoring. Addressed issue with searches in a smart bin. Addressed empty folder in user directory when loading DRP files. Addressed issue with selecting multiple titles and subtitles. Addressed timeline in-out range issues in collaboration projects. Addressed Quick Export not using selected trim pass grade. Addressed issue with geometry thumbnails in the media pool. Addressed Recent 5 Mins mode inserting full clips. Addressed loudness meter not resetting after Cut page scrubbing. General performance and stability improvements. items.title: César Cid turns famous artists into letters in his playful alphabet series
items.summary_what: César Cid turns famous artists into letters in his playful alphabet series: The creative lead at CESS has created a fun new Artphabet featuring 26 notable artists.
items.summary_why: Influences typography, UI/UX prototyping speed, and vector design production assets.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: The creative lead at CESS has created a fun new Artphabet featuring 26 notable artists. It's a testament to an artist's talent that their paintings can be abstracted and remain recognisable. César Cid proves this point 26 times over in The Artphabet, a 3D typographic series that turns famous artworks into letters matching their creators' names. And it all begins with an A-shaped Campbell's soup can inspired by Andy Warhol himself. The Artphabet is a personal project for César, who works as the creative lead at the Madrid-based studio CESS by day. Inspired by the annual typography challenge 36 Days of Type, he wanted to bring his love of art and his 3D work together in a series that could explore different visual worlds. Rather than simply wrapping a famous artwork around typography, César wanted to imagine how an artwork's colours, shapes and materials could become a letter in three dimensions. D from the series is a perfect example, as it adapts the shark and formaldehyde tank from Damien Hirst's 1991 installation The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living. Elsewhere, Banksy's Girl with Balloon becomes the basis for the letter B, and the swirling pastoral imagery from Van Gogh's Starry Night inspires the letter V. Given the nature of the alphabet, though, creative liberties were taken with certain letters. "My initial idea was for each letter to match the artist's initial, but that wasn't possible across the whole alphabet," says César, referring to how the terrified figure from Edvard Munch's The Scream becomes zig-zagged into the letter Z. "The process became a way for me to learn more about art, to look more closely at each artist's work and understand what makes their style distinctive." Once the full range of 26 artworks was completed, The Artphabet soon found an international audience. This encouragement prompted César to release the images in other formats, such as a popular collection of physical prints. "I love seeing people choose these pieces for their homes, and connecting with the project beyond the screen has been especially rewarding," he says. The Artphabet has already grown beyond the original digital project, and a "substantial number" of canvas prints are being bought through private sales and online auctions, but César isn't done with it yet. "A book of The Artphabet will be published early next year, which is a big milestone for the project," he says. "I'm also in ongoing conversations about expanding The Artphabet into other formats, and I'm always open to new collaborations with publishers, brands and cultural organisations. I'd love to keep finding new ways for people to discover and enjoy the collection."

items.title: Uncommon's rebrand of global powerhouse White & Case ditches every law firm cliché
items.summary_what: Uncommon's rebrand of global powerhouse White & Case ditches every law firm cliché: Uncommon Creative Studio's visual identity swaps corporate restraint for kinetic type.
items.summary_why: Influences typography, UI/UX prototyping speed, and vector design production assets.
items.summary_action: Review the full source announcement for technical requirements and deployment details.
items.raw_content: Uncommon Creative Studio's visual identity swaps corporate restraint for kinetic type. We find out more. For decades now, it feels like there's been an unspoken rule about law firm branding. That these are serious institutions and demand serious, conservative-with-a-small-c visual identities. You might think of sober serifs, a navy blue palette, stock photography of gleaming skyscrapers and firm handshakes. Whatever the elements, the theme is: we are trustworthy. Possibly a little boring and samey. But if so, that's a feature rather than a bug. White & Case's new identity, however, is none of these things. Crafted by Uncommon Creative Studio , it's the New York-based global law firm's big rebrand in 13 years. And it's about as cliché-free as you could imagine. Navy blue is out, and an edgy, electric shade dubbed Catalyst Blue is in. Kinetic headline serifs add a welcome spot of verve and dynamism. And there's even a proprietary image tool that turns photography into streams of data. Complexity as an advantage So what's the underlying concept here? Well, in an increasingly uncertain world, the 125-year-old law firm wants to frame complexity not as a bad thing, but as a catalyst for new thinking and opportunity. One poster makes this abundantly clear by teaming the words "Complexity creates risk" with "We see opportunity". In other words, they're not talking down to their audience: quite the reverse. "Our clients are sophisticated business leaders navigating a complex world, and our category is intensely and increasingly competitive," says Jason Hill, White & Case's CMO. "Those factors mean that brand can be a powerful source of differentiation and a driver of commercial growth. Our new design system reflects the catalytic energy and forward momentum of a powerhouse global firm." Uncommon's brief then was to pull the firm out of a "sea of sameness". In the words of global chief design officer Lisa Smith: "The legal sector is drowning in navy blue slabs, borrowing from tired financial and tech clichés, and safe choices. White & Case is a firm built for polycrisis. They are high-stakes gladiators who step into friction when everyone else backs away." Set in stone The new logo draws on the inscriptions on Trajan's Column and Roman stone carving, giving White & Case a sense of permanence and authority. It's a tightly stacked lockup in which diagonal cuts slice through the letters, such as the W, making them seem to lean forward. The ampersand, meanwhile, has been reworked as a standalone monogram. It's designed to celebrate the power of global partnership, and it looks equally at home on a laptop screen, a lapel pin or as a huge marble sculpture in a lobby. Those directional cuts carry through to a set of custom-made headline serifs, designed to embody the idea of momentum and mirror how the firm's lawyers navigate complex legal landscapes. Set in large type, in phrases such as "Forward energy", they give the brand a real swagger. Turning up the voltage The main brand colour Catalyst Blue is drawn from the highest-energy end of the visible light spectrum. It's balanced out by Marble White and Ink Black, with secondary tones named Ion, Thermal, Solar and Ultraviolet, completing what Uncommon calls a "high voltage palette". Then there's Energy Studio, a proprietary tool that applies a signature "energy effect" to brand photography. This stretches part of each image into sharp streaks of colour, so a volcano, a city skyline or a field of wind turbines dissolves into lines of data. The new identity is rolling out globally across digital recruitment platforms, client collateral, pitch materials, paid advertising and a podcast, along with a brand film, The Power of Complexity. Overall, this is a sassy, original and perhaps brave take on legal firm branding. "We built a dynamic, assertive identity that cuts through the noise," says Smith, "proving that design isn't just about how a firm looks, but how it multiplies its force on the world stage."

items.title: Royal portrait painter swaps palaces for a Barnsley chippy, a Catford corner shop and a pub run by 'Slugger'
items.summary_what: Royal portrait painter swaps palaces for a Barnsley chippy, a Catford corner shop and a pub run by 'Slugger': In Coca-Cola's latest campaign, four independent business owners get something usually reserved for kings and queens: an oil-on-canvas portrait by artists who've sat opposite the late Que...

items.raw_content: In Coca-Cola's latest campaign, four independent business owners get something usually reserved for kings and queens: an oil-on-canvas portrait by artists who've sat opposite the late Queen, King Charles and Princess Anne. Before the camera came along, only the very rich could afford to have themselves immortalised in oils. I'm talking royalty, aristocrats, and the odd wealthy merchant; their portraits often hang in prestigious galleries or National Trust properties. Their noble gazes in gilt frames suggest a life of privilege, while everyone else went undocumented. Even today, a formal portrait remains a status symbol. So it's quite unusual to find a portrait of the person who serves you chips on a Saturday night. But that's what's happened in a new campaign by Coca-Cola. The drinks brand has commissioned four of Britain's finest portrait artists, each of whom has painted an official portrait of a member of the Royal Family, to paint a fish-and-chip shop owner, a café proprietor, a pub landlord and a corner shop owner. The finished works will be on show at London's Saatchi Gallery from today until 1 November, and admission is free. It's the latest chapter in Coca-Cola's 'Localness' platform, which celebrates the people behind the pubs, shops and cafés where its drinks are served. It follows last year's documentary and photo series, The Bosses, and Counter Cultures earlier in 2026. This time around, the campaign borrows the visual language of official portraiture. And we love it. Because why shouldn't a Barnsley chippy get the same gravitas as Buckingham Palace? Pindy Kaur by Nicky Philipps Simon Dafforn-Jones by Jamie Coreth Everyone else seems to agree. New research commissioned by Coca-Cola Great Britain found that 79% of people think independent businesses are under-appreciated, while 80% want to see them celebrated more often. "Independent business owners create the places where local life happens, yet their contribution often goes unrecognised," says Rhona Stephen, senior director of communications for Coca-Cola Great Britain. "With Local Royalty, we wanted to celebrate them in a way that felt deliberately unexpected and enduring. By borrowing the visual language of official portraiture and placing these owners at its centre, the campaign gives their everyday impact the status it deserves." So who got their portrait done? First up is Pindy Kaur, who took over a struggling Ocean Fish Bar in Barnsley in the 1990s. More than 25 years on, she and her family have turned it into a much-loved takeaway, known for its regulars and its family-run spirit. Pindy is a devoted admirer of the late Queen Elizabeth II, and she was painted by Nicky Philipps, who painted the Queen not once but twice. Gino Verecchia by Gareth Reid Kaual Patel by Nick Bashall Gino Verecchia's University Café in Glasgow was opened by his grandfather, Pasquale, in 1918, and it's been in the family for three generations. Wow. It blends Italian heritage (including a 100-year-old gelato recipe) with Scottish favourites, and it's a true Glasgow institution. It even once served Anthony Bourdain battered haggis. Gareth Reid, portrait artist to King Charles III when he was Prince of Wales, painted Gino. Down in Dittisham, South Devon, meanwhile, The Ferry Boat Inn sits on the banks of the River Dart. Locals know it as the FBI. Brilliant. Landlord Simon Dafforn-Jones, or "Slugger" to the locals, has run it for almost 20 years, following in his dad's footsteps. He gives local teens their first jobs and champions produce from across the region, so the pub naturally sits at the heart of village life. He was painted by Jamie Coreth, who created the first official portrait of the Prince and Princess of Wales. And finally, Kaual Patel's father bought Torridon Convenience Store in Catford, South East London, in 1984, and Kaual took over in 2000. Over the past two decades, he has made it a real community hub, stocking local producers alongside the bigger household names. His mantra is lovely: "If you're a local producer, there's a space on my shelf for you." Kaual was painted by Nick Bashall, portrait painter to Princess Anne. Kaual Patel by Nick Bashall Gino Verecchia by Gareth Reid Pindy Kaur by Nicky Philipps Simon Dafforn-Jones by Jamie Coreth There you have it. All worthy contenders. All beautifully depicted. Alongside their finished portraits, the Saatchi show includes behind-the-scenes footage from the sittings. It shows how each artist got to know their sitter and turned their character and history into a formal portrait. Each owner also donates to a local charity of their choice and keeps the portrait to hang in their home or business. MHP Group created and delivered the campaign across MHP, Mischief and Studio La Plage. Find out more on Coca-Cola's website . So next time you're enjoying a pint or picking up a chippy tea, take a moment to appreciate the people behind the counter. You might be in the presence of royalty.
